scraped.description: The author of a major review on youth unemployment, due next week, acknowledges the change would mean some young people losing out on benefits.

scraped.h1: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Young people should have a legal guarantee to a job or training, Milburn says

Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.

He claims the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it spends on supporting them into employment , and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.

That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.

Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - £25 to one, and we can take everything to £2 to one".

He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."

The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.

Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say

Can Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?

Milburn said the government is already spending £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive, and that money needs to be spent differently.

He has already said that the under 25s should no longer be able to claim some health benefits – the personal independence payment and the health element of Universal Credit.

In his other major announcement, Milburn spoke of the proposal he calls an "opportunity guarantee" for young people.

This would put a legal duty on government to ensure young people have access to a route into employment.

He said: "It should be a guarantee for a young person. Because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is a very simple thing. To get a benefit. What sort of life is that?"

The "opportunity guarantee" might work similarly to the way that councils have a legal responsibility to offer homeless people accommodation or advice, or accommodate children in care.

Milburn argues previous employment schemes have been temporary, and says a permanent legal entitlement is needed to tackle the long-running problem of young people not in education, employment or training.

The government is expected broadly to welcome the proposals, which will be published in full on Tuesday, with a statement in Parliament and draft laws early next year.

Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training - otherwise known as Neet - according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics .

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.

Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.

Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic.

"It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.

The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning.

Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away.

"It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.

Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."

The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.

They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.

The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".

But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said.

"A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

items.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
items.summary: Milburn is not the first to try and fix the Neets problem - so what’s different this time round, asks Laura Kuenssberg.

scraped.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
scraped.description: Milburn is not the first to try and fix the Neets problem - so what’s different this time round, asks Laura Kuenssberg.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
scraped.body_text:
Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight

It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed, , external he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

Millburn has already said under-25s should no longer be able to claim the personal independence payment and the health element of universal credit

Westminster jargon often describes earnest sets of recommendations published in reports like this as "wide-ranging". This review genuinely is, arguing for changes not just in welfare, but in the health and education systems.

It's a real expansion of the state's involvement in the next generation, from one of the Blairites still standing, with the expensive Paul Smith knitwear to match.

He is not the first government veteran nor is Burnham the first PM, to try to sort out this problem.

But what Milburn and his allies say is different this time round is they're pushing for a whole new system that's permanent, not just another scheme that gets introduced by one secretary of state, then is dropped or scrapped by the next one that turns up.

And the notion of a legal guarantee is designed to make the state, likely through local councils or mayors, take responsibility for making sure young people have something useful to do when they emerge from school – for good.

The recommendations apply to the whole UK, but the precise way the powers might be used in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will be worked out when it gets to the finer details of draft laws.

The scale of the practical challenge can be seen from space. New research from the Lib Dems this weekend suggests that if nothing was done, the number of Neets would hit 1.26 million by 2031.

And Milburn himself cites figures that puts the cost of the issue at £22bn a year.

No politician would argue for the status quo. But agreement that something must be done doesn't automatically translate into consensus over what that something is.

For all Milburn's talk of grand ambition – his plans will not, any time soon, make much difference to the ballooning costs to welfare.

His plan will take as long as a decade before making a real dent in the benefits bill. And it will require taxpayers' cash at the start, although not the £6bn guesstimates that have done the rounds.

He's still coy about the upfront cost, but it will be billions over the years.

And he says plainly there are many young people who are capable of working but don't, although tiptoes carefully around any accusations that some take advantage of the system, saying he's convinced the vast majority of young people do want to work.

Milburn's forthcoming report has been described as a "watershed moment" by PM Burnham

The Conservatives and Reform have both put saving tens of billions from the welfare bill, and fast, at the top of their list.

The Tories said Milburn was right that benefits must be cut - but that "unlike Labour, our plan goes to the root of the problem" including by halving employer National Insurance for young people and creating 100,000 new apprenticeships. Reform said the review "is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away" and it cannot be "another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Milburn and the government can expect sustained criticism that it's not acceptable the plans would take so long to start cutting the enormous bill for the taxpayer. There is no question the expected increases in benefit payments are absolutely eye-watering.

The opposition from that quarter, and indeed from the Greens on the left arguing already that what they have seen so far is "cruel", is entirely predictable to Downing Street. What's harder to read, and therefore more difficult to contend with, is how Labour MPs will respond.

Sir Keir Starmer tried, and painfully failed to make changes to welfare, sabotaging his own authority when he backed down in the face of backbenchers.

That's why Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, has spent hours and hours talking to Labour MPs in the last year, trying to patiently make the case for this plan.

And why Milburn, as he was keen to point out, has continually been in touch with No 10 and 11, trying to get Burnham on board even before he made it to Downing Street. A government source said hopefully, this time "we've done the ground work – it's not a rushed Treasury process driven by numbers".

As my colleague Iain Watson has written, the signs are healthier for Milburn, with a few key critics from last time showing more than an open mind to the new plans.

The political climate is completely different with Labour, for now, cheerier about the polls, and backbenchers reluctant to make trouble.

Burnham still is in possession of course, of the enormous majority that Starmer won.

Pat McFadden - pictured here with Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham - has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms

There will, without doubt, be voices on the left of the party, concerned perhaps about opposition from the Greens or the SNP in their constituency who will never sign up to anything that would mean a cut to payments for anyone on benefits now.

"Look at the chaos Starmer got into," one source on the left warned, saying Burnham wouldn't be so "boneheaded" to do the same as "he wants to be everyone's friend".

So a possible fault line may become whether the reduced benefits apply to those already claiming, as Milburn believes, or only those in future.

A No 10 source is plain the plans would have to apply to those on benefits now, warning they must act as soon as they can, although new laws will take time.

They told me "an argument on welfare is an argument we are happy to have". Let's see if that sentiment stands the test of time.

The Milburn review was set on its path by Starmer. But it will emerge blinking into the light under a different leader, and in a very different political moment.

Perhaps, some in Labour wonder, Milburn's ideas are arriving at a time when a newish prime minister has big rhetoric but perhaps is short of big concrete ideas, mocked by his opponents for reportedly bringing in private consultants to fill out his much-vaunted 10-year plan.

Burnham is widely expected to adopt most of Milburn's genuinely radical ideas. Months of arguments lie ahead, however settled the political picture appears right now.

But Milburn's ideas just might have come around at the right time for a relatively new government . As one senior Labour figure believes: "You need some meat on the bones that isn't just, 'nationalise everything' – this could be it."

scraped.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
scraped.description: The Ukrainian president says US envoys touted the exchange as part of efforts to end the war with Russia.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
scraped.body_text:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The Ukrainian president's comments come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.

Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Russia has now raised the stakes further. It has revived 2021 demands for Nato to halt any expansion in Russia's vicinity and to roll back military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe that became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The US and other Western nations dismissed these demands then - and Moscow invaded Ukraine a few months later.

However, questions of European security were on the agenda of the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Russia has insisted it will not agree to cease fighting until a final peace deal is in place that would include territorial settlements as well as security arrangements.

In the comments, made on Friday but only released on Saturday, Zelensky said that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".

But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be symbolically significant for Kyiv.

Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

items.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
items.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said initial investigations pointed to an issue with contractor L3Harris updating old tech at a remote location. scraped.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
scraped.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said initial investigations pointed to an issue with contractor L3Harris updating old tech at a remote location.
scraped.h1: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
scraped.body_text:
By

Ava Berger

,

Joel Rose

A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images North America hide caption

Friday's nationwide ground stop was declared after an error occurred while a contractor was updating an old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication line, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

L3Harris, a long time contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration, was doing routine maintenance in at least one of FAA's remote locations changing copper wire to fiber, he said. Duffy said the routers in these facilities were manufactured in 2001. These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."

L3Harris did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.

Duffy said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system.

"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"

Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, who joined Duffy at the briefing said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or AI-related issues.

Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after a rare ground stop halted all flights.

The chaos is expected to linger for days.

The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue after yesterday's nationwide ground stop, Duffy said in the press briefing Saturday.

"Based on everything that we're hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they'll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," Bedford said.

Duffy told reporters Friday night: "I think we're going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving."

For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded. That's 14% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, which tracks aviation analytics.

Duffy said Friday that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed "old switches, old routers" for the failures. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.

Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.

On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.

Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.

"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8pm. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"

She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.

The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.

For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.

"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"

"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."

And it did – eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.

"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.

Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media .

items.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
items.summary: Chile's far-right President José Antonio Kast is facing mounting public anger, as rising fuel prices trigger transport strikes and protests across the country. Chile's far-right President José Antonio Kast is facing mounting public anger, as rising fuel prices trigger transport strikes and protests across the country.(Image credit: Esteban Felix)

scraped.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
scraped.description: Chile's far-right President José Antonio Kast is facing mounting public anger, as rising fuel prices trigger transport strikes and protests across the country.
scraped.h1: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
scraped.body_text:
By

John Bartlett

A masked demonstrator prepares to throw a Molotov cocktail as police use a water cannon to disperse students protesting education policies, rising living costs and reduced sentences for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors in Santiago, Chile, Nov. 5, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

Trucks are parked along a road as drivers protest rising fuel prices and operating costs on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, Nov. 12, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

items.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries

scraped.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
scraped.description: This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly.
scraped.h1: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
scraped.body_text:
Ashley Lopez

A voter walks into a booth at the Valley Bible Chalet to cast his ballot on Election Day, Nov. 3, in Indian, Alaska. Lindsey Wasson/AP hide caption

A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly .

Loading...

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

Democrats denied recruiting the independent Sullivan, who made the top-four general election ballot and has defended his candidacy.

However, proponents of Alaska's system have said that the state's ranked choice voting system could blunt the effects of any confusion. Voters had the ability to rank both Dan Sullivans and not rank Democrat Mary Peltola, for example.

Massachusetts voters this year decided not to switch to a top-two nonpartisan primary system. And during the last election cycle, in 2024, several states considered measures that would create a nonpartisan system similar to Alaska's. Voters rejected all of those ballot measures.

scraped.title: New prostate cancer guidelines urge men to start screening at specific age
scraped.description: American Cancer Society prostate cancer screening guidelines now recommend PSA testing every two years for average-risk men starting at age 50, with earlier screening for Black men.
scraped.author: Eric Shawn
scraped.h1: New prostate cancer guidelines urge men to start screening at specific age
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.

The American Cancer Society is recommending regular prostate cancer screening starting at age 50 for men at average risk under updated guidelines released Nov. 12.

The update shifts from emphasizing individual decisions about screening to explicitly recommending regular testing for eligible men.

The new guidelines call for PSA testing every two years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69. Black men should begin annual screening at 45, regardless of family history. Other men with a father, brother or son diagnosed with prostate cancer should also begin at 45, with the frequency depending on their family history.

JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS

Men ages 70 to 74 should discuss whether to continue screening with their doctors; routine screening is not recommended at 75 and older.

The American Cancer Society is recommending regular prostate cancer screening starting at age 50 for men at average risk under updated guidelines released Nov. 12. (iStock)

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death among U.S. men. For disease that has not spread beyond the prostate or nearby areas, the five-year relative survival rate is nearly 100%, according to the American Cancer Society.

MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS

"Men think it is going to happen to someone else," Dr. Ash Tewari, chair of the Milton and Carroll Petrie Department of Urology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Medical Center in New York City, told Fox News.

The doctor, who has performed more than 10,000 prostate cancer operations , said the success rate of treating patients is exceedingly high, but that many men still need to be nudged to get screened.

The new guidelines call for PSA testing every two years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69. (iStock)

A prostate cancer screening involves a simple blood test for PSA , which measures the level of prostate-specific antigen, the protein produced by normal and cancerous cells in the prostate gland.

Under the updated guidelines, a PSA level of 3 ng/mL or higher in men younger than 70 warrants a repeat test to confirm the result. There are other explanations for higher PSA levels beyond the existence of prostate cancer, such as an enlarged prostate, inflammation or an infection.

CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

Screening can also identify slow-growing cancers that may never cause harm. The society recommends discussing screening’s benefits and possible harms with a healthcare provider and offering close monitoring as an initial approach for low-risk cancers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We know how to cure 95% of them," said Tewari, referring to prostate cancer patients. "I can operate, we have developed medications … to get to them in time, my approach is very simple: Go right where they are."

To reach more men, Tewari and Mount Sinai have created mobile prostate cancer screening vehicles that are deployed in neighborhoods so men can be examined where they live.

The society recommends discussing screening’s benefits and possible harms with a healthcare provider and offering close monitoring as an initial approach for low-risk cancers. (iStock)

The first bus, the Mount Sinai Robert F. Smith Mobile Prostate Cancer Screening Unit, was sent out in New York City in 2022. Last month, another bus was deployed to the Atlanta Falcons-Chicago Bears game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta. The Winship Cancer Institute at Emory University offered free screenings in partnership with the Atlanta Falcons during the game.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Tewari and Mount Sinai are engaged in other ways to get the word out to men.

The ACS estimates that more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed in 2026, and about 36,000 will die from the disease.

Last month, actress Brooke Shields joined Tewari and directed a public service announcement advocating screening and early detection. The goal is to screen more than one million men for prostate cancer under Tewari's Million Strong Men Initiative.

"We need to be able to talk about ...down there," a son says to his father in the PSA video .

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I never got to have the talk with my dad early enough," says Shields in the video. Her father, Frank, died of prostate cancer in 2003 at 61 years old.

"Prostate cancer is treatable when detected early," she adds.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Prostate cancer is often a disease that families don't talk about until there is a reason to," said Tewari. "We want to change that. Starting the conversation early can give men an opportunity to learn about their risk, talk with their doctors about screening and act when appropriate."

Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The ACS estimates that more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed in 2026, and about 36,000 will die from the disease.

items.title: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop

scraped.title: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop
scraped.description: Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.
scraped.h1: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop
scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.

By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.

A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.

Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.

In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.

Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.

Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X .

Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.

Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time .

Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

Tom Costello is an NBC News correspondent based in Washington, D.C.

Joy Y. Wang is a senior editorial director for NBC News.

Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

scraped.h1: FAA ground stop throws college football into chaos, while the NFL is safe
scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several teams across multiple sports.

Follow along for live coverage.

Multiple games in college football had to be rescheduled to accommodate new travel plans, while a handful of NBA teams changed their flights as a result of the ground stop. Every NFL game, meanwhile, will be played as scheduled, as all road teams were scheduled to travel Saturday.

Every NFL game will stick to its original start time, a league spokesman confirmed to NBC News. Teams playing Sunday typically do not travel until Saturday, meaning the league was largely unaffected by the Friday ground stop.

The New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions, who are playing in Munich, Germany, both traveled overseas well ahead of the stop.

While the league’s teams and players will arrive as scheduled, the NFL did have to modify officiating crews for Sunday’s games.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” a league spokesman said.

Three backup referees — Duane Heydt, Barry Anderson and Don Willard — will be used Sunday. Heydt was assigned to a game in New Orleans and Anderson to one in Tennessee, while Willard will be the side judge for games in both Indianapolis and Cincinnati. (The kickoffs in those two games are more than seven hours apart, and the stadiums are separated by less than 120 miles.)

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise,” the league spokesman said.

Travel plans for more than a dozen teams were affected by the stoppage, according to The Athletic .

Some schools opted to fly out on Saturday morning for games scheduled the same day, while others — including the Alabama Crimson Tide playing at Vanderbilt — took a bus to their destination.

Several kickoffs were pushed back to later Saturday to accommodate new travel plans, including the games between Baylor and BYU, Arizona State and UCF, and Utah and Arizona.

The game between Oklahoma and Ole Miss, however, was pushed back to Sunday after Ole Miss couldn’t figure out its travel in time — and it drew a strong response from the Sooners.

“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution,” Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny said in a statement . “After multiple conversations with the league office, [SEC] Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”

Denny’s statement added: “Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight.”

A few NBA teams — such as the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Chicago Bulls — had to reschedule flights from Friday night to Saturday morning, but otherwise it’s largely business as usual for the league.

An NBA source confirmed to NBC News all games would take place as scheduled as of Saturday morning, though noted there were a lot of moving parts.

“Flights are late, get stuck on the runway, just like it does in the normal commercial world of flight, so it’s just part of it,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said before the team’s game Friday. “We’ve all been part of it. You just adapt.”

Atkinson’s star guard Donovan Mitchell was not enthused about the new plan, as Cleveland has a quick turnaround to another game Saturday.

“This is unprecedented,” Mitchell said Friday, per Cleveland.com’s Chris Fedor. “Back-to-back. Three-hour flight. It was already going to be a tough one. But if they say we have to play then we have to play.”

Mitchell added he would have liked for the game to be canceled.

The NHL, meanwhile, has not announced any changes to its schedule. The league had only two games on Friday night, allowing most teams to travel for their road games prior to the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

Rohan Nadkarni is a sports reporter for NBC News.

scraped.h1: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins the Alaska governor’s race
scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor’s race, NBC News projects, flipping control of the office from Republicans.

Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory marks the latest gain for Democrats at the state level in this year’s elections. The party will hold 30 governorships next year after flipping control in six states.

At 37, Kreiss-Tomkins will be the youngest governor in Alaska history and next year he will be the youngest sitting governor in the country. Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, defeated three Republicans on the ballot to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

In Alaska, the top four vote-getters in the primary regardless of party advance to the general election, where ranked choice voting is utilized. Kreiss-Tomkins secured a majority of the vote on the first ballot, so the ranked choice aspect did not come into play in the race.

Former state Sen. Tom Begich, a Democrat, had finished second in the August primary just behind Kreiss-Tomkins. But he dropped out of the race soon after to consolidate Democratic support behind Kreiss-Tomkins.

The three Republican candidates on the November ballot were Anchorage businesswoman Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor. Wilson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, finished a distant second.

Kreiss-Tomkins, who often goes by JKT in the state, earned bipartisan support during his campaign. Most notably, he was endorsed by GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski one week before Election Day. “JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now — a freshness of energy, a common-sense guy who has a known ability to be working together,” Murkowski said in an interview with NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage.

Kreiss-Tomkins campaigned on boosting funding for public schools, lowering energy costs, expanding Medicaid and protecting Alaska’s fisheries.

He also called for a moratorium on all new data centers until the state Legislature can pass regulations, and said he would not allow direct or indirect subsidies to data centers for electricity costs.

Sarah Sternhagen is an intern for NBC News.

The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET. "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. ( Download it here .)

Hosted by Jane Pauley

COVER STORY: "November 1963": Did the mob kill JFK? A new film, "November 1963," posits that the assassination of President John F. Kennedy was tied to a Chicago crime syndicate and its boss, Sam Giancana. Correspondent Lee Cowan talks with screenwriter Nicki Celozzi – Giancana's great-nephew – along with star John Travolta and Giancana's daughter, Bonnie, about the mob's alleged connection to a murder that changed the world.

To watch a trailer for the film "November 1963" click on the video player below:

For more info:

ALMANAC: November 15 "Sunday Morning" looks back at historical events on this date.

ARTS: Aiding veterans with the healing arts With her in-person and virtual painting workshops and online tutorials, artist Mary Whyte teaches veterans to use art to deal with isolation and trauma through her "watercolor bootcamps." Correspondent Martha Teichner reports on an arts program, now in 48 states, that helps veterans' self-expression, and allows them to reconnect with fellow vets, their communities – and themselves.

For more info:

MOVIES: Billy Evans on "You Can See Everything" In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks with correspondent Matt Gutman about his role in the Nathan Fielder-Lance Oppenheim documentary "You Can See Everything."

PREVIEW: Billy Evans calls his portrayal in Elizabeth Holmes documentary "crazy" but says: "It's entertainment"

For more info:

PASSAGE: In memoriam "Sunday Morning" remembers some of the notable figures who left us this week.

Correspondent Mo Rocca learns how, a century ago, puppeteer and artist Tony Sarg created the parade's iconic balloons, floats and costumes. Rocca also visits the Macy's Studio in Moonachie, N.J., where preparations for this year's parade are being designed, painted and inflated.

For more info:

For more info:
