items.summary: Fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight and into the morning, Iran's military said Saturday.

scraped.title: Live Updates: 3 oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
scraped.description: Fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight and into the morning, Iran's military said Saturday.
scraped.h1: Live Updates: 3 oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 14, 2026 / 1:33 PM EST / CBS News

Invoking Iran's pursuit to rebuild its nuclear program, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saturday it's time to eliminate the threat from Iran "once and for all" in a speech about forming a new government following a meeting earlier this week with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.

"The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear program," Netanyahu said, translated from Hebrew. "And let this be clear: This murderous regime, which did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people, will not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us."

"It will do so the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons," he continued.

Netanyahu said he met with Eisenkot on Thursday, and the meeting "only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government at this time."

In last month's election , Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies received 53 seats in the Knesset, short of the 61 needed to form a government and keep him as prime minister. Eisenkot's Yashar party and its allies won 48 seats, while the Arab coalition took 19 seats.

Netanyahu wondered aloud why Eisenkot would potentially side with the Arab coalition to form what he called a "fragile and dangerous government." Netanyahu is clinging to hopes Eisenkot will agree to a deal to establish a majority and cut out the Arab parties, who he has accused of stealing the election . On Saturday, he referred to them as "supporters of terrorism."

"We must remove this existential threat from over our heads once and for all," Netanyahu said, referring to Iran. "A narrow government, or a government that relies on supporters of terrorism, will not be able to achieve this monumental goal. But a national unity government can achieve it in time, thereby ensuring Israel's security for many years to come."

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthi militant group said it intercepted and destroyed two drones on Saturday.

The drones were intercepted near Riyadh and over the southern region. The coalition was not more specific about where in the south it had been intercepted. Riyadh, the country's capital, is located in central Saudi Arabia, though hundreds of miles from the Houthis' base of operations in Yemen.

It was a busy week of drone and missile interceptions by the Saudis. The two drones intercepted on Saturday afternoon were the first since one was fired at the eastern, oil-rich region of the country on Thursday. Multiple drones in the east and near Riyadh were interrupted Thursday, while two ballistic missiles were shot down on Wednesday in the western part of Saudi Arabia and three others were shot down near Riyadh, according to the coalition.

Two drones were also intercepted on Wednesday, the coalition said, though one destroyed near Mecca was disavowed by the Houthis, who have said they will not target the holy city.

Multiple drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles were also intercepted over different parts of Saudi Arabia on Monday, the same day the coalition said it took out a weapons manufacturing facility in Yemen.

Iran and the United States should "immediately" allow fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to ease the crisis in some of the most vulnerable countries, a senior U.N. official said Saturday.

Jorge Moreira da Silva, head of the U.N. Office for Project Services, told the COP31 climate talks in the Turkish resort city of Antalya that the lack of fertilizers could push millions into poverty.

While Iran and the United States are still trying to negotiate an end to the conflict, Moreira da Silva said he had the same message for both countries.

"They should continue their negotiations about the comprehensive deal — but that deal should not avoid an immediate, exceptional, limited, and time-bound solution for the fertilizers," he said.

"Basically what we need is five vessels a day with fertilizers," he added.

Before the conflict, a third of the world's fertilizers passed through the Strait of Hormuz, and since the blockades, their prices had risen by 30%, Moreira da Silva said.

Sudan's finance minister recently told him the price of food there had doubled in six months, he added. In Nepal, they told him that farmers could no longer afford to buy fertilizers.

"So it's very important that we are aware that countries such as Mozambique, Kenya, Sudan, Somalia, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka are facing very significant impact," Moreira da Silva said.

The effects of this shortage could be catastrophic, he warned.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have shot down an American MQ-1 "Predator" drone for the second straight day on Saturday.

This was the 17th MQ-1 drone shot down by Iran, according to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though that number was not possible to verify. The U.S. certainly has lost a number of the drones, however, either to them being shot down or crashing.

The drone was shot down over Iran's Qeshm Island, which is located along the northern coast of the Strait of Hormuz. Like Friday, the strike was credited to Iran's alleged new air defense system.

The U.S. has lost dozens of unmanned aircraft during the war with Iran, according to a congressional report dated Oct. 5. Forty-five MQ-9 Reaper drones have been lost, just through mid-August, while at least three Predator drones were previously destroyed, according to the report.

There were at least 81 manned or unmanned aircraft lost during the war in Iran through early October, according to the report. As of Aug. 1, the losses amounted to a cost of between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion.

Iran's military said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran has insisted vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait since war erupted with the United States in February, and has attacked ships that do not comply.

"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.

A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker "navigating through the unsafe and prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking and identification systems switched off, caught fire and was forced to stop after striking a naval mine".

The statements did not provide the names or origins of the vessels but the Guards said one of those hit in south Hormuz was a supertanker.

CBS/AFP

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that explosions rang out on two oil tankers after they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has restricted navigation.

Since war erupted in February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait and has attacked ships that do not comply.

"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Guards' navy said in a statement carried by an Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.

The statement did not provide the names or origins of the vessels, but said one was a supertanker.

The U.S., in response to Tehran's choking of the strategic trade route, has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and provides military support to tankers using the waterway.

In recent weeks, Iran's armed forces have reported several fires or explosions on board ships in the strait, often saying the vessels had struck mines.

On Friday, the Guards released footage of a large plume of smoke rising from a vessel it said was carrying liquefied gas and hit a mine in the south of the strait.

The U.S. military, however, has said it has cleared the main routes through the waterway of mines .

U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq said Friday that civilians across Yemen are increasingly being hit by drones, missiles, airstrikes and shelling in their homes, markets and other places once considered safe.

In one of the deadliest attacks since fighting resumed between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, at least 30 people died in airstrikes on a market in Taiz province on Nov. 6, according to the Houthis.

Under international law, Haq said all parties must take "all feasible precautions" to avoid and minimize the death and injury to civilians.

Oil prices swung a day after President Trump said the U.S. didn't "need a deal with Iran" even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.

Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It was mostly unchanged at $95.89 a barrel at 2 p.m. ET. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.

Rising energy prices because of the U.S. war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising.

The latest wholesale inflation report released Friday also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.

CBS/AP

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani signed a mutual defense agreement Friday in Istanbul, according to Erdogan's office.

In a statement posted on X , the office said the two sides would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the Gulf region and "persuade the parties to resolve their problems through diplomacy."

There were no further details on the defense agreement between the countries, which already share deep military ties.

The deal follows a joint defense agreement signed between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August in which the three nations pledged to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Qatar, in its readout of the deal, praised that defense pact and said this one would carry similar weight.

"(The deal has the) aim of strengthening collective defense and promoting regional security and stability, and a unified stance in confronting any external armed attack targeting either party or both of them," Qatar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on X .

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has signaled an openness to other regional countries joining the pact, including Egypt.

Even though Turkey and the Saudis agreed to the defense pact, Turkey has not yet become involved militarily in defending Saudi Arabia from attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen. Qatar repeatedly came under fire from Iranian attacks during the opening weeks of the U.S.- and Israeli-led war.

CBS/AP

The Iranian military claimed it shot down a U.S. MQ-1 "Predator" drone near Kuhestak, a city on the coast of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official ISNA news agency.

The Iranian news outlet shared photos of the supposed downed drone. The U.S. military did not immediately comment on whether one of its drones was shot down.

The Iranian army said its new air defense system was responsible for shooting it down. There have been several confirmed and more claimed shoot-downs of Predator drones in Iran throughout the war.

"We will not hesitate for a moment in safeguarding and defending the territorial integrity, maritime borders and interests of the Islamic Republic of Iran," the Army Public Relations Office said in a statement.

There was good news in the International Energy Agency's monthly oil report for the first time in awhile: Oil supplies are surpassing demand.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the IEA said in its November report. "Observed oil inventories rose by 52 (million barrels), or 1.7 (million barrels per day), in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand."

The war is still having its effects on the oil market, but the report noted positive movement there as well.

"Despite continued attacks on tankers, Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, reached 18.4 mb/d last month, 26% below pre-war levels," it said. "The recent increase was led by crude, with flows rising to 15 mb/d, equivalent to 82% of pre-war levels in October."

The good news should continue, the report said.

"Our November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in 4Q26, with a more substantial build in 2027," it said, before adding the caveat, "As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery."

Much of the increased oil coming out of the Gulf is doing so under U.S. military protection, even as Iran has increased its attacks on oil tankers exiting through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. is facilitating ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, but it is a costly, and for now indefinite, process.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent came out swinging against Iran in the wake of death threats that have caused him to move to a military base for added security.

"F the Iranian leadership," Bessent told CNBC on Friday. "I'm not going to be cowered that they have initiated death threats against me. The other members of the Cabinet are not going to be cowered. And it means what we are doing with Operation Economic Outcast is working."

"The IRGC, they're like a dangerous, cornered animal," he added.

Bessent has come under added threats since the start of a ramped-up sanctions campaign called Operation Economic Outcast in late August, dubbed at the time as "economic D-Day."

Bessent also said the military action undertaken by President Trump was "100% … worth it."

"President Trump took action that had been needed for 47 years, and we'll get on the other side of this," Bessent told CNBC. "Now, President Trump doesn't think we need a deal, and we're just going to keep squeezing them."

Earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no need to restart military operations in Iran since the economic sanctions were working so well.

The U.S. military on Friday denied a claim by Iranian forces to have destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar installation in Bahrain, acknowledging that Iran had launched two attack drones at the small Persian Gulf nation, but saying "both were shot down by U.S. forces."

The claim, attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), was published earlier Friday by various Iranian state media outlets, along with an image said to show the damaged radar station.

In its "Fact Check" post on social media, the U.S. Central Command said there were no injuries or damage caused by the interception of the Iranian drones.

Iran had peppered Bahrain and most other U.S. Gulf allies with daily rocket and drone strikes earlier in the war, but far fewer attacks have been reported since the summer, when major hostilities ended.

The United Nations nuclear watchdog agency is "increasingly concerned" about its lack of access to an underground Iranian uranium enrichment facility that Tehran has acknowledged exists, but refused to allow inspectors to visit, according to Reuters.

"The Agency does not know IFEP's exact location, status for safeguards purposes or whether it contains nuclear material," Reuters quoted the International Atomic Energy Agency as saying in a quarterly report to member states, referring to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP).

The IAEA asked Iran to allow inspectors to visit the IFEP in February, but Tehran refused , telling the U.N. agency that "conditions resulting from acts of aggression and the continuation of threats have created a situation in which the normal implementation of safeguards is legally untenable and materially impracticable."

The refusal came after the U.S. and Israel pummeled Iranian nuclear sites, including Isfahan, with a wave of missile strikes in June 2025 .

The IAEA said in a September report that, since then, it had observed, in satellite imagery, "regular vehicular activity around the entrance to the tunnel complex at Isfahan," where the agency believes some of the Iran's roughly 900-pound highly-enriched uranium stockpile is believed to have been buried by the June 2025 missile strikes.

"In light of this activity," the IAEA said it requested in February that Iran give inspectors access "as soon as possible," but Tehran has continued to refuse, the nuclear watchdog agency says, citing the attacks on its territory.

The Trump administration has framed Iran's controversial nuclear program as the primary justification for the war, but it has vacillated during the conflict between suggesting Iran would give up its remaining stockpile voluntarily, to declaring the issue largely resolved.

"More than 80 percent of their nuclear industrial base — gone," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declared earlier this week," adding: "CRAZY ISLAMISTS IN TEHRAN WILL NEVER EVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON."

But Iran has agreed to nothing so far regarding its uranium stockpiles or its enrichment program, including renewed IAEA inspections. It has refused to negotiate with the U.S. on the topic until a formal ceasefire is implemented.

On Wednesday, a top Iranian security official insisted Tehran would "not remove even a single particle of enriched nuclear material from the country."

President Trump said Thursday that, "we don't need a deal with Iran," suggesting he may be willing to leave the matter unresolved.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, the first such claim in months.

It couldn't be independently verified.

A report by Iran's official IRNA news agency on Friday quoted a statement by the Guard as saying the attack on the U.S. radar system followed a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik.

Bahrain has been one of the strongest critics of Iran and is home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet.

The statement said the attack on the radar was a serious warning to the U.S. to cease its strikes. It was the first report by Iran of targeting a facility in Bahrain since September.

During an air war that began in February, Iran targeted U.S. bases in neighboring Arab nations including Bahrain in retaliation for U.S. strikes. Since then, Iran routinely targets oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for international oil shipments.

Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without its approval.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Friday that there was an explosion on a ship that struck a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has sought to restrict navigation.

Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorization to traverse the strait and has attacked vessels that don't comply.

In response, the United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and began providing military support to tankers using the vital trade route.

"A few hours ago, a ship carrying liquefied natural gas east of the Strait of Hormuz tried to cross an unauthorized passageway south of the strait, but was hit by a naval mine and exploded violently," the IRGC said on Friday, without giving the name or origin of the vessel.

In recent weeks, Iran's armed forces have repeatedly reported fires or explosions on ships in the strait, often saying they'd hit mines.

The U.S. military, however, claims to have cleared the waterway's routes of mines.

Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that U.S. officials requested that Russian President Vladimir Putin facilitate negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

"It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them," Qalibaf said.

The White House did not directly respond to the Associated Press' query about whether the U.S. had asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.

President Trump's senior envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Russia Thursday, where they met Putin to discuss the ongoing war in Ukraine . In their remarks after the meeting, neither Putin nor Mr. Trump's envoys mentioned any discussion about Iran.

-CBS/AP

President Trump told Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president claims is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.

Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month war, has been blunt in blaming the conflict — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans' sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections in the United States.

But Mr. Trump brusquely told Vance, in a social media post, to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing - and perhaps more politically salient - issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.

"We don't need a deal with Iran," Mr. Trump said in the post. "Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!"

Mr. Trump earlier this week said he believed the war "militarily is effectively over," and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance "to focus his complete and total attention" on his anti-fraud campaign.

His directive came after The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official. The vice president's office did not respond to a request for comment.

- CBS/AP

items.summary: The DHS secretary said there were no indications of a cyberattack.

scraped.title: FAA ground stop live updates: 'Zero evidence of anything nefarious,' FAA head says
scraped.description: The DHS secretary said there were no indications of a cyberattack.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: FAA ground stop live updates: 'Zero evidence of anything nefarious,' FAA head says
scraped.body_text:
The administrator said the ground stop was the result of equipment failure.

The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a rare nationwide ground stop for all airports Friday -- a more than four-hour disruption that snarled travel from coast to coast with canceled flights and stranded passengers.

At a White House news conference Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old technology that became overloaded and called on Congress to provide billions more in funding to modernize critical equipment, calling the situation an "emergency."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication the incident stemmed from a cyberattack, but that officials were still investigating.

Thousands of flights were canceled amid the ground stop.

"I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity," Duffy said when asked how long air travelers should expect delays and cancellations to continue.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign or President Donald Trump should remove him "immediately" on Saturday.

"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch. Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency," Hochul said in a statement Saturday.

"With millions of Americans preparing to travel for the holidays, families deserve answers and confidence in the safety of our skies. Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again," Hochul said.

The ground stop on Friday was the result of faulty equipment, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday.

"We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was," Bedford said.

"When we have that root cause analysis complete, we'll share it with you," Bedford said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does not believe the failure in communications that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday was the result of a cyber attack.

"In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber," Duffy said during a press conference Saturday.

Duffy said this transfer from copper to fiber has been happening in the U.S. for decades, saying virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital.

"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. So specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was gave us issues with our our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds," Duffy said.

When that happened the airspace was shut down for safety, Duffy said.

"Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online, so we don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said operations are "slowly" returning to normal on Saturday with planes pushing back, taxiing and taking off.

"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Duffy said in a post on X.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said.

Duffy also thanked air traffic controllers, pilots, and flight crews who have been working around the clock.

"The nation thanks you for your professionalism and dedication to the flying public," Duffy said.

items.title: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say
items.summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China next week.

scraped.title: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say
scraped.description: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China next week.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say
scraped.body_text:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.

President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.

Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.

Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.

Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.

Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.

An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.

Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.

There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.

The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.

"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.

Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.

While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.

Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.

The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

items.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
items.summary: Sean Duffy, the country's transportation secretary, said his agency is 'going to hold people accountable'.

scraped.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
scraped.description: Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’.
scraped.author: Evan Semones
scraped.h1: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
scraped.body_text:
Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’.

Save

Share

The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.

At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.

Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.

“We had 1,000 connection attempts ever four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Transportation Department.

When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.

“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

Al Jazeera has reached out to L3Harris for comment on the allegations but has not yet heard back.

Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.

“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”

The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added.

As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11 , the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”

Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.

“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

items.summary: Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.

scraped.title: US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
scraped.description: Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
scraped.body_text:
Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.

Save

Share

US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds ⁠of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from ⁠Donbas?” he said. “That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda.”

Zelenskyy said the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine the US asked about were areas Russia does not control. The Ukrainian president said he refused to cede territory.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

Putin has long said that Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy did say that if Ukraine received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, military and reconstruction funds, and a recovery plan from the US and other partners, he would put the question about ceding parts of Donbas to a national referendum.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.

He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.

“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”

Despite the diplomatic push to end the conflict, Russia and Ukraine reported numerous overnight attacks . Russian officials reported on Friday that about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets, while Ukraine reported attacks on a hospital and the port of Odesa.

At the summit in Ireland over recent days, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers – non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – as well as EU officials. They would hold talks ‌with ‌US and Ukrainian officials, but not with Russia.

items.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
items.summary: The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

scraped.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
scraped.description: The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.
scraped.h1: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
scraped.body_text:
The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.

Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit).

Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change .

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."

"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.

"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to organizers.

Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.

"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.

Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.

"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"

Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.

Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.

The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.

Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phaseout of oil and gas.

Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.

COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment , reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.

Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.

A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming.

The figure, set at COP21 in 2015, is the threshold beyond which most scientists believe the world will see increasingly extreme effects of climate change.

A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.

items.title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
items.summary: DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

scraped.title: DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim, Katja Gloger win top journalism prize
scraped.description: DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.
scraped.h1: DW's Abdul Karim, Katja Gloger win top journalism prize
scraped.body_text:
DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau , this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades .

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press . That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta , the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom .

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany .

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism , antisemitism , Islamophobia , discrimination , sexism , and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

This article was originally written in German.

items.title: Copper wire replacement caused air traffic control issue that grounded flights across U.S.: White House

scraped.title: Copper wire replacement caused air traffic control issue that grounded flights across U.S.: White House | CBC
scraped.h1: Copper wire replacement caused air traffic control issue that grounded flights across U.S.: White House
scraped.body_text:
Routine maintenance to replace telecom line led to air traffic control outage: U.S. transportation secretary

Passengers and airlines face domino effect after nationwide ground stop in U.S.

Rental cars, trains or Ubers? Airline passengers search for alternatives during U.S. ground stop

Ground stop aftermath: Why it will take days to get things back to normal

'Mostly the vibe is confusion': Stranded air passenger describes crazy day

U.S. officials blame now-cancelled ground stop on outdated equipment, underfunding

U.S. ground stop order now lifted

U.S. FAA has been 'underwater' for years, says former inspector general

Who controls the runway? A retired air traffic controller explains

The facts about U.S. air traffic controllers

Responding to one of the last questions of the news conference, Duffy said he didn't have any data or reports of passengers who had medical issues as a result of the ground stop.

But he added that airport staff "rallied in those moments yesterday to accommodate passengers."

"We don't want to leave passengers on airplanes," he said.

Duffy ended his remarks with a final appeal for more money from Congress, referring to funding as a "great end-of-the-year Christmas present for the American people." He also said his team will continue to provide updates.

When asked whether the FAA has to swap out copper wire elsewhere, Duffy said yes.

About 75 per cent of the system has been transitioned to fibre so far, he said.

"Is it disruptive? Yes," Duffy said. "People may not get to a wedding. They might not get to a birthday … [but] I want them to get home safely."

Duffy says he's asked for $30 billion US ($42 billion Cdn) to make the upgrades necessary to modernize FAA infrastructure.

But he added that the issue goes beyond telecommunications infrastructure, saying that he wants to look at upgrades to airport infrastructure like runways and air traffic control towers as well.

"We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace," he said.

"It's not a cheap proposition."

As mentioned earlier, Congress has been controlled by Republicans — Duffy's party — for the past two years.

Bedford told reporters that all affected passengers in the U.S. will be supported — either by getting onto a new flight or by getting a full refund. He also said passengers should reach out to their air carriers directly.

Canadian travellers are also urged to track their flight status, and airlines in Canada have rebooked flights and even offered a one-time option to change or cancel some flights without penalty.

Looking ahead, though, Bedford essentially said it's too soon to tell what the FAA can do differently next time. For now, the agency needs to figure out the "root cause" of the glitch, he said, and then they can establish what needs to happen differently.

Officials were asked if they had any message for passengers who were nervous after yesterday's full ground stop, especially since it coincided with the Microsoft outage .

"Bedford said passengers can rest assured that "we will keep planes on the ground unless we are 100 per cent confident that we've got the stability and resilience to operate safely."

He also again stressed that officials are confident that this was not a cyber issue or cyberattack.

But he also added that this incident highlights the need to upgrade their telecommunication infrastructure as soon as possible.

"This is probably the worst kept secret in government, that this FTI system needs to be replaced," he said, referring to the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure.

Duffy said several teams and departments, including Kash Patel with the FBI as well as the Department of War, were involved in yesterday's investigation.

Asked what gave the indication that something was going wrong, Bedford said they started to experience "instability" on their communication lines "that we couldn't explain."

Because they couldn't identify a root cause for this, "we were unwilling to take any risk," he said.

On Friday, Duffy said the FAA experienced telecommunications issues at 3:36 p.m. ET.

The ground stop order was issued 17 minutes later, at 3:53 p.m. ET.

Duffy said that had the maintenance taken place at a big facility — like, say, Newark — it would have taken place at night. But the upgrade in question that led to the ground stop was in a remote location.

"Safety is paramount. If we don't make these upgrades we can't have a safe system," Duffy said, noting that the FAA has to replace copper wire.

"We're making transition not because we want to spend money, but because it is safer and it is more resilient."

Fridays are typically one of the busiest days of the week for airports, according to CLEAR .

Bedford estimates that some 4,000 or 5,000 flights of 41,000 scheduled for today will be cancelled in the U.S. as airlines and airports continue to recover. Still, he struck an optimistic chord.

"I do think the worst is behind us," he said.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford is up next.

Bedford stressed that the mass grounding of flights was done out of an abundance of caution.

"I'm sorry we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons," he said, addressing passengers whose flights were disrupted yesterday.

He added that the ground stop was necessary because they couldn't determine the root cause of the technical problems and needed to take pressure off their system.

"I think that was the right call. We stand behind that."

He also added that this was due to an equipment issue, and they don't believe it had anything to do with AI.

Duffy is again making appeals for more funding, calling it a bipartisan issue — all while claiming that the U.S. has the safest airspace in the world. (Earlier, a Canadian aviation expert told CBC News that U.S. telecommunications and air traffic control systems could indeed use updates.)

The transportation secretary is pushing Democrats and Republicans to work together to approve funding. Congress has been controlled by the Republican Party — Duffy's party — for the past two years.

"This is a time when I think Congress can signal … we're willing to work together," Duffy said. "We can fight on a lot of things, but we're not gonna fight on this."

items.title: Canadian judge decries U.S. sanctions of International Criminal Court as 'attack in favour of impunity'
items.summary: Kimberly Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court, was sanctioned by the Trump administration last August. Despite impacts including cancelled credit cards and frozen bank accounts, she says attempts to intimidate her and other court officials are 'futile.'

scraped.title: Canadian judge decries U.S. sanctions of International Criminal Court as 'attack in favour of impunity' | CBC News
scraped.description: Kimberly Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court, was sanctioned by the Trump administration last August. Despite impacts including cancelled credit cards and frozen bank accounts, she says attempts to intimidate her and other court officials are 'futile.'
scraped.h1: Canadian judge decries U.S. sanctions of International Criminal Court as 'attack in favour of impunity'
scraped.body_text:
The ICC will survive Trump's attacks, Canadian judge says

Kimberly Prost began to feel the effects of the U.S. sanctions immediately.

"These economic sanctions are not symbolic in any way," said Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), who was sanctioned by the Trump administration last year.

Prost's credit cards were cancelled and her access to banking services hindered, she said, because of the U.S.'s wide-reaching impact on the global banking system.

"Every time literally I go to make a bank transfer, I hold my breath because I don't know if it's going to work," Prost said in an interview with CBC News.

"To order an Uber, book a hotel, buy a theatre ticket — everything requires some form of credit card, and so you're sort of struggling to adjust."

Google, iCloud, Amazon accounts cut off for ICC judges amid U.S. sanctions

Based in The Hague, Netherlands, the ICC investigates and tries individuals charged with genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when courts in its 125 member states , including Canada, are unwilling or unable to do so.

The sanctions on Prost are part of a larger U.S. campaign to discredit and dismantle the ICC, which began in earnest after a February 2025 executive order imposed sanctions for investigating American personnel and issuing arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

U.S. President Donald Trump has since sustained his attack on the international court, calling on member states to immediately "resign from this rogue institution" in a September UN General Assembly speech . Just last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" if allies do not "rein in" the court.

In a Sept. 22, 2026, speech at the United Nations General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump urged member nations of the International Criminal Court to 'officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.' (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

Prost says these actions are an attack against the international system of criminal justice and rule of law that has been built since the Second World War.

"It is an attack that foresees a world where victims of atrocity crimes are forgotten. And it is an attack in favour of impunity and ending accountability for these crimes. That's the only way it can be framed."

Prost was singled out for her role in judicially authorizing a March 2020 preliminary investigation into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan since 2003, including by U.S. service members.

Since 2021, however, the investigation has deprioritized the role of the U.S., focusing instead on the Afghan government and Taliban forces.

"To my knowledge, there's no active investigation of the Americans in that case, but I'm sanctioned."

Trump administration sanctions Canadian judge who sits on International Criminal Court

The United States has never been a member of the ICC, and has long expressed concerns that its citizens could be prosecuted.

"As the United States works to bring peace around the world, our diplomats or our soldiers could be drawn into this court," President George W. Bush said the day after the court was inaugurated in 2002 . "It's very troubling to me."

Twenty-four years later, Rubio echoed the same rhetoric about the "dangers" of the global court, warning that American border patrol agents, marines and prosecutors would "be at the mercy of foreign judges," risking imprisonment for defending their own country.

However, Prost says Rubio's arguments are misleading, as the ICC would have "no jurisdiction" if the U.S. asserted its sovereignty and conducted its own genuine investigations or prosecutions when allegations arise.

Prost and two other ICC judges sued the Trump administration in June, opposing the sanctions that they say are "designed to exert extra-judicial pressure" and coerce them into "prioritizing their private interests over deciding cases on the basis of the law and facts."

"We decided that it was so significant and such an impediment to our work — and to the work of the court — to challenge it before the courts of the United States," said Prost.

In July, four former U.S. ambassadors and prosecutors of international criminal tribunals submitted a brief in support of the ICC judges , arguing that the sanctions "penalize independent judicial decision-making."

Ottawa tight-lipped on joining legal case against Trump sanction of Canadian ICC judge

Canadian officials have not intervened in Prost's lawsuit. But in a September interview with CBC News, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said Canada "remains committed to the ICC process."

"As a sovereign country, we determine our foreign policy, and that includes the principles on which our foreign policy is based," Anand said. "One of those fundamental principles is respect for international law."

Mission of ICC 'too important' to abandon, says Canadian judge

Prost said the efforts to intimidate her and other judges are ultimately "futile."

"We continue to judge our cases on the facts and the law and the evidence before us objectively and independently, and that will never change," she said.

In October, the U.S. allowed the ICC to access certain information technology and banking services for six months. The State Department said that time would allow member states to demonstrate "meaningful progress" on U.S. concerns.

EU awards human rights prize to International Criminal Court amid Trump attacks

Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions

Prost says losing access to those systems could have a "very crippling effect" on the court's operations.

Though some member states have signaled support , she says the moment remains "critically important" to safeguard the ICC, which has taken steps to prepare in case sanctions come into full force.

"It's their court. It's not the prosecutors' court, not the judges' court. It's the states' court, and they have to protect it."

With files from Reuters and The Canadian Press

items.title: Carney says he will not boycott APEC 'family photo' with Putin
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will participate in an upcoming group photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit out of respect for the host, Chinese President Xi Jinping.

scraped.title: Carney says he will not boycott APEC 'family photo' with Putin | CBC News
scraped.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will participate in an upcoming group photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit out of respect for the host, Chinese President Xi Jinping.
scraped.h1: Carney says he will not boycott APEC 'family photo' with Putin
scraped.body_text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will participate in an upcoming group photo with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit out of respect for the host, Chinese President Xi Jinping.

"Yes, I will participate in the photo out of respect for the host. We’re in Asia," Carney said, speaking in Manila, the Philippine capital, which is one stop on his overseas multi-country tour.

The photo will be taken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen next week. U.S. President Donald Trump is also expected to attend.

With war in Ukraine continuing and the casualties mounting following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Carney was asked why appearing in the photo is the right move. He said Canada's repudiation of Russia is demonstrated through its broader sanctions policy, not from boycotting the photo.

He pointed to the federal government's recent announcement that it will take steps to prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada for next month's world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

Carney wraps meetings on security, trade with European leaders in Ireland

Canadian government says Russian players with visas will still be barred from WJC

"Canada stands firmly with Ukraine, firmly with democracy, territorial integrity, rule of law — and all of those put us on the other side of Vladimir Putin's Russia," Carney said.

Faced with a similar decision at last month's G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said she would opt out of taking part in a group photo with her Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

Then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, centre, and other world leaders wave during the family photo at the G20 summit in Osaka, Japan, in June 2019. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

The "family photos" are traditional diplomatic protocol at world summits.

Putin will attend this year's APEC summit hosted by China because unlike last year's host, South Korea, China is not a member of the International Criminal Court, which has issued an arrest warrant for Putin.

Former prime ministers Justin Trudeau and Stephen Harper both took part in family photos with the Russian leader. This will be Carney's first face-to-face encounter with Putin since becoming prime minister.

Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia

Meanwhile, the White House has confirmed plans for a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin, coming amid recent U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia.

Asked for his thoughts on the trilateral meeting, Carney reiterated support for NATO allies.

"The security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe, for Europe and NATO, not by Russia," he said.

Producer

Mayson Maharaj is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics and a writer for CBC's Parliament Hill bureau.

items.summary: In youth detention, writing a song means escaping the walls for a while. Kobie Dee and Dobby know what music offers young people inside. Kobie Dee has seen the power of music through his time working with youth in detention.

scraped.h1: Kobie Dee and Dobby on the surprising songs inside youth detention
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Dan Condon

Double J

Topic: Music

Kobie Dee has seen the power of music through his time working with youth in detention. ( Supplied )

Kobie Dee knows the power of music as a positive force that can steer young people towards a less destructive path. He knows the road they're on.

"I was very fortunate that I didn't end up in jail," he tells Double J's Michael Hing.

"I was very much walking down a road that was leading that way. For me, it was, 'If I don't get my life right, if I don't get myself help, these opportunities aren't going to last for me.'

Start your weekday with the songs that soundtrack your life, thrilling new releases and fun chats. Michael Hing hosts Mornings from 9am Monday to Thursday, on Double J.

"There were so many opportunities that came when I was heavy in addiction, and all the stuff I was doing. I missed out on so much stuff. There were big shows that I was supposed to do that I didn't do because I was heavy in addiction."

The 29-year-old Gomeroi man and award-winning musician has recently spent weeks working as part of the Hear Me Out, Music Behind Bars initiative from the Australian Children's Music Foundation, an intensive six-week songwriting pilot for those detained at the Cobham Youth Justice Centre.

He was joined by Rhyan Clapham, a Filipino Murrawarri musician who performs as Dobby. Both rappers believe there are few more powerful and accessible ways to escape.

"We've seen the power of music play out again and again with young people," Dobby says. "It's a platform with which to express themselves, and also to just make dope music."

Both rappers are Indigenous men and take seriously the responsibility of being put up as examples of the power of music in one's life.

"We are so over-represented in these centres," Kobie says. "So, to have other black fellas come in and to be able to speak to stuff that they can be working towards outside, showing them how to make music…

"They got to watch Dobby do his thing in there. Those young fellas' minds were blown. To see that it's also accessible for them to be doing too, I think it's so important."

“It’s not just about me anymore.”

"You've got to see it to be it," Dobby agrees. "It's representation.

"It's also self-fulfilling. When you create something that you can own and hold and say, 'That's my song,' it gives you a sense of pride and motivation to keep creating. I think creativity cannot be taken seriously enough."

The two rappers know creating music needs a safe environment conducive to accepting self-expression in whatever form it takes.

"We're helping create a space in which they feel safe enough to share their story and bring it out in a musical way, whether it be rap, whether it be singing or playing the guitar or whatever," Dobby says.

"Because we're fostering that environment, they're able to sharpen their sword and practice their skills and become a better musician.

"That should be afforded to anyone. It doesn't matter what situation you're in doesn't matter who you are. Music is a universal language, and we can all speak it. It's one of the most powerful forces of energy that we have here to work with."

Music as escapism becomes especially profound when talking about youth in detention. No one wants to be in jail, and Kobie says making music provides a momentary but powerful escape.

"They're completely in the moment of creating and expressing themselves and speaking about things they probably wouldn't be speaking about in everyday life within these centres."

Rap and incarceration have been closely aligned for decades; countless hip hop classics reference prison and the behaviours that will land you in there.

When Aboriginal-Filipino rapper DOBBY made his ARIA award-winning album Warrangu: River Story, it set him on a journey of spiritual self-reflection. Now he's using his voice to send a powerful message around climate, racism and injustice.

"I'm very biased as a rapper, but I think it's one of the most influential forces," Dobby says. "It's so direct.

"It helps tell their story. I mean, hip hop is famously a counter narrative against the mainstream, against the government, against wider Australia in this context.

"Where racist stigma and stereotypes are put upon them, hip hop is a place where they can say, 'No, that's not me. This is my story, let me tell you the real side of what it is'. That's incredibly powerful."

Some preconceptions about the music being made in these sessions are natural, but that doesn't mean it's always correct.

Rap wasn't the only sound participants gravitated towards. And not every song was born from anger.

"When I walked in, I was expecting to hear a rap song," Kobie says. "I was expecting to hear some drill music, just from my own experience of doing workshops in juvies in different states. It's mostly what the kids want to be making.

"I walk in and they're singing a love song, and it was beautiful.

"This is the stuff that is on their minds already."

Making such a song requires a level of vulnerability that can be hard for any young person to access, let alone when in a prison environment.

The program provides a level of safety that hopes to allow participants the chance to air the gamut of their feelings.

"To be able to provide a space where they can let that out like that, I think it's just so important that we're doing this for these young people," Kobie says.

Both Dobby and Kobie know the limitations of a program like this. They know they won't influence everyone, and that those they affect won't always carry these lessons with them.

That doesn't mean it's not worth doing. As active members of Australia's music industry, they see the opportunities that exist.

"Showing these young people, 'This is out there for you. You have the opportunity to change your life through music,'" Kobie says.

"It doesn't have to be being on stage or anything like that; they could even be doing what we're doing right now and teaching other young people music.

"Showing the different opportunities and showing the different avenues."

Vitally, they know the most influential people in a child's life are their peers.

"You could do workshops with 20 kids, and there might be only one kid that comes out with that thought," Kobie says.

"But changing that one kid is so powerful, because that one kid can then go on to start his own programs and save another five or six kids from that lifestyle.

"It's more about showing them what's possible and telling them, like, 'If you want this in your life, there are some things that need to change.' It's sowing those seeds."

Hear Michael Hing's full chat with Kobie Dee and Dobby on Double J Mornings , Monday from 9am.

Topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art

Some of the recent artwork produced from Bidyadanga, WA's largest remote Aboriginal community. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

Artists from Western Australia's largest remote community are increasingly securing their own unique place in the state's vibrant northern arts scene.

Bidyadanga, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, is home to about 850 people.

Its unique location between the red dirt of the West Kimberley and clear blue water of the Indian Ocean gives the community's artists a unique perspective.

Bidyadanga, about 180 kilometres south of Broome, is home to 850 people. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne )

Jenny Butt was painting long before the community's award-winning arts centre opened its doors.

She said Bidyadanga's artistic reputation continued to grow in scale and reach.

"It's been touching; painting, representing your identity with your family's connection to country," she said.

"And inspiring for us too, as we think of back where we've been.

"We grew up near the coast [and have] lived in the desert with family, so we've got two connections."

Jenny Butt makes a sale on opening night. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

Butt said it was particularly heartening to see the next generation of young artists getting involved.

The work highlights the connection of different cultures and everything that made Bidyadanga what it is, according to artist Marika Jadai.

The centre hosts an exhibition in Broome twice a year, giving locals the opportunity to buy artworks direct from the artists themselves.

The artists keep part of the proceeds, while the arts centre also directs some of their take back into the Bidyadanga community.

Sifting through the reams of artwork at Redbill Studio Gallery. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

Behind the scenes, the process of hauling the reams of pieces from Bidyadanga to Broome is no small feat, especially in stifling summer weather.

In the days leading up to the show, artists and staff began cataloguing and listing the pieces, ready to be rolled, packed up and driven to Broome.

Augustine Bada has taken up a position working at the art centre and helps to coordinate the showcase.

Augustine Bada says he was proud to have the pieces on display. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

Mr Bada said he was excited about what next year would bring, with high hopes for the studio.

"It's really important here, because by doing art, we're sharing stories, passing down knowledge and painting country as well."

Jenny Butt says Bidyadanga artists have the rare opportunity to represent both the ocean and desert in their work. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

The opening night of the show, at Broome's Redbill Studio Gallery, attracted a crowd of hundreds.

Attendees sifted through the vast quantity of paintings on display from more than 80 Bidyadanga artists.

Daisy (far right) says the work she buys will remind her of her time in the Kimberley. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

"We're probably moving on soon, so we really wanted something that captured the earthy colours and reminded us of our time up here," shopper Daisy said.

"I work out in Bidgy as well; I know a lot of these artists, so it feels really special."

Redbill Studio Gallery has hosted the Bidyadanga artists twice a year for the past four years. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler )

Redbill Studio Gallery co-owner Melissa Foster said the connection with the remote community and hosting their art shows in Broome came about through "word of mouth".

"It's great for them to have a platform in Broome. They have a lovely following of community," she said.

"We definitely get a lot of good feedback. We always have people come up and ask when the next Bidgy sale is."

At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade.

What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes.

Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system , and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work.
