scraped.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
scraped.description: Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials.
scraped.h1: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
scraped.body_text:
Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials.

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.

Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

According to theoretical models, ultraviolet radiation from the star can destroy small grains of pure ice faster than collisions can produce them. On the other hand, grains of dirty ice, mixed with other molecules, should survive longer.

Betti and her colleagues observed Beta Pictoris on December 7, 2023, using Webb’s Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). They operated it in a mode that records a full spectrum, from 0.6 to 5.2 micrometers, for every point in the image. After subtracting the overwhelming glare of the star, the team measured how much starlight the disk’s dust reflects at each wavelength to look for the fingerprints of ices.

Water ice absorbs light strongly near 3 micrometers, while carbon dioxide ice absorbs either at 4.27 micrometers or 4.39 micrometers when it contains the heavier carbon-13 isotope. The team first mapped the water ice features across the disk and found they were strikingly uniform. They then extracted detailed spectra from two spots on opposite sides of the star, each roughly 100 astronomical units out.

Both spectra showed water and carbon dioxide ices, the latter in both its common form and the rarer carbon-13 version. But the shape of those features turned out to tell us more than the fact they were there.

The carbon dioxide features were shifted slightly toward shorter wavelengths and were much broader than those of pure carbon dioxide ice measured in the lab. The team says in the paper that this is how carbon dioxide behaves when its molecules are trapped inside water ice. In other words, the two ices aren’t sitting side by side as separate grains—they are thoroughly mixed, which makes it the kind of dirty ice that models suggested could survive the star’s ultraviolet radiation.

The team calculated that there is slightly more than one carbon dioxide molecule for every 10 water molecules, meaning it’s about 11 percent of the ice. That falls within the 2.5 to 30 percent range measured in Solar System comets and the 7 to 20 percent seen in the ice of disks around other newborn stars. It means the ices of Beta Pictoris may have formed through the same processes as in our own Solar System, building up on dust grains in cold, dense, water-rich clouds during the earliest stages of star formation.

The structure of the water ice also pointed in this direction. When water freezes at moderate temperatures, its molecules settle into an orderly crystal lattice, and crystalline ice produces a sharp peak in the spectrum just above 3 micrometers. That peak was absent at Beta Pictoris. The ice is almost entirely amorphous, a disordered, glass-like solid that forms when water molecules freeze so fast and so cold that they stick wherever they land. The team estimates that less than 7 percent of the water ice in the system is crystalline, which is somewhat surprising.

Models predicted that ice in debris disks should mostly be crystalline. For amorphous ice to stay in that form, it has to remain colder than about 100 Kelvin, or minus 173° Celsius. Otherwise, something has to keep breaking up its crystal structure, such as high-energy ultraviolet light, cosmic rays, or particles streaming from the star. Either way, the researchers concluded the ice most likely formed in the interstellar medium, long before the planets of Beta Pictoris began to take shape.

The remaining question was how the icy grains got spread so evenly across the disk.

The team argues that this even ice distribution requires frequent collisions among planetesimals. Each collision would release fresh icy dust, including ice that had been buried and protected deep inside the colliding bodies, replenishing what the starlight destroys. We already have evidence that such collisions do happen. Earlier infrared images revealed a curved, lopsided streak of dust in the southwestern arm of the disk, thought to be debris from a violent collision a little less than halfway out from the star.

Betti’s team’s findings support the idea that the disk’s carbon monoxide gas comes from colliding icy bodies and offer an explanation of how ice can survive in an environment constantly exposed to ultraviolet light. What the team could not do is determine exactly how much crystalline ice is present or rule out other molecules hiding in the mixture.

But if a young planetary system 64 light-years away may have started with much the same icy ingredients as ours, then primordial, interstellar ice might be a common ingredient of planetary systems in general. This means the raw materials for water-rich, potentially habitable worlds might be common, too.

scraped.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
scraped.description: Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt.
scraped.h1: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
scraped.body_text:
Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt.

More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.

Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.

As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.

We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change , environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards , about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.

In many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities . But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.

The Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region , a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos , a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas , ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

Sustainability certification and conservation programs, such as World Wildlife Fund Conservation Champions , have helped encourage vineyards to protect biodiversity in the region. Many growers use these sustainability certifications to increase their wine’s marketability. But we found they have also embraced conservation for how it can benefit their vineyards. Rather than viewing conservation as land taken out of production, many said they see it supporting the ecological processes essential to their business.

The majority of South Africa’s vineyards today participate in the Integrated Production of Wine certification system, created by the South African wine industry and researchers in 1998 to reduce environmental harm. The system sets standards governing pesticide use, water management, wastewater treatment and environmental stewardship. It also uses independent auditing of participating farms and wineries to ensure those claiming certification meet the standards.

To manage the water supplies their vineyards depend on, growers described restoring native vegetation , including the removal of alien species, along waterways and reducing erosion to protect wetlands and rivers. Research shows that healthy natural systems can improve water retention in the soil and contribute to the overall resilience of the landscape in the face of more extreme climate conditions.

To boost their soil’s health, some growers are planting cover crops , such as legumes , cereals like oats and rye, and brassicas such as radish and mustard, between vine rows. Growers broadly described using cover crops, compost, mulching and other practices to improve soil structure and increase organic matter in the soil. Cover crops require maintenance and can provide habitat for pests, but research shows that the right cover crops, when well maintained, can benefit vineyards by reducing erosion and increasing water retention and nutrients in the soil.

Several producers also described efforts to reduce their reliance on chemical pesticides, which is beneficial not only for the environment but also their businesses as chemical costs continue to rise . We heard about vineyards that monitor pest populations closely and respond in targeted ways rather than using pesticides broadly.

Some growers encourage beneficial insects and manage habitats that support natural pest control . The creation of habitats for natural pest predators can reduce the overall disease risk too. While chemical treatments remain part of many vineyard operations, growers reported increasing interest in other approaches that prevent disease and pest outbreaks, such as pruning, to reduce their total chemical use.

Sustainable practices like these are well established in South Africa’s wine industry, but our interviews suggest their use has been expanding in recent years. Rather than focusing solely on treating problems after they arise, these approaches emphasize prevention, monitoring and ecological balance.

The stewardship practices we observed in South Africa are investments in long-term business resilience for many growers.

Many of the wine producers we interviewed described facing rising costs and market uncertainty. Exports, labor and chemicals are all expensive. They emphasized that maintaining healthy soils, conserving water and reducing vulnerability to drought and disease are essential to keeping their vineyards productive.

As concerns about drought, climate pressures and profitability rise, the area in vineyard production in South Africa has also decreased . Several growers described diversifying their business models and even switching crops to make their businesses more resilient to hotter, drier conditions.

Farmers around the world are confronting the realities of a changing climate . Our research shows that effective solutions can come from recognizing the interconnectedness of nature and production.

The experience of South Africa’s winegrowers shows that farms can be managed more sustainably when they’re seen as part of larger ecological systems.

Students Zoe Van der Walt , Jack Spining and Dryver Finch contributed to this article.

Hannah V. Herrero is Associate Professor of Geography & Sustainability and Director of Sustainability at University of Tennessee ; Erin L. Bunting is Assistant Professor of Geography at Michigan State University ; Jane Southworth is Professor of Geography at University of Florida ; Jason K. Blackburn is Professor of Geography at University of Florida ; and Stephanie Insalaco-Wyner is Assistant Professor of Geographic Information Sciences at Southwestern University .

scraped.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
scraped.description: One way or another, the company will get some more data on Saturday.
scraped.h1: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
scraped.body_text:
One way or another, the company will get some more data on Saturday.

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified issue, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.

The primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.

This means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.

In that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The company has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

However, SpaceX still has a chance to make history on Saturday with the potential return of the Starship upper stage. SpaceX has never attempted to catch the vehicle’s upper stage.

Doing so will require Starship to pass a series of tests in orbit and subsequently during its return to Earth to ensure it is fully healthy. This is critical because Starship will be passing over parts of Mexico and the United States before returning to Starbase, and SpaceX does not want to endanger people on the ground. Additionally, it does not want to risk damage to its launch towers.

If Starship passes these health checks, it would land at about 3:15 pm local time in Texas (21:15 UTC). If it does not, the company has earlier options to de-orbit the vehicle into an ocean.

Successfully returning Starship’s upper stage would be historic, as well as significant for SpaceX’s efforts to reuse the massive rocket. It would also give the company valuable information about the vehicle’s performance during reentry.

One of the biggest hurdles left in Starship’s development is the vehicle’s heat shield, which must protect the upper stage during its return through Earth’s atmosphere. More than that, SpaceX aims to make Starship rapidly reusable, and to do this, Starship’s tiles must be light and resilient.

SpaceX has been experimenting with tiles since the beginning of the Starship program, trying to find the right combination of low mass, heat resistance, and durability so the tiles require minimal refurbishment between launches. For this flight, SpaceX said it is applying learnings from the previous test flight in September, including additional retention mechanisms on tiles in areas deemed to be at the highest risk of falling off during ascent and addressing areas with a flow path for plasma to get behind the tiles.

Another problem on recent flights has been heat incursion into the small gaps between the edges of the tiles. According to SpaceX, this Starship has a large portion of the heat shield equipped with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles.

Apple’s new foldable , the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock . While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos.

After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID.

Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful.

There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things.

The camera tricks are a little more niche, but some Duo owners have found the following to be helpful.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work.

Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop.

“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own . “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?”

The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added , “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.”

Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis.

Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day.

“There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said.

This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium . And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday.

The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”

“We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said.

When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied , “We call it SI around here, remember? SI.”

Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .

items.title: Nationwide ground stop followed contractor upgrade to L3Harris telecommunication system: DOT’s Duffy
items.summary: The FAA ground stop came after updates to an older communication system managed by L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

scraped.title: Nationwide ground stop followed contractor upgrade to L3Harris telecommunication system: DOT’s Duffy
scraped.description: The FAA ground stop came after updates to an older communication system managed by L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.
scraped.author: Leslie Josephs
scraped.h1: Nationwide ground stop followed contractor upgrade to L3Harris telecommunication system: DOT’s Duffy
scraped.body_text:
In this article

The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system made by L3Harris Technologies , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as travel disruptions lingered for thousands of passengers nationwide.

There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference.

The updates were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiberoptic cable, Duffy said. When a router was switched to fiberoptic cable from copper, it had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, Duffy said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds.

Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports.

"We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford.

L3Harris didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Duffy told the press conference that the FAA is investigating.

"What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said.

Flight disruptions continued on Saturday. More than 3,700 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and close to 2,000 were delayed as of 9:40 a.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of about 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather.

Part of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports.

Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period.

American Airlines , for example, is offering flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips, according to a person familiar with the airline's plans.

Delta Air Lines was offering crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages seen by CNBC. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter.

American and other airlines said they would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans.

Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to aviation data firm Cirium.

The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. ET on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such pause on departing flights in 25 years.

Duffy on Friday blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack.

The U.S. has the world's busiest airspace.

"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday.

The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.

Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority.

"I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing.

The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption.

"We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X.

The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns."

— CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

items.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
items.summary: Two Nvidia investors with about $2.13 billion of stock disclosed as of June 30 are calling for a deliberate leadership search after Huang’s resignation.

scraped.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
scraped.description: Two Nvidia investors with about $2.13 billion of stock disclosed as of June 30 are calling for a deliberate leadership search after Huang’s resignation.
scraped.author: Katie Tarasov
scraped.h1: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.

Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.

The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.

"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.

Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."

Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.

Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .

The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.

President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

items.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
items.summary: Eric Trump-backed robot startup Foundation Future Industries has run low on cash and missed payroll, as CEO Sankaet Pathak faces scrutiny over a $4.6 million company loan.

scraped.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
scraped.description: Eric Trump-backed robot startup Foundation Future Industries has run low on cash and missed payroll, as CEO Sankaet Pathak faces scrutiny over a $4.6 million company loan.
scraped.author: Hugh Son
scraped.h1: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
scraped.body_text:
Foundation Future Industries , a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak , borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts .

Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.

That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands."

Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."

Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors , claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.

"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon -owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury , Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams , said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said . "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

items.summary: Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars’ worth of the world’s most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door. scraped.title: Is Alice Huang a spy? The business behind the mysterious Chinese
scraped.description: Details about Alice Huang's life are vague, making it almost impossible to pin down where she lives, where she works, or when she was born, But her influence undoubtedly spreads far and wide.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Spies and silicon chips: Alice Huang’s tangled corporate web
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Singapore-based tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars’ worth of the world’s most advanced AI chips, but its office was an empty shell when AFP visited, its staff seemingly vanished long before claims of espionage landed at their door.

Megaspeed’s former director Alice Huang was this week outed as an alleged Chinese spy, accused of having an affair with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang while digging up company secrets for Beijing.

Details about Alice Huang’s life are vague, making it almost impossible to pin down where she lives, where she works, or when she was born.

But her influence undoubtedly spreads far and wide, from the nondescript Singapore office, to hulking data centres in Southeast Asia, to the gleaming boardrooms of Silicon Valley.

Her connection to cloud computing firm Megaspeed sits at the centre of the scandal.

Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia’s advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.

But it is also under investigation for serving a murkier purpose.

Under the guise of buying computer hardware for its Southeast Asia data hubs, Megaspeed has allegedly helped Beijing skirt trade restrictions by sending Nvidia chips into China.

Beijing has denied allegations of spying, and Megaspeed said it was investigating if it had complied with export controls on the sensitive chips.

At Megaspeed’s office in the heart of the Singapore business district, no staff could be seen behind its locked glass doors. Neighbours told AFP they had not seen anyone come or go for the past few months.

Likewise in a mall at a newly developed neighbourhood in Johor, the Malaysian region a bridge away from Singapore, no employees were around in subsidiary Speedmatrix’s office.

Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and several other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.

Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore’s probe.

Although no charges were laid, she was barred from the city-state in February 2026 for providing inaccurate information to “downplay her role in Megaspeed”, Singapore’s home ministry said.

Corporate records show Huang’s direct involvement in the birth of Megaspeed.

A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023, the records showed.

Almost immediately, the 7Road name was ditched and changed to Megaspeed International.

Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.

Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game maker to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.

Within 12 months, Megaspeed’s revenue jumped from $0 to almost US$300 million, according to company accounts filed in 2024.

Megaspeed — which described itself as a “cloud hosting services provider” — saw the value of its assets skyrocket from $32 million to almost $3 billion over the same period.

Just one of Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Over two years, Megaspeed reportedly traded in upwards of $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips.

A financial trail weaving through Singapore, Malaysia and the Cayman Islands suggests Megaspeed’s business may have been boosted by a connection to Chinese tech giant Alibaba.

Megaspeed has a Malaysian subsidiary that struck a deal in 2024 pledging assets to Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore as security in case of contractual breaches.

Apex is linked through a parent company to Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, a firm registered in the Cayman Islands, Singapore corporate data shows.

By that time, Huang was no longer registered as a director at Megaspeed.

But Singapore authorities said she remained one of Megaspeed’s “key controllers”.

Megaspeed’s ultimate holding company is a Singapore firm called Swiftdata.

Singapore businessman Tan Yong Pong — who has previously run printing and graphic design companies — is a director of both Megaspeed and Swiftdata.

No one answered when AFP visited Tan’s registered address in eastern Singapore, although dogs could be heard barking behind the door.

“They are friendly. I occasionally bump into the lady at the lift landing when she’s walking her dog,” an elderly neighbour told AFP. “But we have not seen them for months.”

In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a “post-shipment verification”, with Huang present, according to Singapore’s home ministry, adding that it was the first time it found out about Washington’s probe.

That same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police who impounded her passport.

By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.

In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at an afterparty following the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.

Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about their relationship well before it exploded into a public scandal, but said Sunday he did not regret not acting on it.

“No, I don’t think so. I think — you know, he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said.

But the scandal has sparked national security fears.

China and the United States are fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, and Nvidia’s market-leading products have become a major point of contention.

Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.

In the past years, Jensen Huang has emerged as the leading tech boss urging Trump to lift those curbs.

In any case, the restrictions appear to have been widely circumvented.

A Chinese university tied to the nation’s defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.

Singapore’s probe into Megaspeed is ongoing. Separately, Malaysia said Friday it is investigating the company’s subsidiary Speedmatrix to determine if chips imported into the country had been exported to other jurisdictions.

Megaspeed itself said it has retained a US lawfirm to examine its compliance.

“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously,” it said.

Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.

Corporate records filed in Hong Kong list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride hailing platform in China.

Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.

A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details Huang’s rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.

She served in a senior role at HSBC sometime around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.

Singapore business filings described her as a Chinese citizen with a Hong Kong passport.

She was born in China’s landlocked Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported.

A CCTV reporter wrote on Weibo that she worked with Huang at the Chinese broadcaster, but later deleted the post.

items.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China: White House
items.summary: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to […] Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next w...

scraped.title: Trump Xi Putin historical trilateral talk
scraped.description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting at a summit in Shenzhen next week
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China: White House
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Wales said.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump’s second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

“I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a “whole other track” of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official added.

Tesla and Space X boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but won’t be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the US president’s return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump’s meetings with Xi, the officials said.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

“We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration… and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the second official said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before heading to Shenzhen.

scraped.h1: Hong Kong’s Sikh temple lit in blue for ‘Day of Liberation’ festival
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Wan Chai’s historic Sikh Gurudwara has been lit in blue for Bandi Chhor Divas, meaning “Day of Liberation” – a Sikh celebration coinciding with Diwali.

Gurudwara Khalsa Diwan is the city’s only Sikh temple.

See also: In Pictures: Hong Kong’s only Sikh temple reopens as a place of worship, community and more

The annual festival marks the release of 52 princes and the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, from an Indian fort in 1619.

In Pictures: Cooking up equality at Hong Kong’s 116-year-old Sikh temple

According to a Hong Kong Government Religion Fact Sheet, the managing body of the temple estimates there are approximately 15,000 Sikhs in the city.

The light display, which has attracted photographers and visitors from across the city, will take place between 6:30pm and 9:30pm until November 24.

Words: Tom Grundy .

Updated - November 15, 2026 12:08 am IST - HYDERABAD

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi greeting Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy during the valedictory session of the Bharat Summit 2026 in Hyderabad on Saturday (November 14, 2026) | Photo Credit: Nagara Gopal

Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy along with Gig Workers launches the Telangana Gig Workers Social Security and Welfare Scheme at Hitech City, Hyderabad on Saturday, as part of the Bharat Summit. | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi announced a series of social security measures for gig workers in Telangana, including accident insurance of ₹5 lakh, health insurance of ₹10 lakh, dedicated Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones and a mechanism to ensure that 1% of every transaction is credited towards their social security.

Addressing gig workers, Mr. Gandhi said the Congress government in Telangana was fulfilling its promise to protect workers engaged in the platform-based economy and ensure that they received their fair share of the benefits generated by their labour.

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy riding pillion on two-wheelers while participating in a rally from Indira Gandhi statue to Jayabheri Grounds, in Hyderabad on Saturday (November 14). | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL

Describing the 21st century as the age of data, Mr. Gandhi pointed out that while companies such as Google, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Uber operated on data, gig workers had so far been denied access to information about their own work.

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy riding pillion on two-wheelers while participating in a rally from Indira Gandhi statue to Jayabheri Grounds, in Hyderabad on Saturday (November 14). | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL

Under the proposed legislation, workers would be able to access complete details of their transactions, deliveries, working hours, and payments through their mobile phones. “The data belongs to you, the labour is yours, but you were not even allowed to see your own data,” he said.

He said the government would also establish dedicated, Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones in Hyderabad and other cities to enable delivery personnel and other gig workers to park their vehicles, rest and relax during working hours.

Announcing insurance benefits, Mr. Gandhi said every gig worker would receive ₹5 lakh in accident insurance and ₹10 lakh in health insurance. A social security contribution mechanism under which 1% of every transaction, including deliveries and cab rides, would be contributed towards the workers’ future security.

Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy along with Gig Workers launches the Telangana Gig Workers Social Security and Welfare Scheme at Hitech City, Hyderabad on Saturday, as part of the Bharat Summit. | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL

The amount would be collected from companies and routed through the Gig Workers’ Board before being transferred directly to the workers’ bank accounts, he said.

Drawing a political distinction between the Congress and the BJP-RSS, Mr. Gandhi alleged that the latter wanted to turn gig workers into bonded labourers while allowing large corporate houses and platform companies to reap the benefits. In contrast, the Congress believed that workers were the foundation of the country’s economy and should be treated as partners.

“Do not be afraid. The Telangana government, Rahul Gandhi, Revanth Reddy and the Congress team stand with you. We want to make you partners and ensure protection for you and your families,” he said.

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy said the Congress government had fulfilled the promise made by Mr. Rahul Gandhi to gig workers in Telangana by bringing in legislation to protect their rights and provide them with social security.

Speaking at an event in the presence of Mr. Rahul Gandhi, the Chief Minister recalled that during the Bharat Jodo Yatra from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in 2023, which covered nearly 4,000 km, Mr. Gandhi had understood the difficulties faced by people from different sections of society.

“The Gandhi family stands by its word. A promise made by Rahul Gandhi is as good as a commitment written in golden letters. For us, his word is an instruction,” the Chief Minister said.

Labour Minister Vivek Venkataswamy also spoke on the occasion. Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka, Ministers Ponnam Prabhakar, Komatireddy Venkata Reddy, Ponguleti Srinivasa Reddy and TPCC president Mahesh Kumar Goud were present.

Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy plants a sapling to mark the foundation of PHFI’s campus in Hyderabad on Saturday. | Photo Credit: SIDDHANT THAKUR

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy assured the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) of the State government’s full support for establishing its Institute of Public Health Sciences (IPHS) Deemed-to-be University in Hyderabad, setting June 2, 2028, as the deadline for completing the proposed campus and promising assistance with land, funds, permissions and other requirements.

Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony and unveiling of the campus master plan on Saturday, Mr. Reddy said the government was committed to developing the institution into a world-class university that would contribute to public health education, research and healthcare in India and internationally.

He further added that the proposed university was not merely another educational institution but a project of global significance. Expressing confidence in its potential, he said he hoped that in the coming years, people would discuss the PHFI university alongside established institutions such as Harvard and Oxford.

The Chief Minister recalled how institutions such as the Indian School of Business (ISB) had contributed to Hyderabad’s emergence as an educational and knowledge hub. He said individuals who had established successful institutions had helped create a distinct identity for the city and that the PHFI university would add to this legacy.

PHFI Chairman Rajat Gupta said the university aspired to achieve excellence through world-class faculty, students, international collaborations and infrastructure.

PHFI IPHS Chancellor Dr. K. Srinath Reddy said PHFI aspired to become the world’s leading public health institution with the establishment of the university in Hyderabad. Dr. Reddy said the foundation’s work involved advancing multidisciplinary education and research through multi-sectoral implementation and multi-stakeholder engagement. The objective was to improve life expectancy, strengthen health systems, align policies across sectors with population health goals and encourage active community engagement.

Pro-Chancellor Sanjay Zodpey said the university was being conceived as a long-term institution that would serve generations of students, researchers, public health professionals and communities. He said the public health challenges of the 21st century required professionals with interdisciplinary perspectives, evidence-based knowledge and a commitment to equity and social impact.

Vice-Chancellor M. Vishnu Vardhana Rao outlined the university’s academic journey and expansion plans. The Indian Institute of Public Health Hyderabad was established in 2008 under the aegis of PHFI, with the objective of advancing public health through education, research and community engagement. The institution received recognition as a deemed-to-be university from the University Grants Commission in 2025, with Hyderabad as its main campus and Bengaluru as another campus, he said.

With the proposed campus and modern infrastructure, the institution plans to expand its academic offerings to at least six postgraduate programmes, two undergraduate programmes, PhD programmes and institute-level Master of Public Health programmes. It aims to build an academic community of approximately 2,500 students and research scholars over the next five years.

Dr. Rao said the university’s research priorities would include infectious diseases and pandemic preparedness, non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, One Health, mental health and disability. Digital health, artificial intelligence and data science would serve as cross-cutting areas across its research activities, he added.

items.title: Flights Between US and Japan Face Disruption After Air Traffic System Failure
items.summary: Flights between the United States and Japan face continued disruption after American aviation authorities restored air traffic operations following a nationwide communications failure on November 13 that grounded thousands of aircraft, triggered widespread cancellations and left airlines struggling to rebuild their schedules. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Flights Between US and Japan Face Disruption After Air Traffic System Failure
scraped.description: Flights between the United States and Japan face continued disruption after American aviation authorities restored air traffic operations following a nationwide communications failure on November 13 that grounded thousands of aircraft, triggered widespread cancellations and left airlines struggling to rebuild their schedules.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Flights Between US and Japan Face Disruption After Air Traffic System Failure
scraped.body_text:
Flights between the United States and Japan face continued disruption after American aviation authorities restored air traffic operations following a nationwide communications failure on November 13 that grounded thousands of aircraft, triggered widespread cancellations and left airlines struggling to rebuild their schedules.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted its nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, equivalent to 10:15 a.m. on Saturday, November 14, in Japan, after resolving a major telecommunications failure affecting air traffic control centers across the United States. However, officials warned that the consequences could continue for several days as airlines work to reposition aircraft, reorganize crews and accommodate stranded passengers. The shutdown, which lasted more than four hours, was the longest nationwide grounding of American air traffic since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Flight-tracking data showed thousands of cancellations and delays, with some estimates putting the number of canceled flights close to 10,000 by late Friday. Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and United Airlines were among the hardest-hit carriers. The disruption has implications for international travelers, particularly those flying between Japan and major American aviation hubs such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago and New York. Even after air traffic restrictions were lifted, aircraft and crews remained out of position, creating the possibility of further delays and cancellations on long-haul routes. Japan Airlines has reported delays affecting some international services, including flights to the United States and certain European destinations operating through American-controlled airspace. The disruption illustrates how a failure in one country's air traffic infrastructure can affect international airline networks far beyond its borders. For passengers traveling from Japan, the principal concern is the availability of aircraft and crews for scheduled departures. An aircraft delayed or grounded in the United States may be unable to operate its next scheduled service to Japan, potentially creating further disruptions to subsequent flights. Passengers connecting through American airports also face the possibility of missed onward flights and extended waiting times. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the immediate technical problem had been resolved and the air traffic system had been tested before operations resumed. Nevertheless, he cautioned that restoring normal schedules would be a gradual process rather than an immediate return to full service. According to Duffy, the failure began when switches and routers within the air traffic communications network became overloaded with data, producing inconsistencies in information transmitted between control facilities. Authorities imposed the nationwide ground stop as a precaution while engineers investigated the problem and worked to restore reliable communications. The Department of Homeland Security said there was no evidence that the disruption resulted from a cyberattack. Officials also rejected suggestions that the failure was connected to a separate global Microsoft outage, although the detailed technical investigation has yet to be completed. The incident has renewed concerns about the aging infrastructure supporting American aviation. Much of the country's air traffic control network relies on older communications equipment, and federal authorities have repeatedly warned that modernization is necessary to maintain reliability as air traffic volumes increase. Duffy called for approximately $50 billion in funding to replace outdated systems and prevent similar incidents. The administration has argued that incremental upgrades are insufficient to address the underlying weaknesses of the existing network. The shutdown comes ahead of the busy Thanksgiving travel period, when American airports traditionally experience some of their highest passenger volumes of the year. Airlines now face the challenge of clearing the backlog of stranded passengers while preparing for another surge in demand. For travelers between Japan and the United States, the restoration of air traffic operations represents an important step toward normal service, but the effects of the shutdown may continue as airlines recover from one of the most serious disruptions to American aviation in decades. Passengers scheduled to travel over the coming days are being advised to confirm their flight status directly with their airlines before departing for the airport, particularly when their journeys involve connections within the United States.
