items.title: Kyoko Koizumi to Plant 3,000 Trees in Mountains to Feed Bears
items.summary: Japanese singer and actress Kyoko Koizumi has launched a forest restoration initiative aimed at planting 3,000 acorn-producing trees in the mountains of northeastern Japan, hoping to create a richer habitat for bears and other wildlife following a sharp increase in bear attacks across the country. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Kyoko Koizumi to Plant 3,000 Trees in Mountains to Feed Bears
scraped.description: Japanese singer and actress Kyoko Koizumi has launched a forest restoration initiative aimed at planting 3,000 acorn-producing trees in the mountains of northeastern Japan, hoping to create a richer habitat for bears and other wildlife following a sharp increase in bear attacks across the country.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Kyoko Koizumi to Plant 3,000 Trees in Mountains to Feed Bears
scraped.body_text:
Japanese singer and actress Kyoko Koizumi has launched a forest restoration initiative aimed at planting 3,000 acorn-producing trees in the mountains of northeastern Japan, hoping to create a richer habitat for bears and other wildlife following a sharp increase in bear attacks across the country.

Koizumi, who turned 60 this year, completed a nationwide concert tour in May and is taking a break from performing for the remainder of the year. Rather than spending the entire period resting, she has turned her attention to environmental conservation, joining a long-term project to restore forests and provide food sources for wild animals. The initiative emerged from a discussion on a radio program about the growing number of encounters between humans and bears. With bear attacks reaching record levels, Koizumi questioned whether a shortage of acorns and other natural food sources was forcing the animals to descend from the mountains into populated areas. She was particularly troubled by reports that some bears killed after entering residential areas had almost no body fat, suggesting they had been struggling to find enough food. Koizumi proposed planting trees that produce nuts and other food in mountainous areas, hoping that animals would have less reason to venture into towns and villages. "If there were trees bearing fruit that animals could eat higher up in the mountains, perhaps they wouldn't need to come down," she said. The idea developed into the Forest of Tomorrow Project, which aims to plant 3,000 acorn-producing trees and nurture them into a healthy, sustainable forest over the coming decades. Koizumi encouraged fans to support the project during her nationwide concert tour. In an unusual departure from customary entertainment industry practices, she declined all flowers and gifts from concertgoers, instead asking them to contribute to the forest restoration effort. Although she appreciated receiving flowers and presents, Koizumi had long felt uncomfortable about being unable to take everything home or make full use of the gifts. By redirecting that generosity toward environmental conservation, she hoped to turn the support of her fans into something that would benefit future generations. The appeal attracted donations from more than 3,400 people, providing support for the planting initiative. Koizumi visited Mount Kurikoma in the Tohoku region in October to take part in the planting work herself. Heavy rain leading up to the event had left the mountainous terrain muddy and slippery. Participants had to climb a steep slope extending about 50 meters, where losing their footing could easily result in a fall. Despite the difficult conditions, Koizumi joined volunteers in digging holes, planting saplings and installing protective shelters around the young trees to prevent deer and other animals from eating them. The work proved considerably more physically demanding than she had anticipated, with participants struggling to maintain their footing while clearing obstacles and finding suitable locations for each sapling. During a lunch break, Koizumi joked that she could already tell her muscles would be aching the following day. One of the project's central members, Hiroshi Oi, who has observed changes in the mountain environment for nearly 30 years, explained that restoring a healthy forest requires patience and sustained human involvement. The surrounding woodland has gradually become darker and less hospitable, highlighting the importance of carefully managing forest growth and maintaining an environment where a variety of trees and plants can thrive. According to Oi, newly planted trees will take approximately eight to 10 years before they begin producing acorns, while developing a mature, healthy forest will require several more decades. "Trees don't grow in one or two years. It takes 50 or 60 years," Oi said, emphasizing that people must take responsibility for nurturing the forest over the long term. After approximately four hours of work, Koizumi's team had planted around 50 saplings, while participants across the site planted approximately 500 trees in total. Koizumi said she felt a personal responsibility to participate directly because so many people had contributed money to the project. "I felt that just talking about it wasn't enough. Since everyone had entrusted us with their support, I needed to experience planting the trees myself," she said. Her involvement extends beyond the initial planting. Young trees require regular maintenance, including grass cutting, weeding and other protective measures to ensure they survive and grow. Koizumi has expressed her intention to return to the forest periodically to help maintain the trees and monitor their development. The project is intended not simply as a short-term response to bear attacks but as an investment in the environment over the next half-century. Koizumi acknowledged that environmental problems can sometimes appear overwhelming, with people suggesting that meaningful action is already too late. However, she argued that giving up would accomplish nothing and that even modest individual efforts could become significant when combined. "It's easy to say that we're already too late or that nothing can be done," she said. "But I hope we can continue bringing together these small efforts and keep working toward a better future without giving up." Koizumi also recognized that she may never see the forest reach full maturity. "By the time this becomes a truly rich forest, I probably won't be here anymore," she said. "But I hope we can pass these feelings on to the younger generations and children who come after us, and entrust the future to them." While the planting initiative was inspired by the increasing frequency of bear attacks, its broader objective is to restore a more diverse natural environment where wildlife can find food and shelter without relying on human settlements. The project also reflects a growing recognition that forest conservation requires continued management rather than simply planting trees and leaving them to grow. For Koizumi, the work represents a shift from expressing concern about environmental problems to becoming directly involved in finding solutions, with the hope that the forest planted today will provide lasting benefits for wildlife and future generations. items.title: Nara's Famous Deer Turn Dangerous as Tourists
items.summary: The number of people taken to hospital after being injured by deer in and around Nara Park has reached a record high in 2026, with foreign tourists accounting for more than 70% of cases, prompting warnings about the dangers of approaching the wild animals during their autumn mating season. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Nara
scraped.description: The number of people taken to hospital after being injured by deer in and around Nara Park has reached a record high in 2026, with foreign tourists accounting for more than 70% of cases, prompting warnings about the dangers of approaching the wild animals during their autumn mating season.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Nara's Famous Deer Turn Dangerous as Tourists
scraped.body_text:
NARA - The number of people taken to hospital after being injured by deer in and around Nara Park has reached a record high in 2026, with foreign tourists accounting for more than 70% of cases, prompting warnings about the dangers of approaching the wild animals during their autumn mating season.

Footage filmed at Nara Park in September showed a deer suddenly charging at a woman who had approached it, knocking her to the ground before repeatedly headbutting her. The incident highlights growing safety concerns at one of Japan's most popular tourist attractions, where large numbers of visitors have gathered ahead of the peak autumn foliage season. Nara Park is home to wild deer that are believed to have inhabited the area for more than 1,300 years and are designated as a national natural monument. Their population has increased every year for the past five years, reaching approximately 1,687 animals as of July 2026. According to Nara City Hospital, the number of people transported by ambulance after suffering deer-related injuries has also been rising over the past five years, reaching a record 51 as of November 5. Foreign tourists accounted for more than 70% of those brought to the hospital, with the growing number of international visitors identified as one factor behind the increase in injuries. Yasuhiro Nakanishi, vice chairman of the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation, said many foreign visitors mistakenly believe the park is a place where they can freely approach and interact with the animals. "Some people think this is an area where they can interact with the deer, but that's not quite right. These are wild animals," Nakanishi said. Pointing to a young male deer, he recalled a serious incident involving a foreign child last year. "This is a young male. Last year, its antler pierced the chest of a child from overseas." Nakanishi warned that autumn is particularly dangerous because it coincides with the mating season for male deer, when they become more aggressive and sensitive to people approaching them. "During autumn, the males become more emotional. If people get too close or force themselves toward the deer, the animals may attack," he said. To reduce the risk of injuries, the foundation has been cutting the antlers of male deer in the park. Deer antlers begin growing around spring and become large and hard by autumn, making them potentially dangerous weapons if left untrimmed. Nakanishi explained that the antlers of two deer observed in the park had been removed specifically to prevent accidents. Medical professionals have also warned that antler injuries can be extremely serious. Ryusuke Kawaguchi, a doctor at Nara City Hospital, said deer antlers can cause deep penetrating wounds and potentially life-threatening bleeding. "Deer antlers can cut like knives. If they penetrate a major blood vessel, there is a risk of severe bleeding," Kawaguchi said. In response to the growing number of injuries, the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation carried out its annual antler-cutting operations earlier than usual in 2026. Meanwhile, the expanding deer population has created additional problems beyond Nara Park, with increasing reports of animals wandering into nearby residential neighborhoods. Deer have even entered the Nara Prefectural Government building. According to a prefectural official, a deer walked into the government offices through an automatic door in late September, prompting authorities to replace the entrance mechanism with a push-button system to prevent further intrusions. The presence of deer outside the park remains a concern. During a visit to the area near the prefectural government offices on November 12, male deer were observed fighting with each other. The Nara Deer Preservation Foundation is urging visitors to exercise particular caution during the current mating season, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a safe distance from the animals rather than attempting to approach or touch them. While Nara's deer remain a major attraction for domestic and international tourists, officials stress that they are wild animals whose behavior can become unpredictable, particularly during autumn.

Foreign tourists accounted for more than 70% of those brought to the hospital, with the growing number of international visitors identified as one factor behind the increase in injuries.

Yasuhiro Nakanishi, vice chairman of the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation, said many foreign visitors mistakenly believe the park is a place where they can freely approach and interact with the animals.

"Some people think this is an area where they can interact with the deer, but that's not quite right. These are wild animals," Nakanishi said.

Pointing to a young male deer, he recalled a serious incident involving a foreign child last year. "This is a young male. Last year, its antler pierced the chest of a child from overseas."

Nakanishi warned that autumn is particularly dangerous because it coincides with the mating season for male deer, when they become more aggressive and sensitive to people approaching them.

"During autumn, the males become more emotional. If people get too close or force themselves toward the deer, the animals may attack," he said.

To reduce the risk of injuries, the foundation has been cutting the antlers of male deer in the park.

Deer antlers begin growing around spring and become large and hard by autumn, making them potentially dangerous weapons if left untrimmed.

Nakanishi explained that the antlers of two deer observed in the park had been removed specifically to prevent accidents.

Medical professionals have also warned that antler injuries can be extremely serious.

Ryusuke Kawaguchi, a doctor at Nara City Hospital, said deer antlers can cause deep penetrating wounds and potentially life-threatening bleeding.

"Deer antlers can cut like knives. If they penetrate a major blood vessel, there is a risk of severe bleeding," Kawaguchi said.

In response to the growing number of injuries, the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation carried out its annual antler-cutting operations earlier than usual in 2026.

Meanwhile, the expanding deer population has created additional problems beyond Nara Park, with increasing reports of animals wandering into nearby residential neighborhoods.

Deer have even entered the Nara Prefectural Government building.

According to a prefectural official, a deer walked into the government offices through an automatic door in late September, prompting authorities to replace the entrance mechanism with a push-button system to prevent further intrusions.

The presence of deer outside the park remains a concern. During a visit to the area near the prefectural government offices on November 12, male deer were observed fighting with each other.

The Nara Deer Preservation Foundation is urging visitors to exercise particular caution during the current mating season, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a safe distance from the animals rather than attempting to approach or touch them.

While Nara's deer remain a major attraction for domestic and international tourists, officials stress that they are wild animals whose behavior can become unpredictable, particularly during autumn.

Source: FNN

Flights between the United States and Japan face continued disruption after American aviation authorities restored air traffic operations following a nationwide communications failure on November 13 that grounded thousands of aircraft, triggered widespread cancellations and left airlines struggling to rebuild their schedules.

The number of people taken to hospital after being injured by deer in and around Nara Park has reached a record high in 2026, with foreign tourists accounting for more than 70% of cases, prompting warnings about the dangers of approaching the wild animals during their autumn mating season.

A shrine in Gunma Prefecture has used a high-pressure cleaning drone to wash Japan's largest statue of Daikoku, cutting a maintenance job that previously took two to three weeks to just one day while reducing costs to around one-tenth of the conventional method.

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 12 following allegations involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence has raised concerns in Japan over the potential impact on semiconductor investment, financial markets and the yen, as uncertainty surrounding the American AI chipmaker threatens to disrupt the global technology industry.

Japan launched a new national disaster management agency on November 2nd to strengthen its response to major emergencies, just days before a powerful earthquake struck Aichi Prefecture, injuring 24 people and renewing concerns over the possibility of a catastrophic Nankai Trough earthquake.

Visitors flocking to a popular autumn foliage destination in Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward have sparked growing concerns among residents, with photographers repeatedly stepping into the middle of busy roads to capture pictures and drivers illegally parking near bus stops and residential streets.

Universal Studios Japan (USJ) is launching its winter season events on November 13, featuring one of the largest food festivals in the park's history, with more than twice as many menu items as last year and opportunities for visitors to dine alongside popular characters.

Tokyo's Toshima Ward announced on November 11th plans to impose administrative penalties of up to 20,000 yen for street smoking and littering, extending its smoking ban to heated tobacco products as complaints about public smoking and illegal dumping continue to rise.

The ginkgo-lined avenue at Hiroshima Shudo University in Hiroshima City has reached its peak autumn color, transforming the campus into a golden landscape as trees display their brilliant yellow leaves.

A woman was seriously injured in a wild boar attack in Nishinomiya, Hyogo Prefecture, as sightings of unusually large boars increase across the Kansai region, with some weighing nearly 150 kilograms and capable of running at speeds of 45 kilometers per hour.

Arriving in Japan after a long-haul flight is so exciting. But dragging a 25kg suitcase through a busy train station is less so.

Northern Japan experienced record-breaking cold on the morning of November 11th, with temperatures plunging to minus 20.2 degrees Celsius in Horokanai, Hokkaido, marking the first time in Japan's recorded history that temperatures have fallen below minus 20 degrees during the first half of November.

East Japan Railway (JR East) announced on November 10th that it will introduce touch-free ticket gates at 40 stations, including every station on Tokyo's Yamanote Line, from spring 2028, allowing passengers using Mobile Suica to pass through without taking their smartphones out of their pockets or bags.

scraped.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
scraped.description: I deliberately bet like a problem gambler to test the company’s user safety net. After the investigation went viral, DraftKings downplayed my reporting, closed my account — and sent me a check for 94 cents.
scraped.author: Jake Pearson
scraped.h1: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

The Big Gamble

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. This story first ran in Dispatches, our weekly newsletter from our reporters about their recent investigations. Sign up to receive stories like this one in your inbox every Saturday.

Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news.

“Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”

I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said?

In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler , recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists.

As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses.

If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files.

The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”

So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.

In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X .)

So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly?

DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks.

The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story.

Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action . In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.

On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact .

That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers.

I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry.

In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here . If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and [email protected] .

I’m an investigative reporter covering the intersection of business and government.

scraped.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
scraped.description: The complaint follows a ProPublica investigation that found Alicia Jackson, a high-ranking federal health official, publicly endorsed a change in hormone therapy policy while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.
scraped.author: Corey G. Johnson and Brandon Roberts
scraped.h1: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”

Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.

In a letter to the department’s inspector general , the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.

Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.

In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.

At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures .

It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.

Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.

The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.

“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.

The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.

ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson . The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.

Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.

The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.

Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.

HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote . President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.

ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database , a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

I am a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter at ProPublica.

I welcome tips about ethical conflicts or misdeeds inside the federal bureaucracy. I’m interested in policies, contracts and regulatory issues that affect people’s lives. If you have any insights, please reach out via email or Signal.

I’m a journalist using data and code to hold power to account.

If you have a tip about a dataset, a use of technology or a complicated government process, reach out.

During his congressional campaign, Forstag, 32, who as a leader in the National Federation of […] Former smokejumper Sam Forstag heads to Congress with plans to rebuild federal land management agencies, strengthen wildfire prep...

scraped.title: A Wildland Firefighter Ends Montana Democrats’ Three-Decade Drought in the US House - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Former smokejumper Sam Forstag heads to Congress with plans to rebuild federal land management agencies, strengthen wildfire preparedness and protect Montana’s public lands.
scraped.author: By Mosabber Hossain
scraped.h1: A Wildland Firefighter Ends Montana Democrats’ Three-Decade Drought in the US House
scraped.body_text:
For three decades, Montana voters had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. House of Representatives. That changed earlier this month when Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, defeated Republican Aaron Flint in Montana’s 1st Congressional District.

During his congressional campaign , Forstag, 32, who as a leader in the National Federation of Federal Employees represented some 800 U.S. Forest Service workers in the Lolo, Bitterroot and Gallatin national forests, promised to strengthen federal land management agencies and improve wildfire preparedness.

In an interview with The Wild Idea Podcas t before the election, Forstag called for simplifying the permitting process for prescribed burns and increasing wildland firefighters’ base pay to reduce their dependence on overtime. He argued that investing in measures such as prescribed burning and forest thinning could reduce the risk of destructive wildfires and save taxpayers money. He also proposed pursuing standalone legislation to fund those efforts.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Forstag has also expressed support for the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act , which would strengthen workers’ rights to form unions and bargain collectively. Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill in the House in March 2025, with a companion bill introduced by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. The legislation remains in committee and has not passed either chamber of Congress.

In a post-election email to supporters, Forstag outlined four priorities for his first term in Congress: affordable housing, healthcare, reducing the cost of living and campaign finance reform. Although wildfire preparedness and Forest Service staffing were central to his campaign, neither appeared among the four priorities listed in that email. But, in a separate message thanking supporters, Forstag reaffirmed his commitment to protecting Montana’s wild places for future generations.

Forstag has already begun challenging the Trump administration’s plans for federal public lands. In a Facebook video posted Nov. 12 from the U.S. Capitol, he criticized a new Interior Department proposal to reduce federal land holdings.

“They’re trying to sell off our public lands, but we won’t let them,” Forstag said. He also said he had reached out to Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, whom he is replacing, hoping the outgoing congressman would oppose any effort to sell federal lands. Zinke’s office separately confirmed his opposition to federal land sales and transfers.

Forstag has also expressed interest in working with Republican Rep. Troy Downing, who represents eastern Montana. In a Facebook post, on Nov. 11, Forstag identified protecting public lands as an area where the two lawmakers could find common ground, despite their political differences. “”We can get so much more done for Montana when we work together in Congress,” he wrote.

Forstag said he would seek a position on the House Natural Resources Committee after taking office in January, giving him an opportunity to influence federal land policy. The Interior Department’s five-year strategic plan proposes selling some federal lands to states, tribes and local governments, although officials have not identified specific parcels. Whether Forstag can influence the administration’s plans will depend partly on congressional cooperation and the legal limits on such sales.

During freshman orientation in Washington, D.C. last week, Forstag said he was seeking congressional committee assignments that would give western Montana a stronger voice on housing and rebuilding federal public lands agencies. He also said he planned to join both the moderate Blue Dog Coalition and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, hoping to work across different wings of the Democratic Party to advance economic policies that benefit working people.

In a separate Facebook post , Forstag congratulated the newly elected members of Montana’s American Indian Caucus, which will have a record 14 Native American lawmakers into the state’s 2027 legislative session, and expressed support for tribal sovereignty, treaty rights, and Tribal water and land rights. He said the caucus would be an important voice for Native communities in the state Legislature.

Forstag’s victory marks a historic political shift in Montana, where Democrats have not won a U.S. House election since 1994 . His win also brings a former firefighter to Washington at a time when federal workforce cuts have raised concerns about wildfire preparedness, Forest Service staffing and public lands management. During his campaign, Forstag pledged to restore staffing at federal land management agencies and expand fuels reduction crews as well as simplify the permitting process for prescribed burns and increase the use of such treatments to prevent costly wildfires.

While supporters hope his experience will help address those challenges, political observers caution that turning campaign promises into federal policy will not be easy for a first-term congressman.

“Forstag by himself cannot do much, of course,” said University of Montana political scientist Abhishek Chatterjee .

His ability to influence federal policy will depend on cooperation with other lawmakers, said Chatterjee. Other newly elected lawmakers may share Forstag’s goals to increase funding for wildfire prevention, he added, but presidential veto power and Senate filibusters could limit such efforts.

Chatterjee also expects Forstag to be a part of increased congressional opposition to certain proposals involving public land swaps or transferring federal lands to state governments.

The Forstag campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

According to unofficial results from the Montana Secretary of State, Forstag received 132,003 votes, or 50.34 percent, compared with Flint’s 122,694 votes, or 46.79 percent. Libertarian Nick Sheedy received 7,522 votes.

Forstag’s victory ends a three-decade absence of Democrats from Montana’s U.S. House delegation. Pat Williams , the last Democrat elected to Montana’s U.S. House delegation, retired in 1996.

County-level election results show that Forstag received strong support in several of western Montana’s larger population centers.

In Missoula County, he received 41,232 votes, or 68.24 percent; in Gallatin County, which includes Bozeman, he took 59.42 percent: and in Silver Bow County he garnered 61.55 percent.

Together, Missoula and Gallatin counties gave Forstag a combined advantage of 35,226 votes, helping him overcome Flint’s leads in several rural counties of the district.

Forstag’s personality may have contributed to his success, said Bill Hallinan, a member of Montana Conservation Elders and Wild Montana who noted that he was not speaking on behalf of either organization.

Hallinan described Forstag as “sincere and relatable” and suggested that his campaign may have been better organized in larger cities. Forstag may have better addressed economic concerns that influenced voters, he suggested, while Flint presented himself as a loyal supporter of President Donald Trump.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Several factors may have contributed to Forstag’s victory, Chatterjee said, including his background as a wildland firefighter and union leader, federal workforce cuts under the Trump administration and broader dissatisfaction with the administration’s policies and economic conditions.

“Gas prices in particular would have played a role,” Chatterjee said in an email to Inside Climate News.

Before entering politics, Forstag worked as a wildland firefighter with the U.S. Forest Service, including as a smokejumper, parachuting into remote areas to fight wildfires. He also represented workers in the National Federation of Federal Employees.

That experience became central to his campaign as it focused on protecting federal employees and challenging workforce reductions under the Trump administration.

Forstag’s victory has raised expectations among environmental advocates who believe his firsthand experience could help bring attention to the challenges facing federal land management agencies.

His campaign platform outlines several proposals to strengthen wildfire protection, protect federal jobs and improve public lands management. He has pledged to expand federal land management agencies, rather than just return them to the staffing levels they had prior to the second Trump administration’s cuts, and increase funding for forest management and operations to reduce loads of vegetation that can fuel severe wildfires, creating more jobs while shifting resources toward wildfire prevention. He also supports responsible timber harvesting and federal grants to modernize Montana’s timber mills, while opposing the use of emergency authorizations and fast-track programs to bypass environmental protections in forest management projects. Forstag’s platform calls for ending the use of emergency authorizations and fast-track programs that bypass environmental protections, while improving the review process for forest management projects.

Amy Cilimburg , executive director of Climate Smart Missoula, a nonprofit organization, said Montana could benefit from having a representative who understands wildfire response and the importance of federal agencies.

“Congress has the power of the purse, and federal agencies, including scientific bodies, need to be consistently staffed and funded,” Cilimburg said in an email. “The needed response to climate risks like reduced snowpack, hotter temperatures, longer fire seasons, and drought is to lean into credible science and rebuild our public agencies and work forces,” she said.

Hallinan also hopes Forstag will support stronger Forest Service staffing and continued federal grants for wildfire preparedness and education.

“More forest service staff means more hands to organize, assist, coordinate and administrate,” Hallinan said.

He emphasized the importance of protecting communities in the wildland-urban interface, where homes and developed areas meet flammable forests and open spaces.

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. scraped.title: An Obscure Utility Calculation Is Putting a Thumb on the Scale for Gas in Georgia - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: As Georgia Power decides on its next generation of grid suppliers, a little-known piece of math may be giving the edge to fossil fuel projects.
scraped.author: By Ryan Krugman
scraped.h1: An Obscure Utility Calculation Is Putting a Thumb on the Scale for Gas in Georgia
scraped.body_text:
The growth of data centers and rapid electrification is driving Georgia Power toward another major expansion of its electric grid. The state’s largest utility is preparing to add between 2,000 and 6,000 megawatts of new capacity to its grid for 2032 and 2033. The utility is considering a mix of resources, including natural gas and battery storage, to meet its future electricity needs.

But how much each resource counts toward that expansion depends on a calculation called Effective Load Carrying Capability, or ELCC. It is the “critical renewable energy concept you’ve never heard of,” according to the Union of Concerned Scientists . And the way Georgia Power is using that calculation in its latest effort to secure new power generation is drawing scrutiny from renewable energy advocates across the state.

Prior to the rise of renewable energy, determining how much capacity a new power project added to the grid was relatively simple. Utilities projected peak electricity demand and ensured they had enough power plants available to meet it.

But because renewable resources like solar and wind are variable, planning grid expansions has become more complex. The sun is not always shining and the wind is not always blowing, making it more difficult to determine how much reliable capacity renewable projects actually add to the grid.

ELCC is a way of measuring how much capacity a power resource can reliably contribute to the grid. A resource with a 100 percent ELCC can be counted on for its full capacity when determining how much electricity the grid can reliably support. Natural gas typically has an ELCC near 60 to 80 percent, while solar and wind projects without battery storage can have ELCCs between 4 to 40 percent. With batteries, renewables can have ELCCs around 95 percent, but that value can fall as more batteries are added to the grid.

In its previous planning, Georgia Power assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity, 75 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts and 50 percent for the next 3,000 megawatts. As more batteries are added, they become less valuable during peak demand because they increasingly compete to provide power at the same time. Based on the amount of battery storage on the grid and planned for the future, the utility’s previous calculations suggest the current ELCC should be set at around 75 percent. The latest procurement, however, uses a much lower figure.

According to Bob Sherrier, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center and the Advanced Power Alliance, which both testified about the issue to Georgia regulators, Georgia Power is now using an ELCC of just 20 percent for battery storage in its upcoming procurement. That means a 1,000-megawatt battery project would count for just 200 megawatts toward the utility’s capacity needs. A 1,000-megawatt natural gas plant with an 80 percent ELCC, by comparison, would count for 800 megawatts. ELCC calculations are based on modeling under different conditions and assumptions. Georgia Power did not provide details on the calculations but did tell Inside Climate News they have been consistent and are committed to accurate evaluations of all resources. In response to additional questions about the request for proposal, a company representative said “the company is in the middle of several ongoing resource procurements and cannot comment on specifics of requests for proposals.”

The steep drop in ELCC from Georgia Power’s previous calculations could put battery storage at a disadvantage as the utility evaluates projects for its planned 2,000 to 6,000-megawatt expansion, Sherrier said. With a lower ELCC, developers would need to build more battery capacity to earn the same capacity credit as a natural gas project.

He called the change a “thumb on the scale for gas,” arguing that it makes battery storage artificially less valuable in the procurement.

“Batteries are going to look significantly more expensive than gas,” Sherrier said. “We know that is not the case anymore.”

Recent cost estimates show that utility-scale solar can be cheaper than new natural gas generation. Pairing solar with battery storage raises the cost, but can still make it competitive with gas while allowing electricity to be stored for use when it is needed.

If the ELCC for batteries remains unchanged, Sherrier fears the new expansion could once again be dominated by natural gas.

For its 2029-2031 expansion, Georgia Power planned nearly 10,000 megawatts of new capacity, including roughly 6,000 megawatts from natural gas, with the remainder coming from solar and battery projects. At the time of planning in 2024, the utility’s planning assigned battery storage an ELCC of 95 percent for its first 3,000 megawatts of capacity.

More than 6,000 megawatts of natural gas capacity, if operated at full output year-round, could produce an estimated 20 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, roughly the same emissions as 4 million cars.

If the 2032-2033 procurement goes the way Sherrier expects, Georgia Power could lock in millions more tons of annual emissions.

Georgia Power is reviewing proposals for its 2032-2033 expansion, with battery storage still assigned an ELCC of 20 percent. But the issue is not settled. The utility and regulators are expected to discuss which projects to move forward with early next year.

According to Sherrier, however, some of the damage may already be done. By assigning batteries a lower capacity value, Georgia Power may have discouraged battery developers from submitting proposals in the first place. The impact of the ELCC calculation will become clearer when the utility’s selected projects are submitted for regulatory approval in mid-2027.

If the issue is not resolved in this procurement, SELC and the Advanced Power Alliance plans to push for a higher ELCC in the next round of expansion planning, which is expected to begin in 2028.

scraped.description: A Texas district known for its petrochemical facilities is getting a representative with a background in environmental health.
scraped.author: By Lauren Nutall
scraped.h1: A Clean Air Advocate Will Represent Part of America’s Oil Capital in Congress
scraped.body_text:
Leticia Gutierrez’s upset victory in a Houston-area congressional district means an environmental-health advocate will represent part of the country’s oil capital, and environmental groups say that could help communities choked for years by petrochemical pollution.

Gutierrez, who spent more than a decade as Air Alliance Houston’s government relations director, pledged to support policies to improve air quality and regulate AI data centers’ water consumption and electricity usage. The Democrat beat a vastly better-funded former oil-industry executive whose contributors included petrochemical companies and Elon Musk.

“There is now, dare I say it, a green Houston congressional contingent,” said Jennifer Hadayia, executive director of Air Alliance Houston. She counts Reps. Christian Menefee, Sylvia Garcia and Lizzie Fletcher, all of whom won re-election in their Houston-area districts, among that group.

“We know that they understand Houston is the energy capital of the world,” Hadayia said. “That also means we’re the pollution capital of the world, and I feel very confident that that group together is going to advocate for our best interests when it comes to things like efforts by the current EPA, [which] has been stripping the community of its rights to weigh in on pollution decisions.”

Gutierrez’s 9th Congressional District was among those redrawn by Texas Republicans in 2025 in an unsuccessful effort to maintain the party’s control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Instead, the blue-wave election last week swept numerous Republicans out of office in Texas and nationwide.

The redrawn district includes parts of Harris County and the Houston Ship Channel, a major source of pollution lined with hundreds of petrochemical facilities . During the campaign, Gutierrez pointed to the health consequences of living near those facilities. The Texas Department of State Health Services, studying part of east Harris County near the ship channel and other pollution sources, found higher-than-expected rates of certain cancers in 2015, and a 2025 update still found notably higher rates.

Advocates were heartened by her election because they say people in the region need representatives pushing for pollution control.

“I think a really big issue for Harris County and for District 9 is how we’re treating our national emission standards for hazardous air pollutants,” said Clara Goodwin, staff attorney at the Environmental Integrity Project.

Last year, the Trump administration invited companies to email requests for “ presidential exemptions ” to a number of rules designed to reduce Americans’ exposure to air pollution hazards, including cancer-causing chemicals. Goodwin estimated that 30 facilities in the district have sought such exemptions.

Hazardous material dredged from the Houston Ship Channel and moved to dump sites in the region also pose risks to residents in parts of Gutierrez’s district. In 2024, sample testing of dredge material from part of a channel expansion that began in 2022 found toxic substances, including high levels of cancer-causing arsenic . Despite this finding, current U.S. Environmental Protection Agency policy does not treat dredge material from ship channel expansions as dangerous, Goodwin said.

Gutierrez will join a Congress in January newly under Democratic control. New laws controlling pollution may be impossible for the next two years—President Donald Trump can veto them—but Hadayia said there will still be opportunities to act. The major rollbacks of EPA rules that began last year are an environmental injustice, because the harms fall unequally across the country, she added.

Democrats “can hold ethics investigations and expose some of the corruption that’s going on, including the destruction of the Environmental Protection Agency by the Trump administration,” said Josiah Rector, an associate professor and urban environmental historian at the University of Houston.

He also thinks there’s room for action on tax breaks for petrochemical companies along the Houston Ship Channel that contribute to local air pollution. Rector said those policies have left school districts and other public entities with inadequate funding while people, many of them lower income, pay with their health.

“Now with the defeat of [Gov.] Greg Abbott and the GOP in Texas, there’s a real opportunity for Democrats, both in the congressional delegation representing Harris County but also in the Texas state Legislature, to start phasing out these tax breaks for corporate polluters to incentivize renewable energy,” he said.

Some advocates are tempering their expectations about how quickly Gutierrez can act on her campaign promises.

“Obviously, she’ll be a freshman,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas, “and it’s difficult to be able to immediately have an impact when you’re a freshman, but I think I’m excited to see what committee she gets appointed to and what she does to hold the EPA’s feet to the fire.”
