scraped.title: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
scraped.description: A wildfire exposure study in Hawaiʻi created a new blueprint for public health research and support after disasters — but funding was drying up. Could the organizers keep it afloat?
scraped.author: Keerti Gopal
scraped.h1: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.

This one felt different.

Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.

A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests, and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

On August 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents, and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.

Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.

Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support, and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.

The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain — grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.

Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.

Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.

At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height, and weight. A mental health screener.

At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.

“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.

He was determined to make that happen.

The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.

The building — run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend — sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.

The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.

Lisa Panis, a participant in the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, has struggled with her mental and physical health since the fires, and her family is still in temporary housing. Keerti Gopal​​

Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.

MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.

Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires:12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“We tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”

“Are you still doing that, or pau ?” Maunakea asked.

“ Pau ,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

The Panis siblings’ father is descended from Filipino immigrants who came to the island to work on the sugar plantations more than a century ago, during a period when American and European companies brought indentured laborers from the Philippines to work under brutal conditions for extremely low pay. The plantations, established before Hawaiʻi’s illegal annexation by the United States and continuing another century after, sucked water out of Lahaina’s once green and fertile hills.

That set the stage for modern-day wildfire risks, now worsened by climate change, and cemented a pattern of local disenfranchisement that continued as the tourism industry took hold.

For years, the Panises had experienced the harder realities of life in Lahaina, like gentrification and unstable housing and employment. On the day of the fires, Nilsson was meant to fly back from Las Vegas to spread the ashes of two siblings who had passed away just weeks apart that spring. Lisa was living with an aunt whose home would not survive. She remembers standing on the field next to the post office where she and her brothers played football as kids, watching as flames engulfed the town above and below her.

After they finished checking into the study, the Panis siblings moved through the stations, a sort of medical assembly line: urine samples, then blood tests, then blood pressure, then spitting into a tube. A few feet away, Juarez coached another participant on how to blow into a spirometer to test lung function.

“ Sigue, sigue, sigue ,” he said, reminding the man to keep breathing out. Throughout the day Juarez greeted Spanish-speaking participants, acting as one of a handful of interpreters who walked people through the study’s tests in English, Spanish, and Tagalog.

Juarez was pulled into Maui’s recovery because of his connections to Lahaina’s abundant immigrant community. One-third of Lahaina residents were born outside the U.S., many in Asia or Latin America. Juarez moved from Mexico to Houston for a doctorate at Rice University, then to Oʻahu for a job at the University of Hawaiʻi. There, he met Maunakea, and as neighbors in the university’s faculty housing, they fell in love.

When they met, Juarez’s research was focused on social networks and Maunakea’s on health disparities in disease. After the fires, Maunakea was drawn to Maui by his connections with people working to address the disproportionate public health burdens faced by Native Hawaiians across the islands. Although he lives on Oʻahu, his great-grandmother, a Native Hawaiian healer, was born in Kula, an upcountry Maui community that was also badly impacted by the 2023 fires.

He and Juarez met with community leaders and healthcare workers on Maui soon after the fires. They became part of the MauiWES advisory board, consulting on design and implementation. For many study participants, that grounding made a big difference.

Mikey Burke, a Native Hawaiian mother of four who grew up in West Maui, remembers an influx of mental health practitioners from the continent who swarmed to Maui after the fires. They roamed the lobbies of hotels where she and other displaced families were sheltered. But though they were well-intentioned, they felt largely unapproachable. She gravitated toward local organizations like Maui Medic Healers Hui, which was working with MauiWES. It was something in their mannerisms, the way they spoke to her, the normalcy and familiarity they offered.

In the months after they lost their home, Burke, her husband Rob, and their four young sons were shuttled between temporary shelters, family homes, and rental properties. She could see that her twin boys, just 8 years old when the fires hit, were struggling. But it wasn’t until they got screened by MauiWES that addressing their mental health shot to the top of her lengthy to-do list. The study team told her that both boys were showing serious signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and got them connected with a free therapist right away.

The Burkes aren’t an anomaly. The study found widespread emotional distress and trauma in adults and children, and connected many with therapists.

During a weekend collection event in May, the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center was bustling with families, healthcare workers, and researchers. MauiWES has seen 2,500 participants in three years. Keerti Gopal​

On an island with a severe shortage of physicians, MauiWES was also most early participants’ first time seeing a doctor after the fires. Over the past three years, the team made some big saves.

In August 2024, one year after the fires, a former trauma nurse named Amy Jackson had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t registering on MauiWES’ testing system. The team urged her to go to the emergency room immediately. Jackson had signed up for the study because the cash would be a good birthday present for her daughter. If it wasn’t for that, she wouldn’t have gotten checked out at all.

At the hospital, she remembers a doctor telling her he was amazed she was still alive. She was admitted and treated, and she credits MauiWES with saving her life.

In February 2024, another participant presented with symptoms suggesting a serious lung infection. Volunteer physicians were concerned and said she needed medical attention right away. But she was an undocumented immigrant and one of the 10 percent of study participants who had both lost their jobs in the fire and weren’t eligible for state insurance.

Juarez coordinated with Roots Reborn — a local organization supporting Maui’s immigrant community — and reached out the next day to ask an insurer with a charitable health coverage program to consider an emergency enrollment.

She got the insurance and then the treatment she needed. She’s one of more than 200 participants Juarez estimates have been connected with private insurance via Kaiser Permanente because of interventions from MauiWES and Roots Reborn. He was happy to see her now, in good spirits and good health, coming in for her follow-up at the May collection event. He thought the immigrant population had the most to lose from the study ending.

The team still had so much to do.

After her lung test, Lisa Panis stood underneath the stain on the lobby’s ceiling and waited for her brother. The Panis siblings stay strong for one another. But she’s experienced depression since the fires, like many other survivors, and her tests revealed elevated levels of several toxic metals in her body.

In their first, smallest cohort, about six months after the fires, Juarez, Maunakea, and their colleagues found that about half of study participants were experiencing breathing problems that suggested ongoing, residual impacts from wildfire smoke. They’ve also found that poor lung function was linked to elevated levels of heavy metals in participants’ urine, including some of the same metals the health department found in the burn zone.

After looking at so many test results, Maunakea can guess with considerable accuracy what neighborhood a participant lives in just by seeing the distribution of metals in their body. Some of that contamination may predate the fires. But the health implications are the same.

Before Nilsson Panis left for the day, Juarez gave him a T-shirt with the MauiWES logo — a sun rising behind the island — and a hundred-dollar bill. Then he ushered him over to the front desk, where a case manager who works for the Department of Health was waiting.

She asked Nilsson if there was anything he might need help with.

He paused for a moment before answering. Maybe some assistance with food, he said. He also asked about opportunities to volunteer and help other survivors.

The case manager took down his email.

The next day Maunakea supervised a group of staff and volunteers administering lung function tests. A participant wearing a neon-yellow baseball hat and flower-patterned shorts walked in and took a seat.

“It’s unfortunate that you guys didn’t get more additional funding from the legislative session this time,” Ekolu Lindsey said to Maunakea as he took a break from breathing hard into a plastic mouthpiece.

It had been MauiWES’ most recent funding attempt: A bill sponsored by the state senator for West Maui, Angus McKelvey, would have allotted $3 million to keep the study going and expand the number of children it could serve. But at the last minute, the bill failed to make it through.

“I get it, they went for the bigger-ticket items, but the health part is also a big-ticket item that didn’t take precedence,” continued Lindsey, who is the president of a grassroots land trust organization on Maui. “I don’t think they understood, because probably none of them went through it.”

Maunakea agreed. He had thought that public health would be more of a priority in the wildfire recovery, especially in a state with a doctor as a governor. But funding MauiWES has been an ongoing challenge.

The study’s first cohort, in early 2024, began with charitable funding from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation and Kaiser Permanente, while the researchers pursued government support. That summer, they got $2.3 million from the state. And almost one year after the fires, they received a $1.4 million grant from the National Institutes of Health’s minority health disparities program.

That support quickly turned precarious after Donald Trump retook office and slashed funding for programs focused on diversity or health disparities, along with a wide swath of academic research.

The MauiWES researchers hoped to renew their federal funding and keep the study going for at least a decade. But heading into the May event, applications they submitted to the agency had been languishing without a decision for more than a year. By that time, the NIH had lost 23 percent of its staff under the Trump administration, almost double the reduction across the entire federal government, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News.

The MauiWES researchers started getting national recognition in the disaster recovery space, speaking on panels and presenting at conferences on the mainland, hoping that might drum up more cash. But private funding wasn’t enough to keep the study going, and the speaking engagements had yet to pay off. More state funding seemed like Juarez and Maunakea’s best hope.

Initially, the team had strong backing from the state’s Department of Health, which wrote enthusiastic letters of support for federal grants. But as the study progressed and the researchers began publicizing their results, the agency pushed back.

The Department of Health had earlier screened 557 West Maui residents for lead in their blood, saying in May 2024 that so few had elevated levels that it was not necessary to screen the general population for toxic substances identified in the burn zone.

“On the basis of these results with lead as an indicator of exposure, we do not expect to find health impacts caused by toxins in the wildfire ash,” agency director Kenneth Fink said in a statement at the time.

But lead is just one of the toxic substances the department found at elevated levels in burn zone ash, and it’s undetectable in people’s blood relatively quickly after exposure, unlike some other substances found in the burn zone. Environmental health experts questioned why the department used a limited sampling of lead to draw broad conclusions about the burn zone as a whole.

Then MauiWES found elevated levels of heavy metals associated with heart and lung issues and cancer risks in a cohort of more than 1,200 fire survivors.

The findings seemed to contradict the Department of Health’s assertion that the burn zone was safe. Emails and letters Inside Climate News obtained through public records requests suggest that agency staff quickly moved into damage-control mode.

The day after Honolulu Civil Beat published a story about the preliminary findings last year, a naturopathic doctor on Maui emailed state toxicologist John Jacob for information about the effects of heavy metals like arsenic, nickel , cadmium, mercury, and lead on psychological function. Her clients had been tested by MauiWES and registered high levels of those metals, she wrote.

Jacob forwarded the email to colleagues at the Department of Health.

“I don’t want to affirm what UH is stating,” he wrote, referring to the University of Hawaiʻi. “The panic has begun!”

A few days later, agency staff discussed whether to stop assisting MauiWES with data collection. Fink, the director, said staff could continue for now, but he felt the department’s recommendations on study design had been either inadequate or disregarded. “If the latter, I would need to reevaluate our involvement,” Fink wrote to colleagues.

In October, the Department of Health sent a letter to the University of Hawaiʻi, criticizing MauiWES’ reliance on sampling survivors who showed up — as opposed to a randomized cohort — and its findings of elevated heavy metals in their urine.

The university defended the research in its response and explained that MauiWES was not claiming a definitively causal relationship between the fires and the heavy metals.

Although the team remained committed to working with the state, Juarez said he saw the Department of Health’s letter as an attempt to censor their research. Academics not involved with MauiWES told Inside Climate News the exchange seemed unusual for a university and a state agency, and they did not think the health department’s dismissal of burn-zone dangers was warranted based on the limited information it had collected.

The agency’s director said in a statement to Inside Climate News that discussions about the best way to approach research “are a normal and healthy — and often essential — aspect of scientific collaboration.”

“While our perspectives may differ, both DOH and UH remain committed to respectful dialogue and evidence‑based inquiry,” Fink wrote in his statement. “Most importantly, the public needs clear, accurate, and consistent information about how the wildfires may have affected their health. Residents deserve timely communication they can trust — free of speculation and grounded in the best available data.”

In an emailed statement to Inside Climate News, Jacob acknowledged that the researchers’ approach was acceptable but said that not disclosing limitations could “result in confusion among the general public.”

In defense of the agency’s own approach to quantifying post-wildfire health risks, a department spokesperson said in an email that a structured soil sampling technique allowed staff to use the lead screening as a “reasonable indicator for population exposure.”

In internal emails in January, agency staff discussed a bill with funds earmarked to keep MauiWES alive. They agreed to keep a close watch on the effort. “Especially since we are not satisfied with their science,” wrote Jacob, the toxicologist.

In the end, a department subagency was among those submitting testimony in support of the funding. But that wasn’t enough to push it through. When the bill fell short with still no word on federal money, it looked like the end of MauiWES.

At nearly 5 p.m. on Sunday, the team packed up while finishing tests for the last few stragglers. Most of the staff and volunteers had to catch a flight back to Oʻahu in a couple of hours, but Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist working on the study’s research team, would stay on Maui a few more days to see patients in person.

Knightsbridge was overcome with pure frustration. All weekend, he’d done mental health check-ins with participants still focused on getting by, day by day. He felt certain the study was having an impact. He saw it every week. And he was still concerned about what he’d been hearing in his sessions. He wanted his patients to wake up and feel like they were living, not simply fighting to survive. For that, they needed more support, not less.

Knightsbridge poured everything he had into supporting survivors’ mental health in recovery. He spent half of most weeks away from his wife and young children on Oʻahu to see patients still dealing with ongoing crises: survivors in temporary housing and unstable employment, people with cancer diagnoses, young children whose lives were turned upside down by the fires. He’s seen serious PTSD symptoms, depression, and even suicidal ideation from kids as young as 6.

That same week, he sat in his video gaming group for kids at the health center with two of Mikey and Rob Burke’s sons, the twins dealing with PTSD. Knightsbridge was seeing both boys for therapy and organized the gaming group as another form of support, a low-stakes place for kids to open up. But the federal emergency grant supporting his position — separate from MauiWES’s funding — was also about to run out.

On the other side of the lobby, Juarez stood in a doorway, gutted. The study had made painfully apparent the gaps in healthcare access on the island, and it felt like their work was just beginning. The thought brought him to the brink of tears. Throughout the weekend, he heard from worried participants who asked if the study was going away. He didn’t want to let them down.

Near the entrance to the courtyard, Maunakea carried a table from the hallway back into one of the offices, tired but heartened by how many people had come through. Sitting with returning participants, learning about their recovery journeys and watching how they were putting the pieces back together was energizing for him. Healing is a communal task in Lahaina. The study leaned into that.

Maunakea knew the next disaster was just around the corner. He believed Maui could adapt and offer a model to the rest of the world for building resilience to the steep challenges climate change brings.

Maybe, he thought, that would be the ultimate lesson from the study: that documenting and addressing health inequities in the wake of a disaster helps communities withstand what they cannot escape.

Toward the end of the day, more survivors arrived without appointments after hearing about the study from family and friends. By closing, he estimated the team had turned away more than a dozen new people, taking down their names in case funding came through. Maunakea met people that weekend who said they’d known about the study for several years but hadn’t felt ready to participate until now. It hammered home to him how crucial it was for their work to go on.

The team would find a way to continue the study, Maunakea felt certain. He didn’t know how, but he saw no other choice. If his great-grandmother was alive, she would have said: ‘O ka pono ke hana ‘ia a iho mai nā lani . Continue to do good until the heavens come down to you.

He believed that this study is pono , and that the community wanted and needed this service. So, somehow, iho mai nā lani . The heavens would come down.

Inside Climate News’ Peter Aldhous contributed to this story.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Friday that it is giving states an additional six months to begin enforcing Medicaid work requirements.

States have been racing to prepare their Medicaid systems by Jan. 1 to include the work requirements passed last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill. The legislation required states that expanded Medicaid after Democrats passed the Affordable Care Act to ensure all working-age recipients without dependent children are employed, in school, or volunteering at least 80 hours each month, unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or “medically frail.”

A federal judge recently rejected the federal government’s medical frailty definition and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems.

scraped.title: New addiction society guidance on medetomidine’s brutal withdrawal
scraped.description: Medetomidine, a potent synthetic sedative in illicit opioids, causes withdrawal so severe new ASAM guidance says specialized ICU treatment may be needed.
scraped.author: Theresa Gaffney
scraped.h1: New addiction society guidance on medetomidine’s brutal withdrawal
scraped.body_text:
Home

What's the word?

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Theresa Gaffney

Nov. 13, 2026

Addiction Reporter

Theresa Gaffney

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Clinicians first noticed medetomidine in the Philadelphia drug supply during the spring of 2024. There was a cluster of overdoses one weekend, leaving patients more sedated and with lower heart rates than normal after receiving the reversal medication naloxone.

It raised some red flags, but amid a constantly changing drug supply, not many. None of the patients died, and most went home from the hospital the same day. It wasn’t until autumn, when patients started coming in with excruciating withdrawal symptoms, that doctors knew something had dangerously shifted.

Advertisement

“It took a while for our patients to consistently have a supply that was exposing them to this enough so that when they stopped, they would rapidly develop withdrawal,” said Jeanmarie Perrone, an emergency medicine physician and director of the Penn Medicine Center for Addiction Medicine and Policy. “It’s the withdrawal that has caused so many problems.”

While clinicians in Pennsylvania and other hotspots are now familiar with the signs of medetomidine withdrawal, the American Society of Addiction Medicine this week released the first national guidance for recognizing and treating patients who have taken the sedative. Technically, the document consists of “considerations,” not guidelines, since researchers have not yet conducted larger studies that could validate the inferences clinicians are making on the ground.

If people are using medetomidine, it’s nearly always in combination with illicit opioids, experts say. That means naloxone should still be the first step if somebody appears to be overdosing. But it also means the patient may not be responsive even after they start breathing again. When it comes to acute medetomidine intoxication, low heart rate and low blood pressure can be treated with IV fluids and other basic care, the guidance notes.

Advertisement

The first symptoms of medetomidine withdrawal tend to be nausea and vomiting, without the diarrhea that accompanies opioid withdrawal, said Perrone, one of the co-authors. That’s when they recommend clonidine, a medication that, like medetomidine and xylazine before it, acts as an alpha-2 agonist. If that doesn’t help or patients can’t keep it down, they could develop very high blood pressure and a fast heart rate within a few hours. That may signal the need for the related IV medication dexmedetomidine, or Precedex.

“It’s scary. We thought we were already living in unprecedented times with the adulteration of fentanyl with xylazine,” said Kory London, an emergency physician and addiction specialist at Thomas Jefferson University. (He didn’t contribute to the considerations, but he works with many people who did.) Unlike withdrawal from other illicit drugs, coming off of medetomidine may require a stay in the intensive care unit.

“We are giving doses [of clonidine and dexmedetomidine] that, as an experienced addiction provider, I would not have given five years ago when dealing with the initial xylazine adulteration,” London said. “Unless you’re experienced with this, giving enough medications to avoid getting somebody to the ICU is really challenging.”

Before medetomidine started taking over, xylazine was the dominant adulterant in much of the American drug supply. It leaves users with horrific wounds and is such a powerful sedative that it could knock people out for hours, often leaving them vulnerable in public.

Medetomidine doesn’t seem to cause the same wounds. But as a sedative, it’s far more potent.

By the end of 2025, medetomidine had been detected in at least 18 states . It’s important for physicians to know whether medetomidine is present in the local drug supply, experts emphasize, as the symptoms may resemble other conditions, including sepsis. In general, it’s critical to stay familiar with the local supply and to consider what effects different adulterants could have on users, said Michael Lynch, a co-author of the considerations and an emergency medicine doctor specializing in medical toxicology at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.

Advertisement

“The next thing, and then the next thing, and then the thing after that are coming,” Lynch said. “We can try to predict what they’re going to be, but we can’t always.”

Not every community has the resources to do rigorous, regular drug checking. But “if we do a good job at describing our experience in places where we do have resources and have that early experience, hopefully other places can see the clinical manifestation,” Lynch said. There are drug testing strips for medetomidine.

While the clinical considerations offer doctors a blueprint for treating medetomidine withdrawal, experts say that more research is needed to understand the drug’s long-term effects and to develop better treatments.

Some patients who make it through withdrawal and begin to take medications for opioid use disorder can still experience cravings, experts said. They might think that the cravings are for opioids and begin to use again, but really, the cravings are for medetomidine.

“We’re going to have to recognize that there are now patients who are developing a sort of novel substance use disorder of alpha-2 agonist sedative addiction,” said London. “We urgently need both ways to understand that and ways potentially to help treat patients.”

scraped.description: Advocates said the bill was necessary because of protests outside synagogues hosting real estate expos for Israeli settlement land.
scraped.author: Matt Sledge
scraped.h1: Will Senate Religious Freedom Bill Actually Protect Land Sales for Israeli Settlements?
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Advocates said the bill was necessary because of protests outside synagogues hosting real estate expos for Israeli settlement land.

A proposed “buffer zone” around religious facilities across the country — touted as protecting the right to worship — is alarming free-speech advocates who say the Trump administration could use it to crack down on protests.

The new bill, a national version of a controversial law passed in smaller jurisdictions, could hamper demonstrations against illegal sales of land in the West Bank to Jewish settlers that occur inside U.S. synagogues , the advocates say.

The bipartisan legislation could face another layer of opposition from a surprise corner, however, in the form of reproductive rights groups worried it would undermine an existing law that protects abortion clinics.

“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other Constitutional rights.”

Called the Right to Worship Act, the bill cosponsored by Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., will be the subject of a Tuesday hearing in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

The bill has drawn backing from Christian, Jewish, and minority religious leaders who say it could be used to prevent hate crimes. Major Muslim groups, however, have been notably absent from supporter lists.

That isn’t just because Cruz regularly demonizes Muslims . Muslim leaders also worry that while in theory the law would be used to promote religious freedom, in practice it would be used to punish non-violent, pro-Palestine protesters, said Dahlia Taha, the director of the First Amendment Center at the Muslim Public Affairs Council.

“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other Constitutional rights,” she said. “We believe that this can have very detrimental and long-term impacts. And under this administration, specifically, we’re concerned about those long-term implications.”

Slotkin and Cruz’s offices did not respond to requests for comment.

Under the bill, the Department of Justice could seek civil fines or injunctions against anyone who engages in a “course of conduct” that disrupts religious services, or disrupts access to them, within 100 feet of a church, mosque, synagogue, or other religious facility. Worshippers and state attorneys general could also file lawsuits.

Numerous states have already passed similar legislation creating “buffer zones” around religious buildings. In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani vetoed a buffer zone for protests near schools and colleges, while allowing another one for religious institutions to pass.

Read our complete coverage

Supporters of the federal bill argue that it is needed to protect worshippers from harassment or worse.

“Attacks on synagogues, mosques, churches, and other houses of worship are unfortunately on the rise in Michigan, and across the country,” Slotkin said in an August press release. “No one should ever fear going to their house of worship. Period.”

The law’s authors tout it as a narrowly tailored guardrail, but critics say that the “course of conduct” subject to fines and lawsuits is so ill-defined that the Trump administration could use it to target peaceful protesters.

“There is no relationship between this legislation and the prevention of violent acts at synagogues, mosques, or churches.”

One of critics’ top fears is the “religious services” protected by the law could be defined to include real-estate pitches for land illegally seized from Palestinian people in the West Bank. In a press release, the Anti-Defamation League cited two West bank land-sale protests in New York City as examples of the need for the legislation, along with the March ramming attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan.

When it comes to violent attacks, argued Eli Williams-Szenes, the director of advocacy and political affairs at the progressive Jewish group Bend the Arc, synagogues are better protected by an existing federal law called the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act. The FACE Act makes a federal crime out of force, threats, or physical obstruction near both religious institutions and abortion clinics.

“There is no relationship between this legislation and the prevention of violent acts at synagogues, mosques, or churches,” Williams-Szenes said of the new bill. “The idea that telling someone that if they wave a pamphlet 97 feet from the entrance to a synagogue, they’ll get a $10,000 fine would be the reason that someone didn’t try to drive a car into Temple Israel is crazy.”

The Right to Worship Act faces long odds in the final weeks of the Republican-controlled Congress. Still, Williams-Szenes said he is concerned that even a hearing could set the stage for eventual passage.

Abortion rights groups are also worried. They fear that if the Right to Worship Act passes, Republicans will be inclined to repeal or weaken the FACE Act because of its protections for abortion clinics.

One of President Donald Trump’s first actions upon taking office last year was to pardon anti-abortion rights protesters convicted of blockading a clinic under the FACE Act.

“The Right to Worship Act is a wolf in sheep’s clothing,” Kelsey Ryland, a policy counsel at the National Abortion Federation, said in a statement. “The impact of this policy could become a backdoor FACE Act repeal, weakening enforcement against violent disruptors at abortion clinics.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Democrats must stand with their voters and block the NDAA's provisions to cooperate even more closely with Israel.

Josh Ruebner is policy director of the IMEU Policy Project and author of the forthcoming book “ The United States and Palestinian Nakba: A Transnational History, 1947-1950 .”

After President Biden’s unrelenting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza helped pave the way for President Trump’s reelection in 2024, Trump’s own foolish decision to launch an Israel-backed war against Iran played a large role in putting Democrats back in control of both chambers of Congress — a fact Vice President JD Vance diagnosed in no uncertain terms.

Now Democrats and Republicans alike have the opportunity to demonstrate they’ve finally learned the lesson voters have tried to deliver to both parties over the last three years: The American people do not want to be entangled and complicit in Israel’s aggression and atrocities. Their first opportunity to heed that call is arriving sooner than one might expect.

Right now, the House Armed Services Committee and Senate Armed Services Committee are engaged in an informal but highly consequential conference to finalize the text of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which sets policy for the Pentagon. A disturbing provision in current versions of the texts passed by the House and Senate committees would integrate Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon procurement process at an unprecedented level — opening a back door to almost untraceably send billions of taxpayer dollars to Israeli weapons makers without congressional oversight. The House bill would create a new “executive agent” position within the Pentagon to steer this integration —a level of amalgamation that exceeds collaboration with nations in NATO.

Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle are opposing this provision. On Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen and nine other Democratic senators, plus independent Bernie Sanders, demanded it be removed. In the House, Democrat Ro Khanna and Republican Thomas Massie have made clear they will also try to strip the NDAA of this measure. In doing so, they are representing what the vast majority of Americans want—and their colleagues should take note.

In our August polling with Data for Progress, 75 percent of Democratic voters oppose this provision, as do 58 percent of independents and 42 percent of Republicans. In addition, polling shows a majority of Americans now want to see taxpayer funding to Israel reduced or ended. Passing the NDAA with this measure would mean that even if Congress zeroed out annual weapons funding to Israel, currently at $3.3 billion per year, in the State Department budget — earlier this year, 103 Democratic representatives joined Massie in a move to do just that — there could still be a major increase in actual dollars flowing to Israeli companies that the American people never hear about.

The negative repercussions extend beyond funding Israeli weapons makers (some of which are government-owned) with our tax dollars. This sort of integration could allow for Israeli weapons and surveillance technology that have been tested on Palestinians to be used in the U.S. to advance the Trump administration’s cruel mass deportation program. Israeli weapons maker Elbit Systems’s U.S. subsidiary is expected to install more than 300 surveillance towers along the U.S.-Mexico border, developed from its technology deployed along portions of Israel’s apartheid wall in the West Bank.

Most Read OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Look Inside the Windowless New York Skyscraper Linked to the NSA Ryan Gallagher, Henrik Moltke

Melding Israel into our government procurement process should also set off alarm bells in the U.S. national security world. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vetoed Biden’s decision to send U.S.-Israeli co-produced missile systems to Ukraine three years ago for Ukraine’s war against Russia, even though the missiles were paid for by American taxpayers. The integration measure proposed in the NDAA would massively expand the scope of weapons over which the Israeli government could exercise a unilateral veto.

Congress should be unwinding intelligence cooperation with Israel, not only on the moral grounds that no part of the U.S. national security apparatus should assist in genocide, but also because Pentagon officials raised the threat of Israeli spying to its highest possible level earlier this year. But instead of diminishing our intelligence sharing with Israel, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence’s FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated into the final NDAA version, includes a provision (Sec. 618) actually mandating the president engage in even more intelligence cooperation.

This should give us pause because of the faulty nature of Israeli intelligence and the way Israel used this intelligence to build a case for dragging the United States into war. It was reportedly Israeli intelligence that claimed the Iranian government could be overthrown within weeks, if not days, of Trump launching the war. Instead, Trump and Netanyahu are now stuck in a quagmire, and the war has imposed a terrible cost on the American people, U.S. servicemembers, and people across Iran and the region. Energy prices around the world have skyrocketed, the cost of the war has already exceeded $2,000 per U.S. household on average, and the U.S. is running low on interceptor missiles that will take years to replenish.

None of this seems to concern the main backers of U.S.-Israel military and intelligence integration, like Foundation for Defense of Democracies President Mark Dubowitz. In a column published in Israel Hayom , the right-wing newspaper owned by the Israeli-American GOP megadonor Miriam Adelson, Dubowitz said: “Israel and the United States should deepen their military, technological, intelligence, and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”

In an interview , Dubowitz added that the U.S. and Israel should be so intertwined that any accountability measure against Israel, such as sanctions being enacted by American allies in Europe, would “impose costs on the U.S. itself.” In no uncertain terms, advocates for the integration envisioned in the NDAA want to try to make it impossible for the U.S. to disentangle itself from a regime that is increasingly perceived by many as a rogue actor.

The NDAA is usually considered a “must pass” bill in Congress — in fact, Congress has passed annual defense authorizations for 65 consecutive years. But Congress is under no statutory obligation to pass it this year, and doing so without stripping these provisions to become even more entrenched with supporting Israel would be an immediate betrayal of the will of voters. At a time when even Republicans are openly admitting the midterm election was a referendum on U.S. support for Israel, it would be an unforgivable choice for Congress to pass an NDAA with these integration provisions. If Republicans use their committee majorities to force their inclusion in the bill’s final text, Democrats have every bit of leverage to filibuster and block the bill’s passage in the Senate, which requires 60 votes.

Saying no to bringing the U.S. into a closer relationship with Israel in just about the most expensive, opaque, and dangerous way imaginable should be the easiest political decision Congress makes during its current lame-duck session.

scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:

Tanja Nijmeijer’s memoir tells of how Colombia’s FARC was forced into a long and painful retreat. Her account of its political setbacks suggests that power doesn’t always flow from the barrel of a gun.

Tanja Nijmeijer is a Dutch veteran of Colombia’s FARC guerrillas. Her new memoir strikingly recounts the decline in the group’s fortunes, as hopes of a popular uprising crumbled under the devastating counterinsurgency. (Marcelo Salinas / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

Review of Into the Jungle: My Life as a Guerrilla in Colombia by Tanja Nijmeijer (Pluto Press, 2026)

I n the early hours of September 23, 2010, Tanja Nijmeijer was awakened by a bomb in a FARC guerrilla camp in the Colombian jungle. The strike landed on her commander’s bunker, followed by screams from her comrades. Moments later, dozens of aircraft roared above and launched another wave of bombs. Nijmeijer grabbed her rifle and dived into her foxhole. As the ground shook around her, she closed her eyes, tensed her body and thought: Aquí fue — this is it.

Seven years earlier, when the Dutch internationalist had first entered the jungle to join the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC), the war looked very different. She remembers it as “the calm before the storm,” with abundant supplies, comparatively large and settled camps, and a degree of security.

Nijmeijer’s autobiography, Into the Jungle , recently published by Pluto Press , traces her trajectory from guerrilla warfare to the negotiations that produced the 2016 peace agreement and the troubled transition that followed. Yet what makes the memoir especially politically revealing is that Nijmeijer joined the FARC at almost exactly the moment when the war started to change so decisively against it.

I nitially traveling to Colombia in order to teach English to the children of the rich, Nijmeijer quickly encountered the extreme inequalities dividing Colombia. She witnessed gated communities, stark disparities separating the northern part of capital Bogotá from the south, and the concentration of wealth and power among an elite while poorer neighborhoods suffered neglect and repression.

Nijmeijer came into contact with FARC militants through her work and began to question the dominant image of the guerrillas as little more than “narco-terrorists.” Instead she encountered people prepared to sacrifice their lives in pursuit of a revolutionary project. Gradually developing a socialist outlook, she began to recognize that the ruling class was blocking any prospects of meaningful, peaceful change. She increasingly regarded armed struggle as not only legitimate but necessary and was convinced that the guerrillas could “take power and plant the seed for a new world.”

Although it was not apparent then, when Nijmeijer went into the jungle, the FARC’s decline was already underway. Right-winger Álvaro Uribe won the presidential election in 2002 on the back of mounting hostility to the FARC following the collapse of the 1999–2002 peace process. Harnessing hegemonic narratives that portrayed the FARC as having acted in bad faith and merely exploited the peace process as an opportunity to expand, Uribe promised a “military solution,” relying on massive US support through Plan Colombia to modernize the armed forces.

By late 2003, seven months after Nijeimer went into the jungle, the counterinsurgency offensive organized through Plan Patriota had reached Sumapaz, where military operations targeted guerrilla fronts in a region central to the FARC’s strategic plan for surrounding Bogotá. Areas over which the FARC had historically enjoyed complete control were now being contested.

The guerrillas later discovered evidence of around sixty helicopter landing sites, army surveillance of guerrilla roads and infrastructure, and reconnaissance teams operating inside jungle territories that the insurgents had assumed were impenetrable.

The state’s expanding war chest enabled significant increases in military personnel, specialized mountain battalions, and airpower. This was supported by satellite imagery and geospatial intelligence , communications interception , and other technologies challenging the guerrillas’ traditional reliance on rugged terrain as a form of defensive protection.

The military’s expanding reach is already evident earlier in Nijmeijer’s account, when she describes the penetration of her units by infiltrators who pulled various stunts as part of a tactic to undermine morale — unlocking weapons, defecating in huts, and cutting up the guerrillas’ rubber boots. The result was that “nobody trusted anybody else.”

Whereas in the past, counterinsurgency campaigns were temporary, with troops eventually withdrawing due to budget cuts and other constraints, now the Colombian army established a permanent offensive presence and pursued the guerrillas into rearguard zones and jungles, closing in on commanders once thought invulnerable.

The shifting conditions led the FARC’s leading military commander, Mono Jojoy, to declare before a crowd of five hundred guerrillas, “Thanks to President Álvaro Uribe Vélez, we are going to learn how to live as guerrilla fighters again! We must go back to basics.”

Improvements in airpower gave the state forces a decisive advantage. Vehicles disappeared, supplies and comforts were reduced, marches replaced a comparatively settled life, and concentration gave way to greater mobility and dispersion. “Our days of easy living,” as Nijmeijer puts it, “were over.”

For the FARC, going back to basics meant adopting an increasingly defensive posture: land mines, often described as a “ weapon of the weak ,” became an especially useful tool for slowing the encroachments of army patrols. However, they also caused civilian casualties and left the FARC exposed to criticism for disregarding human rights.

To reduce the risk of interception when communicating with urban militants, the guerrillas began sending encrypted messages via satellite internet. But this wasn’t a comprehensive solution. Air surveillance, increased extensively under Plan Colombia, could still intercept such communications. They had to switch off the equipment whenever an approaching plane was suspected, but the introduction of small, largely undetectable drones enabling real-time surveillance in 2006 made it harder to know when they were being watched.

The transition to a more defensive mode of operating affected daily life. Camps were built with deep foxholes; smoking and flashlights were prohibited after dark; vines were strung along paths so fighters could navigate without light; fireflies were used as improvised illumination. The nightly hour of cultural activities, essential for political education and boosting morale, became a thing of the past in Nijmeijer’s units. Meanwhile, massed forces of guerrillas were restricted — a setback from the FARC’s war of movement strategy at the end of the 1990s, in which large concentrations of troops overwhelmed military bases.

T rue, this was a form of adaptation. Yet adaptation increasingly meant preserving the guerrilla organization under adverse conditions rather than recreating the offensive possibilities of the previous decade. Nijmeijer recounts, “The war changed, and it changed in the army’s favor.”

The psychological impact is described in a way that military histories and government documents rarely capture. Nijmeijer recalls the “pure terror” as bombs drop around her, with nowhere to run for safety, and no visible opponent to shoot at, only the hope that the jungle canopy might offer some protection.

Having to be constantly on the move, often in treacherous terrain, had its physical costs. Long marches left the guerrillas hungry and low on calories, and illness and fatigue, inevitable in such conditions, spread and grew more difficult to overcome. The army had repeatedly blocked Mono Jojoy’s attempts to meet up with Manuel Marulanda, the FARC’s founder and long-standing leader. Nijmeijer describes the resulting two-month march through particularly arduous territory on inadequate rations, which left her body aching so badly that she could barely manage to endure the night watch.

The psychological and physical impact had broader organizational repercussions. Demoralization deepened, and desertion rates increased , which the counterinsurgents exploited to the full. One guerrilla defector recorded the coordinates of Raúl Reyes’s location while sitting on the FARC leader’s bed . Iván Ríos, then the youngest member of the FARC’s secretariat, who had decided to remain with a guerrilla front to tackle problems of indiscipline and disorganization, turned up dead alongside his girlfriend — killed by his own head of security, who hoped to collect a lucrative bounty. Even people imagined to be staunchly politically committed ended up deserting and providing crucial intelligence.

As my own interviews with various former FARC leaders confirm, from around 2007, the counterinsurgents took the FARC by surprise, systematically hiding tiny GPS trackers in items that the guerrillas relied upon to survive. They identified stores in guerrilla areas and forced merchants to cooperate and even pressured family members and the children of guerrillas, as revealed in an interview with a retired strategic intelligence analyst in the Colombian navy. The trackers guided precision strikes on guerrilla camps, such as in the case of Mono Jojoy, whose boot concealed a GPS tracker.

Nijmeijer reflects that “if I had to pinpoint a moment when I began to see we wouldn’t take power by military means, it would be some time before Mono’s death in 2010.”

Yet her growing recognition that the FARC could no longer take power militarily was also linked to the organization’s broader political isolation.

As many former FARC commanders have admitted, kidnapping and extortion, justified by the organization as “revolutionary taxation,” inflicted enormous political costs and enabled the ruling classes to paint it as a group of terrorists and bandits, especially in urban areas where most people were based.

The FARC’s communications strategy — deemed a complete failure by Nijmeijer — also left it politically vulnerable. The state had dedicated task forces whose entire purpose was to undermine the FARC’s claim to political legitimacy. According to Nijmeijer, FARC leader Manuel Marulanda had decided “there was no good reason to respond to falsehoods the state made up.”

Given that the FARC was overwhelmingly rooted in the countryside, and the country was increasingly organized around the big cities, political communication was fundamental. Yet Nijmeijer recounts how long the FARC ignored this issue.

Nijmeijer concludes that while the conflict had no straightforward military victor, the FARC “certainly lost the ideological battle.”

T he FARC’s strategy had always theoretically left open the possibility of negotiations alongside the more ambitious goal of taking power through a popular insurrection.

But as the FARC faced military blows and narrowing strategic possibilities, the idea of a negotiated settlement gained prominence.

In November 2011, the FARC’s supreme leader — Alfonso Cano — was assassinated by the counterinsurgents, the first time this had occurred in the organization’s half-century history, a moment Nijmeijer remembers as a “heavy blow” that left even the more radical commanders Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich sitting in stunned silence, repeating, “We have to go on, anyhow.”

While the FARC was capable of sustaining the war over many more years, its influence had been significantly weakened. Key figures, including Nijmeijer, no longer realistically envisaged taking power through a popular insurrection and the point of war, they saw, was to win it, not simply endure it.

Unable to foresee victory or a realistic possibility of retaking the strategic initiative nationally, the FARC turned to negotiations from a position of relative weakness. The state only agreed to talks on the condition that changes to its fundamental economic model were off the cards — thus leaving intact the exploitative social relations that sustained the conflict.

Ultimately, from the perspective of a former guerrilla fighter who experienced firsthand the FARC’s military reversal, the book reveals that political power does not necessarily grow from the barrel of a gun. To be sure, the FARC became one of Latin America’s most powerful communist organizations, with many thousands of guerrillas, control over territory, and access to an enormous war chest. And yet, this capacity to sustain an insurgency did not translate into nationwide appeal or a credible strategy for taking power.

Oliver Dodd is an Economic and Social Research Council postdoctoral fellow in politics and international relations at Aberystwyth University.

scraped.title: Organizing for Tenant and Political Power in Montana
scraped.description: We spoke to a Montana tenant union leader about organizing renters in the state and the midterms victory of Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper, a union leader, and the first elected House Democrat in Montana in three decades.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

We spoke to a Montana tenant union leader about organizing renters in the state and the midterms victory of Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper, a union leader, and the first elected House Democrat in Montana in three decades.

Organizing tenants in a rural, red state like Montana isn’t easy. We spoke to the president of Bozeman Tenants United about how they’ve done it. (Jered McCafferty / Bozeman Tenants United)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

S am Forstag, a smoke jumper and union leader, flipped western Montana’s US House seat blue in last week’s midterm elections. He is the first Democrat from Montana elected to the US House in more than thirty years, having run on a grassroots progressive campaign that brought together labor unions, environmental organizations, indigenous groups, and tenant unions.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez played a significant role in Forstag’s upset victory in the Democratic primary. She endorsed Forstag when he was trailing by 20 points and traveled to Missoula for a get-out-the-vote rally. Missoula County carried Forstag to a narrow primary victory, with Democratic primary turnout increasing 23 percent from 2024.

Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorsed Forstag for the general election and campaigned for him in Gallatin County, which had the highest increase in Democratic votes between the primary and general election. The county has recently become a destination for wealthy transplants, driving up housing costs. Since the start of the pandemic, the median home price in Bozeman has nearly doubled to over $700,000.

BTU was formed in 2022 and was a cofounding organization in the national Tenant Union Federation in 2024. Benjamin Finegan was a cofounder of BTU and currently serves as president. Jacobin contributor Willem Morris spoke to Finegan about Forstag’s win and how to organize tenants in Montana.

Willem Morris

Who is Sam Forstag, and why did Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorse him in his race for the US House of Representatives in Montana’s 1st congressional district?

Benjamin Finegan

This May, Sam Forstag drove two hundred miles from Missoula to Bozeman to join the picket lines of BTU members on a rent strike at two major mobile home parks, the first major rent strike in Montana in fifty years. Sam really went out of his way to support the strike. He used his social media platforms to rally public support for the strike and raised money for our strike fund.

Forstag also committed to a co-governance pledge with BTU. He committed to consulting tenants on policy, maintaining ongoing engagement with the union, and working to hold landlords accountable.

That’s who Sam Forstag is. He knows what it’s like to have to choose between gas or groceries in order to pay the rent. He’s also someone who has proven that he will stand with working Montanans against multimillionaires and billionaires.

BTU is an independent group of tenants with many different political backgrounds. We have been very selective with our endorsements, avoiding establishment picks from both parties, and have focused mostly on local races. Our decision to endorse Sam was the first time we have endorsed a federal candidate. The vote was nearly unanimous, with enthusiastic support across political differences. Our members remembered that Sam was willing to stick his neck out and fight for tenants during their strike at such a high-risk and high-profile moment.

Willem Morris

Missoula carried Forstag to victory in the primary. Your home in Gallatin County made a significant difference in the general election. Who are these voters in Gallatin County?

Benjamin Finegan

Gallatin County is home to Montana State University in Bozeman. It’s also home to the thousands of workers who staff nearby playgrounds for the ultrarich, Big Sky and the Yellowstone Club. The wealthiest people in the world pay $500,000 to join the Yellowstone Club. Working people serve as their landscapers, cooks, and maids.

BTU’s membership comes from these two main groups: students and young professionals centered around the university, and families renting apartments and mobile home parks, many of whom work in the service industry or live on fixed retirement incomes.

Willem Morris

BTU formally endorsed Forstag in September. How did BTU contribute to his race in Bozeman?

Benjamin Finegan

BTU organized our members to vote in large numbers for Sam Forstag, and we led mass canvasses in Bozeman.

The majority of tenants that struck the trailer parks this summer voted for Sam. This includes folks who I know are more conservative and have historically voted Republican.

One of our members is an older retired veteran who went on strike; he told me, “We are getting chiseled, we are getting gouged, we are being sheared like sheep.” He has voted Republican but was one of the folks that voted for our union to endorse Sam in the election. The solidarity that Sam showed us during the strike ultimately meant a whole lot more to our members than the party label.

After our endorsement vote, folks hit the doors to get their neighbors committed to vote for Sam. The union is generally pretty trusted by tenants in our city, even if they’re not members. We have a reputation for fighting for tenants and against landlords. Last year, we won a law for tenants to have the right to counsel before eviction, which got city-funded legal representation for tenants. We have organized to enforce that law.

So when we knocked doors, we were able to say: “We’re with the tenant union. We won this law called right to counsel, and you can call this number if you ever are in trouble with your landlord. And we’re trying to get this candidate elected who is willing to fight alongside us, Sam Forstag. We trust him, and you can trust him too.”

Willem Morris

Forstag’s support extended well beyond Missoula and Bozeman. He dominated in Butte, Anaconda, and Glacier County. These three areas are traditional Democratic strongholds where MAGA had made inroads over the last decade. The largest shift for Forstag compared to 2024 was in Butte. Why was Forstag able to succeed in these three counties?

Benjamin Finegan

The AFL-CIO threw down for Sam Forstag. They led impressive turnout operations across the state. Sam comes from the labor movement, and unions organized to send one of their own to Congress. Butte and Anaconda, two old union mining towns, are almost legendary places in our state’s labor history. Sam Forstag ran almost 20 points better than Kamala Harris in these two places.

Native American voters were very significant for Sam too. Prominent Native leaders supported Sam, and the Blackfeet Nation and Reservation turned out for Sam in Glacier County. Public lands advocates are always important in every Montana election too. These are the forces that came together and were able to lead Sam to such an important victory.

Willem Morris

What else has BTU been organizing around this year?

Benjamin Finegan

Our bread and butter is organizing tenants to fight and win the changes we need from their landlords and from the government: getting members talking to their neighbors in apartment buildings or mobile home parks; developing leaders; deciding on demands; and taking action together. Our membership needs to be able to stay in their homes, regardless of who wins an election.

BTU is also one of the five founding locals of the national Tenant Union Federation ( TUF ). We came together with tenant unions from the South Side of Chicago, Connecticut, Kentucky, and Kansas City, Missouri, to form TUF.

In the last few months, TUF ran a three-month intensive training on tenant union organizing. We trained nearly a thousand tenant unionists from over 130 cities in forty states who learned how to organize tenant unions and fight for their homes.

This training series has already been getting results around the country and leading to brand new tenant unions in places like Colorado, Idaho, New York, and in the South, and winning collectively bargained leases, repairs, and rent reductions.

Willem Morris

Four years ago in Jacobin , I tried to think about how environmental, labor, and indigenous movements could start to rebuild the Left in Montana. I left out tenants. What does this election show about the potential power of organized tenants?

Benjamin Finegan

Tenant unions and tenant voters were a significant force in the midterms. And tenants are going to be decisive in 2028 and every election going forward.

Tenants make up nearly one-third of all Americans. We are facing higher rents for worse conditions and have less and less control over one of our most fundamental needs. Tenants want the government to take action on capping the rent, and I believe this will continue to mobilize more and more people to the ballot box.

I’ll also say that many tenants are poor and working-class people who live off a fixed income or work jobs not typically covered by labor unions. And even for tenants who are fortunate to have a labor union, rent increases can outpace wage increases. Organizing at our homes in addition to the workplace is necessary to have a stable, dignified life. As more tenants unionize across Montana and around the country and control our rent, we will wield more power in the economy too.

Last, when tenants unionize their apartment building or mobile home park, they experience collective power together, often for the first time. The experience serves as a training ground for democracy for regular people. It shows them how to negotiate and how to make decisions together. It teaches people that taking risks and exercising power collectively can get results. And they take those lessons to other parts of their life.

One of our members is a woman in her seventies who works at a nursing home, and she was elected by her neighbors to sit on the bargaining team for her union. We forced a representative from the corporation that owned their building to come to negotiate. During negotiations, I could see her literally shaking as she talked to this landlord representative demanding that they fix parking lot lights outside her building. Afterward, she told us: “I’ve never felt stronger in my entire life.”

Benjamin Finegan is the president of Bozeman Tenants United in Montana.

Willem Morris is the cochair of the Young Democratic Socialists of America's National Labor Committee.
