scraped.title: The Politics of Beef in the 2026 Midterms
scraped.description: Beef has long symbolized the promise of American material abundance. The midterms illustrated the political consequences of failing to deliver it.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Beef has long symbolized the promise of American material abundance. The midterms illustrated the political consequences of failing to deliver it.

Republicans have learned the political cost of failing to deliver roast beef. The Left now has to figure out how to put it back on the table. (Michael Macor / The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I n 1840, following the devastating economic contraction of the Panic of 1837, Whig presidential candidate William Henry Harrison defeated incumbent Martin Van Buren by promising “Two dollars a day and roast beef” for every worker. His opponent, meanwhile, was derided for offering workers just “fifty cents a day and French soup.”

Nearly two centuries later, Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom has become the first black person elected to the United States Senate from his state since Reconstruction.

Many pundits have identified the pivotal moment in his campaign: an advertisement mocking Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for responding to soaring beef prices by telling Americans, “You have so many proteins to choose from.”

Colom’s punch line : “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Harrison had promised American workers roast beef. Colom made the inability to afford it an indictment of the Republican Party.

Mississippi wasn’t an isolated case. From Texas’s historic Democratic sweep of statewide offices to extraordinary Democratic gains in Kansas, the 2026 midterms revealed the political consequences of the Trump administration’s failure to manage the American beef economy.

Caught between two constituencies with conflicting interests — cattle ranchers struggling to sustain their businesses and consumers increasingly unable to afford beef — the administration failed both. Meanwhile, immigration policies threatened the workers responsible for processing the country’s cattle.

The result was a political nightmare for Republicans and a lesson for progressives and leftists about the difficulty of delivering the material abundance that American workers have long been promised.

B eef occupies a special place in the American social contract. It has long symbolized material abundance: the promise that an ordinary person ought to be able to afford the occasional steak. Beef, according to a famous industry campaign, is “What’s for dinner.”

Heading into the midterms, Republicans found themselves caught between two constituencies, both struggling, with conflicting interests. On one side were America’s 622,000 cattle ranchers , of whom nearly 90 percent have only twenty cows on average. In 2018, roughly three in four identified as Republican. Many struggled financially with rising input costs, which resulted in the lowest national herd per capita in recorded history. Consumers, meanwhile, faced beef prices up 111 percent since 2019.

Ranchers need higher cattle prices to sustain their businesses, while consumers need lower beef prices to continue buying it. As Bloomberg reported in late 2025, “The Beef Market Is Broken for Everyone.”

High prices normally induce cattle ranchers to raise more cows. But ranchers have been forced to prepare their heifers for slaughter instead of raising baby calves due to climate-change-induced water shortages and rising primary input costs ( namely feed, fertilizer, and fuel — all driven higher by droughts, tariff disputes, and the war in Iran). Last month, Bloomberg reported that more than half of our country’s cattle live in areas suffering from droughts — meaning many of them will have to be sold for slaughter earlier than ranchers would prefer. And even if ranchers want to rebuild their herds, it takes three or four years of financial risk to do so.

T hrough much of the second Trump administration, Republicans chose a policy of supporting domestic ranchers with high beef prices, implicitly asking consumers to change their eating habits: “Pick another protein.” They were aware, however, that if beef prices rose too much, they’d face a political crisis.

In late 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that cattle ranchers “would be doing just as they’ve done for the past 20 years — Terrible!” if not for his 50 percent tariff on Brazilian cattle coming into the United States. He noted, though, that “it would be nice” if cattle ranchers also understood that “they also have to get their prices down, because the consumer is a very big factor in my thinking.”

While tariffs supported high beef prices, this ultimately proved politically untenable after beef prices continued to surge.

In August, Trump announced an expansion of the quota for imported lean beef trimmings eligible for reduced tariff rates. The goal was to increase imports of lean beef trimmings used to produce ground beef, bringing down beef prices before the midterm election.

Cattle prices subsequently fell roughly 15 percent from their May levels, exposing producers who had purchased cattle at elevated prices to substantial financial losses. Although other market forces also influence cattle prices, the administration’s decision to expand imports certainly contributed to the reduced value of ranchers’ herds.

Imagine you spent $50,000 to buy cattle in April. Now, their market value has fallen $7,500, or 15 percent. If you borrowed money to make the purchase, that decline would represent an even larger percentage of your own investment. When your cows reach market weight — or when you can no longer afford to feed and water them — you will be forced to sell. And if the prices don’t recover, you will lock in those losses.

At the same time, the policy shift came too late to benefit consumers; retail beef prices continued to surge heading into the midterms.

This is likely because consumers don’t immediately see the benefits of increased supply. The process requires importers to purchase and ship the beef, the imported beef to arrive and receive customs approval, the meatpackers to blend the imported and domestic beef, and the ground beef to move to wholesale distribution. After that, the supermarkets receive the shipment and adjust their prices. Just importing the beef takes two to eight weeks.

While cattle prices crashed, consumers paid even higher prices at the supermarket. The administration had failed struggling cattle ranchers without ensuring the ordinary American could afford to eat a steak.

T he consequences were particularly striking in Texas, where Democrats swept statewide offices in a historic electoral breakthrough.

In August, following the expansion of the in-quota allowance for beef imports, Republican Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller broke from Trump, warning that some Texas Republicans would lose statewide offices in November due to rural voter outrage. In fact, Democrats ended up winning every statewide Texas office, including his seat after he lost to his Republican challenger in the primaries.

Some of the state’s most remarkable swings toward Democrats occurred in counties with significant cattle-ranching economies. Kleberg County swung approximately 28 points toward Democrats relative to 2024, Brewster County 24 points, and Wilbarger County 16 points. While these shifts were comparable to the roughly 26-point Democratic swing statewide, they were substantial relative to the approximately 7.5-point swing across rural Texas more broadly.

These results do not prove that cattle prices caused ranchers to abandon the Republican Party. The election was a referendum on the Trump administration, and voters had plenty of reasons to reject its candidates.

But the Democratic gains in cattle country suggest that the administration’s agricultural policies may have broken a key part of the Republican coalition.

B eyond the consumers in Mississippi and the cattle ranchers in Texas, there was another constituency caught in the administration’s contradictory beef policy: the workers who process American cattle.

The meatpacking industry, which handles the slaughter and processing of livestock, depends heavily on immigrant labor. In September, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducted raids around meatpacking plants in Kansas, the second-largest meat-processing state. Many of these plants were already on the verge of closing because the herds they could buy were too small to continue operating profitably. ICE raids caused further shutdowns and delays, as immigrant workers stayed home out of fear of arrest. Without workers, the supply of beef fell, and beef prices continued to rise.

Kansas’s three largest meatpacking counties — Ford, Seward, and Finney — swung 39, 52, and 37 points toward Democrats, respectively, compared with a roughly 21-point Democratic swing statewide relative to 2024. The Kansas Reflector reported that they were the three counties that helped the Democrats take the Kansas Senate seat, even though less than one in four voters in these counties are registered Democrats.

While the Trump administration increased beef imports in an attempt to lower consumer prices, its immigration policies threatened the workforce responsible for processing this beef. Ranchers faced losses on their cattle; consumers worried about affording steak again; endangered meatpacking workers faced uncertainty about their livelihoods.

Given these widespread grievances, it’s not surprising that a Kansas Senate seat turned blue for the first time since the Great Depression.

B eef prices alone did not determine the 2026 election — high gas prices and the war in Iran drove a lot of political messaging and actual voting. Texas and Mississippi have distinct political histories, and voters had plenty of reasons to reject Republican candidates beyond the cost of hamburgers.

But beef offers a useful lens through which to understand the election. The Republican Party had built a coalition promising to defend rural producers, restore working-class prosperity, and protect traditional American abundance. But its beef market policies broke each of those promises.

When the administration tried to protect domestic producers, it left consumers with unaffordable groceries. When it tried to help consumers, it hurt ranchers. And its immigration policies threatened the workers essential to the entire industry.

Ultimately, the administration asked all three constituencies to accept a lower standard of living.

For centuries, the ability of ordinary Americans to afford beef has been part of the country’s informal social contract. It is a small expression of a larger promise: that even if inequality explodes to unprecedented heights, economic growth should trickle down into tangible improvements in everyday life.

In 1840, William Henry Harrison understood the political power of promising workers roast beef. In 2026, Republicans discovered the political cost of telling them they could live without it.

For progressives and leftists, the lesson is that governing for working-class prosperity requires more than promising lower prices or higher wages. It requires understanding how the goods Americans depend on are actually produced and developing policies capable of expanding supply while protecting the livelihoods of the workers and producers as well as the natural environment that make that abundance possible. Republicans learned the political cost of failing to deliver roast beef. The Left now has to figure out how to put it back on the table.

Nicholas Brown works at Upsolve, a nonprofit that erases debt for low-income Americans through free bankruptcy assistance. He previously worked in investment research at Bridgewater Associates.

scraped.description: The Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief explaining why the tariffs violate statutory requirements, and also run afoul of the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.
scraped.body_text:

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Tariffs

The Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief explaining why the tariffs violate statutory requirements, and also run afoul of the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

Ilya Somin | 11.14.2026 10:45 AM

Yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp. v. Trump , the first case challenging Donald Trump's massive 50% Section 338 tariffs against Canadian imports. The plaintiff is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That case resulted in the tariffs' invalidation by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch , and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.

We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice. Here is a summary of our key arguments, which should soon be posted at the Cato website:

This brief explains why Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 cannot be used to impose the tariffs enacted by Defendants, and why doing so violates the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

The Court should strike down the Section 338 duties for three reasons. First, Section 338 requires that any tariffs imposed be in response to discriminatory trade restrictions enacted by foreign trading partners, and that those tariffs "offset" the barriers imposed by those countries. The Section 338 tariffs imposed by the Trump administration violate both of these requirements. In addition, Section 338 has been superseded by later statutes and is no longer operative.

Second, the major questions doctrine forecloses interpreting Section 338 to permit the President to impose extraordinary import taxes whenever another country imposes any trade restrictions or declines to purchase American goods. to "speak clearly" when it assigns to the executive "decisions of vast 'economic and political significance.'" The sweeping power claimed by the administration in this case undeniably raises a major question, and it is at the very least unclear that Section 338 actually grants such vast authority.

Third, stripping the statute's qualitative conditions of operative force violates the nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegation of legislative power to the executive. An extremely high rate ceiling of 50 percent cannot substitute for clear legislative limiting how and when tariffs can be imposed.

Cato and I (together with Prof. Michael McConnell) also recently submitted an amicus brief in litigation challenging Trump's massive Section 301 tariffs.

NEXT: Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter , and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain .

scraped.title: Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case
scraped.description: It is on behalf of the Cato Institute and myself.
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Immigration

It is on behalf of the Cato Institute and myself.

Ilya Somin | 11.14.2026 10:35 AM

On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).

The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes. It relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump , the tariff case I helped litigate. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds .

We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono. Stanford Law School Prof. and former federal judge Michael McConnell, also worked with us on the brief. He is one of the nation's leading experts on executive power, a prominent conservative originalist constitutional law scholar, and was our lead counsel in the Supreme Court phase of the IEEPA tariff case.

Here is a summary of our arguments:

As the Supreme Court emphasized in its recent decisions striking down Donald Trump's Massive IEEPA tariffs, "the Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people." Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump , 607 U.S. 229, 241 (2026) The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, "the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union." Just months ago, the Supreme Court in Learning Resources applied those fundamental principles to hold that the President may not use a general grant of authority to "regulate … importation" to impose tariffs, because the power to "regulate" is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power. This case asks whether the same President—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a "restriction" on entry—may accomplish by a different label what Learning Resources forbade.

The exaction here is a tax. Its "defining feature" is that it raises revenue. Learning Resources , 607 U.S. at 241. It is neither a mere fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. The power to "restrict" entry is not the power to "tax" entry. To limit or qualify entry says nothing about charging for it, and the Government can identify no statute in which the words "restrict" or "restriction" confer tax authority.

The Immigration and Nationality Act contains express, detailed provisions for fees and payments, setting each amount and specifying how the funds are collected and spent. This confirms the absence of a generalized, unlimited discretionary presidential taxing power. Congress does not "hide elephants in mouseholes," and this case involves a very large elephant. Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass'ns , 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001). In more than a century, no President has used Section 212(f) or Section 215(a) of the INA to raise revenue, a point the Government does not dispute. As the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, that absence is "strong evidence" the power does not exist.

In addition, the government's interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political issue to the executive. The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive.

I have previously criticized the $100,000 H-1B fee on both legal and policy grounds here , here , and here .

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 14, 1922

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter , and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain .

Show Comments (2)

Nate Jurewicz | 11.14.2026 7:00 AM

scraped.title: Iran War Day 260: Iranian Tanker Attacks Continue
scraped.description: State of the Union: CENTCOM denied that Iran struck a radar installation in Bahrain.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
Iran continued its campaign against civilian shipping in the Strait of Hormuz with another strike on a tanker Saturday morning.

The IRGC claimed the tanker struck a mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. Iran’s state-affiliated Tasnim news service reported five such incidents since Thursday night.

Despite continued Iranian pressure on maritime traffic, world oil production has rebounded to roughly prewar levels. Because of reduced demand after several months of severe energy market disruption, a supply surplus is now glutting world markets. Increased production costs and limited refinery capacity has kept consumer prices well above their prewar levels.

The IRGC also claimed Friday to have struck an American radar installation in Bahrain. CENTCOM denied the report, saying it had intercepted the attack.

Brent crude closed Friday at $96.29 per barrel. AAA reported Saturday’s national average prices per gallon as $3.84 for regular gas and $6.07 for diesel.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

items.summary: Iran would be unwinnable for any president. But Trump is particularly ill-suited to run a forever war. The post For Republicans, the War Is a Political Gordian Knot appeared first on The American Conservative. Politics For Republicans, the War Is a Political Gordian Knot Iran would be unwinnable for any president. But Trump is particularly ill-suited to run a forever war. scraped.title: For Republicans, the War Is a Political Gordian Knot
scraped.description: Iran would be unwinnable for any president. But Trump is particularly ill-suited to run a forever war.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Iran would be unwinnable for any president. But Trump is particularly ill-suited to run a forever war.

In the final weeks before Democrats officially replace the GOP “ trifecta ” with majorities so large they effectively repeal the 1994 “Republican revolution,” one of the most important questions in American politics is: What was President Donald Trump thinking when he listened to the Iran hawks?

Of course, that question will be explored thoroughly in the coming decades, regardless of whether Trump’s Oliver Hardy successfully extricates himself from the latest fine mess the neoconservatives’ Stan Laurel has gotten us into.

So perhaps a more interesting question is what the Iran hawks were thinking when they decided Trump would be the best vehicle for their aims. How could they expect him to see through to the end the war that even George W. Bush wouldn’t—and couldn’t—give them?

When trying to escape blame for the midterm rout the war inflicted on Republicans, these hawks often point out that Trump’s job approval ratings were already low before he attacked Iran.

Indeed, Trump’s numbers would have been bad enough for a normal midterm election loss, assuming he didn’t find ways to resuscitate them (such as by allowing inflation to continue to fall rather than by causing it go back up ). But they weren’t bad enough to lose Kansas or Mississippi, nor had the president yet completely blown his credibility on the economy.

But the question Iran hawks ought to have pondered (and apparently didn’t) is how a president who was already underwater in the polls, and who has usually been underwater for most of his decade in national politics, was going to sustain public support for a military venture likely to last longer than the Venezuela operation.

Trump himself had never attempted an intervention with such obvious and long-lasting electoral and economic consequences. His decision not to make a real case to the voters or seek authorization from Congress are among the signs he did not expect an engagement of this duration.

Our old friend George W. Bush spent down his once sky-high approval ratings in the sands of Iraq, putting them near record lows well before the 2007-08 financial crisis. Even W’s father, who received a tremendous boost from his shorter and more successful Persian Gulf adventure, couldn’t sustain those numbers once the 1990–91 recession hit and public perceptions of the economy soured.

This caper was like a combination of the type of war that annihilated Dubya’s political capital and Poppy’s “read my lips” campaign-promise violation. And just as the elder Bush’s tax increase arguably worsened preexisting economic problems, Trump’s Iran energy shock indisputably poured gasoline—high-price gasoline at that—on the embers of an inflationary fire that might otherwise have burnt itself out.

Trump has never really agreed with the Iran hawks about what was necessary for success, even as he gave them their war. He has never been willing to pursue a military operation of that size. He did not lead a political coalition that would be unified in support of such a war, and was reliant on working-class voters who would not and could not absorb its domestic economic costs.

For the coalition necessary to keep Trump’s party in power, the war and the economy cannot be so neatly separated as hawks like to imagine . And the war itself was unpopular right from the beginning, before it produced the biggest costs for ordinary Americans.

Republicans who might have waged the Iran war in the way its supporters envisioned didn’t, for three reasons. One is that Bush—the likeliest champion of a drive to Tehran—was already bogged down in Iraq and Afghanistan. The second is that Bush’s conflicts did not go well enough to make the political case for another war, even if there had been the money or military capacity available to fight it. Third, Republicans who wanted new wars or continued to defend the old ones couldn’t get elected president.

Trump solved all these problems for the Iran hawks. Convinced that the relative successes of his more limited military interventions across two terms compared to Bush’s more open-ended ones meant he had found the cheat code to avoiding forever wars, he stumbled into an entirely new problem.

Will it be worth the cost, even by the Iran hawks’ own standards? The war doesn’t yet seem likely to end the regime, and over the longer term it could have the opposite of its intended effect on Tehran’s nuclear ambitions. Trump was a leader who was simultaneously supportive of Israel and skeptical of Middle Eastern wars. Now leaders who wish to signal the latter increasingly eschew the former. But maybe the damage inflicted on Iranian military capacity will be sufficient to justify this campaign in the minds of its supporters.

The voters, at any rate, feel differently. And while some of the Republicans who lost their elections as a result may deserve it, the Trump 2024 voters enduring higher gas and diesel prices surely don’t.

W. James Antle III is executive editor of the Washington Examiner magazine and a contributing editor of The American Conservative .

(ANTHONY WALLACE/AFP via Getty Images) Both President Donald Trump and China’s leader Xi Jinping have taken steps to prevent the Taiwan issue from becoming a m...

scraped.title: Beijing’s Taiwan ‘Reunification’ Dreams Are Fanciful
scraped.description: Taipei may become friendlier to Beijing, but the Taiwanese cherish their sovereignty.
scraped.author: Ted Galen Carpenter
scraped.body_text:
Taipei may become friendlier to Beijing, but the Taiwanese cherish their sovereignty.

Both President Donald Trump and China’s leader Xi Jinping have taken steps to prevent the Taiwan issue from becoming a major source of tension in bilateral relations. Their joint goal was especially evident during the two summit meetings between Trump and Xi this year. Despite Beijing’s recent conciliatory approach, however, there is no indication that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has relinquished its long-term goal of absorbing Taiwan and ending its status as a democratic, de facto independent state.

Xi’s regime appears to be pursuing a two-pronged strategy to achieve that objective: Beijing sustains an uncompromising, sometimes even militarily menacing, policy toward the current Taiwanese government, which is controlled by the officially pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party (DPP); at the same time, PRC officials drop abundant hints that Beijing would be willing to adopt a less confrontational posture toward the DPP’s more moderate rival, the Kuomintang Party (KMT) that last governed Taiwan from 2008 to 2016. Beijing has already extended political olive branches to the KMT leader Cheng Li-wun, especially during her visit to the mainland in April 2026.

In an October 6 article in Foreign Policy , Michael Poznansky, a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, and Ian Easton, a senior nonresident fellow at the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security, contend that U.S. leaders need to examine the possibility of a

bloodless annexation, whereby an elected government in Taipei concludes a treaty effectively ceding Taiwan’s territory to the People’s Republic of China. Such a strategy, known by euphemisms like “winning without fighting” or “peaceful reunification,” is Beijing’s preferred outcome . And Washington is unprepared for it.

Xi and other PRC leaders undoubtedly would prefer to achieve Taiwan’s reunification with the mainland through political and economic means. Using military force to do so would be highly dangerous and unpredictable. Indeed, such a course would probably lead to war with the United States and Japan, the island’s principal military protectors.

PRC leaders have long proposed the formula of “one country, two systems” as a model for reunification. Taiwan would become part of a reunited China, but it would not be controlled from Beijing. In essence, the promised one country, two systems arrangement is similar to the agreement that Chinese leaders signed in 1997 when possession of Hong Kong was transferred from Britain to the PRC. The provision for Hong Kong’s political autonomy was even written into its Basic Law and guaranteed for 50 years. The one country, two systems model for Taiwan would include even greater promised autonomy, including on military affairs. Moreover, unlike the agreement regarding Hong Kong, current PRC policy does not specify an end date for Taiwan’s autonomous status.

Nevertheless, Beijing is unlikely to succeed in ending Taiwan’s de facto independence solely through greater political and economic influence. Extensive damage to Beijing’s credibility with the Taiwanese occurred when the PRC executed a security crackdown on Hong Kong in June 2020 . The territory’s promised autonomy was so drastically narrowed as to become virtually meaningless. The media mogul Jimmy Lai and other vocal democracy activists subsequently received long prison sentences, and a suffocating atmosphere of coerced political conformity settled over the once ideologically vibrant city.

Taiwan’s population was watching, and most Taiwanese did not like what they saw . Indeed, the Hong Kong lesson was a major factor in the DPP’s subsequent surge in political power.

Granted, current President Lai Ching-te of the DPP has dissipated much of that gain because of corruption within his administration, as well as his own authoritarian abuses. Many Taiwanese also worry about Lai’s extremely hardline, confrontational rhetoric and policies toward Beijing.

Yet there is a crucial difference between a growing desire by Taiwanese voters to rein in DPP excesses and a willingness to abandon Taiwan’s status as a de facto independent country. Numerous opinion polls have confirmed that no more than a tiny percentage of Taiwanese favor reunification with the totalitarian, one-party state across the strait. The hostile reaction to the PRC’s crackdown on Hong Kong indicated that the Taiwanese are determined not to let their island suffer a similar fate. Even most KMT supporters do not want to see Taiwan become Beijing’s puppet or their party to become subsumed into the PRC.

If Xi and other PRC leaders are content with seeing a more conciliatory, less confrontational government emerge in Taipei, they have a very good chance of achieving their objective. That benign outcome is especially likely if they are simultaneously willing to reduce the PRC’s military presence in and around the Taiwan Strait.

But if they continue to press for reunification (even solely by peaceful means) they are likely to be disappointed. Indeed, even if Beijing pursued a more limited goal of transforming Taiwan into an obedient, albeit still nominally self-governing, client under the KMT, such an effort would likely fail.

In her March 3 Foreign Affairs article, Cheng Li-wun, the KMT leader, conveyed her party’s orientation rather pointedly:

As Beijing and Washington compete for influence in the Pacific, how Taiwan manages cross-strait relations affects whether the region remains peaceful and stable. Many observers assume that Taiwan must choose to align itself with one side or the other. But this binary framing is misleading. Taiwan is strongest when it preserves space to pursue its own needs, not when it becomes a frontline outpost for one country or a subordinate partner to the other.

There is not a yawning gap between the views of most KMT leaders and those of the more sensible elements of the DPP regarding policy toward Beijing. Lai, though president, is among the more extreme (and sometimes recklessly assertive) pro-independence party activists. Voters may well reject that faction in the next national election in favor of the KMT, but such an outcome would not signal a popular mandate for Taipei to embrace an appeasement policy toward the PRC.

It is appropriate for U.S. policymakers to carefully monitor developments, but there is no need to panic nor to conjure improbable worst-case scenarios involving a clever PRC ploy to conquer Taiwan via a political offensive.

Ted Galen Carpenter is a contributing editor at The American Conservative , a senior fellow at the Randolph Bourne Institute, and a senior fellow at the Libertarian Institute. He also served in various policy positions for 37 years at the Cato Institute. Dr. Carpenter is the author of 13 books and more than 1,200 articles on international affairs. His latest book is Unreliable Watchdog: The News Media and U.S. Foreign Policy (2022).

scraped.title: John Brennan's Son Arrested For Alleged Possession Of CSAM
scraped.description: The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was arrested Friday for possession of child sexual abuse material.
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Ex-CIA Director John Brennan’s Son Arrested For Alleged Possession Of Child Sexual Abuse Material
scraped.body_text:
Editor’s note: This article addresses the alleged possession and distribution of sexually explicit images of children.

The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was arrested Friday for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material, otherwise known as child pornography.

The 40-year-old Kyle Brennan was arrested at his place of work in Virginia, and the FBI executed a search warrant on his cell phone, which allegedly contains “sexually explicit” materials of children. He is being charged with “transportation of child pornography.”

Court documents allege his phone contained “approximately 88 images that appeared to depict minor girls, including prepubescent girls, engaged in sexually explicit conduct,” which included an explicit image of a toddler.

According to documents, there was a “fully nude, pubescent minor girl on a locker bench” whose “wrist and ankles were bound and her mouth was gagged.”

“There is probable cause to believe that on or about April 7, 2024, BRENNAN knowingly transported child pornography using a means or facility of interstate or foreign commerce,” court documents state.

The Warrenton, Virginia, Police Department responded to two CyberTipline Reports from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), according to the Department of Justice. The local police identified an account registered to Brennan, which appeared to have been used to upload CSAM, which included an image the Fauquier County Sheriff’s Office was able to identify as a 12-year-old girl, the Department of Justice said. Warrenton is in Fauquier County.

According to the Department of Justice, the Fauquier Sheriff’s Office searched Brennan’s residence and devices in the summer of 2024, and the office referred the case to the FBI on Oct. 2, 2026.

Brennan faces a minimum sentence of five years and up to 20 years in prison. He did not return a comment request from the Daily Mail.

The arrest comes as John Brennan is himself under investigation for concocting the Russia collusion hoax. Evidence shows Brennan and other Obama administration officials, such as Federal Bureau of Investigation Director James Comey and former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper, conspired to perpetrate the hoax.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe has suggested Brennan and Clapper are still liable for their alleged crimes, even as some argue the statute of limitations is up.

scraped.title: I Froze My Eggs. Was It Worth It? Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Weekend Press: Is egg freezing worth it? Why does Oprah’s agent eat worms? Is ‘You’ve Got Mail’ a rom-com or an ode to capitalism? Suzy Weiss on Silicon Valley’s sex spies. And more!
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
Welcome back to The Weekend Press ! Today, Suzy Weiss sits down with the Hollywood superagent who’s texting Elon Musk and beefing with Harvey Weinstein. Liel Leibovitz argues that the “You’ve Got Mail” reboot will make capitalism romantic again. “Tech bro whisperer” Molly O’Shea says the richest men in the world would rather chase samurai swords than women. And more!

But first: Poppy Damon on what drove her to freeze her eggs . . .

I think egg freezing might be a false promise. But last month, I visited a Manhattan clinic to drop $8,000 on doing exactly that.

I knew fertility start-ups had been bombarding me with advertisements on Instagram because there’s money to be made off millennial women’s anxiety. I also knew most women who freeze their eggs don’t come back for them.

And yet, for two weeks, I injected myself with medication every day, and abstained from drinking and sex and weight-loss drugs. I was grumpy, sore, and constantly hungry. And I did all this to obtain the nebulous feeling that I had a little bit more time to fulfill my dream of becoming a mother.

In the media, the woman who does this is a stereotype. A career-obsessed urban thirtysomething who blithely thinks she can painlessly press pause on her biological clock. Certain men online might assume that my childless existence at the age of 33 is “my fault.” That I’m single because I’m too “picky.” Or that I am choosing to be a “geriatric mother” because I want to prolong my hedonistic lifestyle in New York City.

But the truth is, I was married at 24, and started trying for a baby at 28—and nothing went the way I imagined it would. This is the story of what happened instead.

— Poppy Damon

Hollywood superagent Ari Emanuel—who represents Oprah Winfrey, Adele, Larry David, Mark Wahlberg, and Martin Scorsese—starts the day with a cup of live worms (“to eat the bad bacteria in my gut”) and is a big advocate for smoking toad venom. But he was drinking black coffee when Suzy Weiss asked him about the sexiest man alive. “I don’t think about that,” he said. But he does think about his brother Rahm, who he says will be the next president; his friend Elon Musk; and his enemy Harvey Weinstein, whom he was very rude about in his recent memoir—causing Weinstein to insult him right back via a representative. “I can’t believe he can afford a publicist,” Emanuel tells Suzy. “I thought he was broke.”

You might think “You’ve Got Mail” is a romantic comedy about two bookshop owners. Think again! According to Liel Leibovitz, it’s actually an ode to capitalism, which is “always innovating and always growing and inviting us all along for the ride.” So this week, when Warner Bros. announced that Nora Ephron’s cult classic is getting a reboot, Liel thought: “What better time for it? After all, we seem to have forgotten the point of capitalism, which is to make all of us happier and more comfortable.” In this week’s Things Worth Remembering, he honors a film in which “shopping is no mere material exercise in wasting time and spending money, but a form of self-expression.”

Not one, not two, but three sex scandals have hit the second-most valuable company in the world this week. And all of them involve the same man, the now-ex-CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang. So who better to have on Second Thought than “Tech bro whisperer” Molly O’Shea, who travels the country interviewing the world’s top founders? She chatted to Dan and Suzy about why the midterms will make Big Tech woke again, why none of these guys will ever find love—and why they’re developing genetically advanced dogs that can go into battle. “These guys think they’re warriors,” Molly says.

Click the link below to watch the episode, or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This week, Dr. Bryant Lin wrote about using AI to cure his own cancer; Rod Dreher reviewed the “gripping” new movie by Ben Shapiro; and Kat Rosenfield analyzed the Cornell 7’s texts. Catch up here:

A new batch of ads from single Free Press ers is live on our site. Click here to meet two bachelorettes in Australia, or another bachelorette in Chicago. Your special someone could be just one email away! If you’d like to take a chance at Free Press love, write a paragraph that defines you, including your age, where you live, and what you’re looking for, and send it over to Cupid@TheFP.com.

How should you spend the rest of your weekend? We asked our contributor Larissa Phillips for her recommendations . . .

🌮 Cook . . . It’s almost Thanksgiving, so I should be making piecrusts to freeze, waking up my sourdough starter, and cleaning out the fridge—but I am more likely to spend my time making foods I actually want to eat right now. This will include at least one recipe from my favorite food Instagrammer, Corre Larkin , who just released a cookbook ( Season to Taste ) filled with comfort foods that are perfect for the coming cold weather. Her Hachis Parmentier (basically a French-style shepherd’s pie) is a staple in my house, but this weekend I’m making her Asian tacos —pork or beef sautéed inside squares of Napa cabbage, then rolled and dipped in a soy-ginger sauce. I’ll get back to American-style carbs in a couple weeks.

🎧 Listen . . . The second season of Sold a Story (hosted by Emily Hanford for American Public Media) is out, and I’m two episodes behind, so I’ll be catching up on this while I make my tacos. In 2022, the pod’s first season addressed the flawed methods used to teach reading—and arguably caused a seismic shift in instructional methods across America. Season 2 zeroes in on the most effective method to teach almost anything: direct instruction, duh. It’s shocking to hear how a “mountain of data” was repeatedly brushed aside in favor of vibes and romantic notions about children finding their own paths. Both seasons of SAS are essential listening for anyone interested in their own children’s education—and for the rest of us, who might hope for a widely literate populace at some point.

📚 Read . . . I generally don’t consume mysteries or thrillers but I make an eager exception for the strange, smart, twisted novels by my fellow FP columnist Kat Rosenfield , which have literally caused me to gasp out loud at some shocking plot revelation. If you miss the days when you regularly dissolved yourself into the pages of a book in order to follow the convoluted path of a person completely unlike yourself, gathering clues the writer has dropped like tiny crumbs that you have to whack your way through an overgrown thistly glen to gather, until the thoroughly satisfying end when all those disparate bits come together, have I got a recommendation for you. How to Survive in the Woods is ideal for this first chilly weekend, when you are more or less required to spend some time curled up under a blanket with a good book. You have a couch, so use it. This is actually far more important than cleaning out the fridge or making pie dough.

They write. They edit. They post. And now: They pose! This week, a few Free Pressers spent a rainy New York afternoon modeling for our new-and-improved merch shop. Click here to order!

scraped.description: Drinking his coffee black, Ari Emanuel talks about losing Taylor Swift, his brother running for president, and feeling like ‘a pimple on the ass of an ant.’
scraped.author: Suzy Weiss
scraped.body_text:
About 40 seconds after I sit down across from Ari Emanuel, his phone rings. “I think you’re going to owe me money,” Hollywood’s superagent tells his interlocutor.

Emanuel—who represents Oprah Winfrey, Mark Wahlberg, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Adele, Denzel Washington, and many more—doesn’t do hellos. His friend on the phone lost a bet and owes him two bucks. But Emanuel, a billionaire and compulsive dealmaker, tells him that he’ll settle for just one dollar, “framed and signed.”

An assistant—there’s a battalion of them—hands Emanuel a black coffee in a to-go cup.

It’s 9 a.m., but Emanuel, 65, tan and trim, has been up since 4, running though his health regimen. It includes a workout, a dip in a cold plunge, and a cup of live worms “to eat the bad bacteria in my gut”—as he explains in his recently released memoir, Roll the Calls , which details his 30-odd years in the entertainment business. On the health score, he writes: “If you want to win at life, then isn’t Job One having more life?”

scraped.title: I Froze My Eggs. Was It Worth It?
scraped.description: Maybe egg freezing is a waste of money. Maybe it’s the only way for me to have a baby, writes Poppy Damon.
scraped.author: Poppy Damon
scraped.body_text:
In the story of the emperor’s new clothes, the fashion-obsessed monarch is fooled by two con men into buying something he’s told is the latest trend. They weave the outfit out of nothing at all, promising it is only visible to those who are discerning enough to see it. None of the adults in the story are brave enough to say anything; in the end, it is a child who points out that the emperor is in fact going around stark naked.

This fairy tale came into my head when I went for my first appointment at a fertility clinic in Manhattan. I was about to spend close to $8,000—granted, mostly covered by insurance—for something invisible. I was about to freeze my eggs. As many of them as I possibly could.

In the media, the woman who does this is a stereotype. A career-obsessed urban thirtysomething who blithely thinks she can easily and painlessly press pause on her biological clock. But generally speaking, women aren’t that naive. As a journalist who has reported on the economics of fertility, I knew I was being sold a feeling of assurance, rather than a true insurance policy for motherhood. I also knew that, two years ago, a review of 27 studies that together looked at 13,724 patients found that only 11 percent of women who froze their eggs for nonmedical reasons returned to thaw them. Of those women, only 29 percent achieved a live birth. In other words: Most women who freeze their eggs either don’t become mothers, or find another way to get there.

I also knew that fertility start-ups were bombarding me with advertisements on Instagram because there’s money to be made off millennial women’s anxiety. One offers women the chance to freeze their eggs for free if they give half their haul away to strangers in need. I knew, too, that a lot of companies offer young women the chance to put their dreams of becoming a mother on ice, to keep them at the grindstone as long as possible.

And yet, with open eyes, I was handing over close to a thousand dollars of my own money to do this.

Was I the emperor?

scraped.title: The moral confusion of MeToo
scraped.author: John Maier
scraped.h1: The moral confusion of MeToo It is built to sow anxiety
scraped.body_text:
MeToo has tabloid urges. (Credit: Lia Toby/Getty)

MeToo has tabloid urges. (Credit: Lia Toby/Getty)

Being a student during the high-water mark of MeToo, 10 years ago, was a curiously chastening experience. The authorities at my university resolved that all undergraduates should participate in a mandatory “consent workshop” during freshers’ week. Gathered in circles on the floor, mixed-sex groups of hungover 18-year-olds, whose lifetime sexual experience tended overwhelmingly toward zero, were made to assess a series of hypothetical case-studies. The first few examples eased you in (accounts of clear-cut criminality). But the exercise quickly took on a more Talmudic quality: the vignettes assuming such a level of baroque moral intricacy — crucial information about the sexual encounter strategically withheld, characters multiply wrong-footed by their epistemic environments, the gravity of the transgressions in play held in a kind of suspended animation — that it became radically unclear who, if anyone, was to blame for what.

Luckily by that stage our instructor, a worldly wise third-year, had made it helpfully clear that this was a test with only one correct answer. If you looked closely enough, it always turned out that, in attempting to have sex, things had gone disastrously, perhaps irreparably, morally wrong for our male protagonist. He was the perennial villain of the piece. Indeed, the more creatively unforgiving you could make your interpretation of his offense, the more notional “points” you seemed to earn in the resulting discussion (the rule of thumb, I suppose, being that the more esoteric an injustice, the graver it is, because the more often “marginalized” by society at large).

As the vignettes took on the textual complexity of High Victorian literature, I saw a seasick look creep into the faces of some of my heterosexual male peers. Most of them were self-aware enough to realize that the odds were already stacked against them in the sexual marketplace; but this degree of liability was greater than they could ever have feared. One asked, subversively, why, if workshops like these in fact helped to reduce sexual wrongdoing, they were not used by the state to combat other kinds of crime. I interjected that his rhetorical question sounded rather “problematic” to me and mentally awarded myself another point. By the end of the struggle session, I watched these defeated young men trudge from the room contemplating an immediate future of nervous celibacy.

By Kathleen Stock

Of course, no political ideology is ever flattered by having its central tenets filtered through the minds of zealous, under-socialized, Oxbridge freshers. Yet, within the MeToo movement proper, there is significant reason to fear that the tendency toward a certain kind of moral hallucination is a feature, rather than a bug — the pressure to discover heightened moral seriousness in minor as well as major infractions being key to the movement’s forward propulsion.

One tension within MeToo has always been that it is simultaneously a project of vigilante sexual justice (aiming to take out select famous and powerful men) and a social movement that aspires to recast collective social norms in a more progressive mold.

In achieving the first aim (claiming famous male scalps), all kinds of sensationalist smear tactics are usually deemed to be fair game. Revelations merely trashing the characters of the rich and famous share frontpage space with allegations of more obvious criminal seriousness. When there is no smoking gun, the strategy can seem to devolve into something like “death by a thousand reputational cuts” — no single anecdote or detail needing to be probative, the prosecution’s case resting on the quantity, rather than quality, of the loosely gathered evidence.

Indeed, there is an unsettling sense in which MeToo attack jobs sometimes indulge the very same, unnervingly tabloid, urges of the era they claim to despise. Their fixation with inspecting the lives of celebrity targets for unedifying (but often non-criminal) behavior is frequently only faintly disguised by the new puritanical lens used to justify their exposés.

This all is, you may think, part of the bargain the famous strike for notoriety. But the approach prototypical MeToo activists take to indicting their celebrity targets spells disaster when coupled with the movement’s other aim — that of motivating better collective social-sexual norms. In this conflation of the criminal and the creepy, the clear-cut and the vague, the movement has sown moral confusions that end up pathologizing vast swathes of ordinary life. This tendency would probably more often be called out were it not that criticism of the movement’s tactics was in turn so often glibly conflated with condoning the wrongdoing of the criminals it sometimes unmasks.

Just look at recent weeks. Russell Brand will spend 10 years in prison for a rape conviction; following a long-anticipated joint ITV and Guardian investigation, David Walliams now too stands accused of potentially serious criminal wrongdoing in his behavior towards young girls who were below the age of consent. (The Met has announced it is now investigating historical claims against Walliams, too.) Yet in the same breath as these bleak allegations are relayed, further aspersions are attached of a less obviously criminal, more dubiously moralistic kind: exploiting their “power” and “status”, and behaving in lewd or “inappropriate” ways. Rolled in as part of a package deal frontloaded with graver allegations, the implication seems to be that the wider public should accept that these lesser offenses too are now grounds to socially and professionally destroy someone.

By Julie Burchill

The move to indict grubby but consensual sexual behavior becomes destabilized when one remembers that, in their wider thinking about social-sexual norms, many MeToo activists are uncompromisingly “sex positive”: they think of mutual consent as the final word when it comes to judging the moral appropriateness of all sexual interactions.

The underlying tension that results is unmanageable. The reluctance to articulate stable standards of wrongdoing that go beyond consent-violation leads to a heavy reliance on less specific insinuations. Wrongdoers are typically accused of “manipulating” or “exploiting” their “positions of power”. (When interpreted in a thinly relational way, it can become quite unclear who the “powerful” can enjoy a morally acceptable sexual “dynamic” with — only those, perhaps, exactly as rich and powerful as themselves?) In news reports, women who were young adults at the time they met Walliams are spoken of as having been “ groomed ” by him: a phrase once reserved for children, now applied freely to fully adult, but vulnerably non-famous, people too. The rhetorical effect of such “ concept creep” is to extend the scope of a term while attempting to smoothly retain its original moral severity (a bit like calling every political development you dislike “fascist”).

The Guardian’s extensive investigation into Walliams’s sexual life certainly suggests it was an insalubrious affair. Walliams, it is alleged, routinely courted women many years younger than himself, often contacting them through friends at modeling agencies; he would send them unctuous handwritten notes; when one woman sofa-surfed at his London townhouse he “pawed” at her to come and share his bed. While serving as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent, Walliams allegedly “stared at [the] chest” of a female runner on the show “in a way that made her feel uncomfortable”; later he was overheard referring to her as “the one with the arse”. A different complainant recollects that, while visiting Walliams’s TV dressing room as part of a larger group, “the door was shut and we were alone with him” in a way that “she now feels that was inappropriate”. Sitting alongside far grimmer (and potentially criminal) allegations, it is difficult to know what to make of reports of mere creepiness or indeed anecdotes that read as something closer to innuendo (since when was “shutting doors” any part of a case for wholesale reputational ruin?).

On occasion, the quoted verdicts of complainants are used as interpretive ballast: Walliams was, in their words, “pushy”, “highly inappropriate”, and “a weird old man, like, trying his luck”. One woman, while acknowledging that her sexual contact with Walliams was consensual, elaborates at length : “OK, it’s legal… but the context of who you’re having sex with — if that person is double your age, if that person has known you from a young age and promised you things and is in a much bigger position of power than you, both in age, in work, in finance, in stature and size, like, everything, I really don’t think that’s OK.” By leaning rhetorically on such anguished, but somewhat hard-to-parse, attempts to theorize the non-criminal moral transgressions of men like Walliams, activists operating within MeToo’s moral paradigm attempt to let themselves off the hook: allowing the standard that he is supposed to have flouted to remain morally lively but conveniently impressionistic. Added to which, every last lurid detail then becomes admissible as evidence in the chaotic moral case being constructed.

But the collateral damage of this approach is to foist the same newly moralized standards onto the wider public, too. There, the movement’s effect has often been to pathologize benign behaviors, sowing doubts about the propriety of relationships between colleagues, “age gaps”, “power imbalances”, and quotidian kinds of romantic indiscretion.

Many people sense that the standards MeToo has conventionally employed in taking down the powerful sit uneasily with life as they know it to be. The famous injunction to “believe all women”, for example, was a clearly socially irresponsible piece of public anti-epistemology (what are you supposed to do when, as sometimes happens, two women disagree with each other?).

In placing so much evidential weight on retrospective reassessments of past sexual episodes, many onlookers are also left with the uneasy sense that MeToo’s baroque morality can make the ethical status of physical encounters virtually impossible to read in the moment they are occurring. The philosopher Bernard Williams famously coined the term “moral luck” to describe a feature of actions whose justificatory status depends essentially on future contingencies the decision-maker is not in a position to assess at the moment of action. (Should Anna Karenina run off with Count Vronsky?, Williams asks, to illustrate his concept: the decision would be retroactively justified should their romance eventually flourish, catastrophically unjustified otherwise.) On MeToo’s background logic, it can seem that many powerful men, and by extension men in general, are subject to a radically pervasive kind of “sexual luck”: their every sexual overture and action held hostage to later becoming a catastrophic moral error, depending on the contingent twists in how the recipient comes to think of its “appropriateness” years down the line.

By Poppy Sowerby

Though exquisitely sensitive to the nuances and power differentials of “problematic” sexual encounters with famous men, MeToo remains strangely deaf to the subtly malign effects its own ideology has on wider sexual culture. The movement’s proponents are an odd mixture of cynicism and naivety. Cynicism — for example, in constantly dialing up the moralistic mood music to 11, pitching all manner of sins in the same hysterical key. The movement’s politics, on the other hand, are often naïvely obtuse. With each new scandal, the media finds another opportunity to declare a fresh crisis, reasoning that every country, profession and industry is eligible for its own bespoke “MeToo moment”. On occasion, sympathetic commentators allow themselves to wonder in amnesiac fashion whether this time may at last prove to be the decisive cultural reckoning — the moment that, somehow, finally straightens out whatever crooked feature of certain human beings’ natures inclines them towards such transgressions. In the end, the implicit hope that one last push in the direction of regulation or censorious vigilance will finally give force to a rule against rule-breaking is an obvious chimera.

MeToo has, to its undoubted credit, exposed a fair number of utter villains. But a movement that so unforgivingly holds others accountable for their every transgression cannot exempt itself from questions about its own methods. Its worst excesses see it increasingly lump together bona-fide criminality with behavior that veers closer to the simply debauched, emotionally cruel or merely awkward. It then relies on the graver cases to moralize the weaker ones by brute association. While leaning heavily on flexibly impressionistic assessments, it pretends its rigoristic judgments are the outputs of a confidently worked-out theory of sexual morality, one fit to be approved and adopted by all. Such pretenses do the wider world an inadvertent wrong — and more than an impressionistic one.

John Maier is an UnHerd columnist and PhD student at the University of Oxford

scraped.title: Who whacked Jensen Huang?
scraped.author: Tom Ough
scraped.h1: Who whacked Jensen Huang? Conspiracy, not canoodling, undid him
scraped.body_text:
Was it a honeypot? (JG Fox/Getty)

Was it a honeypot? (JG Fox/Getty)

Rubin, Nvidia’s flagship GPU, is a technological marvel almost beyond compare. No bigger than a mid-sized charcuterie board, it nonetheless boasts 336 billion transistors, 224 streaming multiprocessors, and 896 specialized processing units called Tensor Cores. Deployed wisely, the resulting computational horsepower is just about equal to the task of juggling one wife and three mistresses.

Or not. Farewell, then, Jensen Huang, whose philandering was almost as remarkable as his leadership of Nvidia. In 1993, he and two other engineers sat in a booth in a Denny’s diner and sketched out a plan for a new chip company. Huang led the startup from the outset, and it was thanks to his vigor and foresight that Nvidia came to supply the chips that today power the AI revolution.

Nvidia became the world’s most valuable company; Huang, evidently, became one of the most irresistible men in commerce. In the past few days, though, the now former CEO’s clandestine love life has unraveled. On 29 October, The New York Times disclosed that he had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese intelligence asset. Alice is no familial relation, but there was certainly some incestuousness to the acquaintance: not only was she an executive at a firm supplied by Nvidia, she was also, it soon transpired, Jensen’s mistress. News of another mistress, this time one of Huang’s direct reports at Nvidia, soon followed. Huang, under investigation, resigned. Hours later, a third mistress came to light.

Huang’s story, then, is both an epic, corporate bildungsroman and a riotous, geopolitical bonkbuster. But it is also a whodunnit, for intelligence reports tend not to leak accidentally, and Huang had many foes. Silicon Valley is ablaze with rumor: who wanted Jensen gone, and why?

There are several competing theories. The less refined conspiracists, noting that three Israeli executives were among those who could replace Huang, have immediately blamed you-know-who. “I don’t have enough evidence for it,” said the Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker of this fanciful hypothesis, “but that’s not going to stop other people from suspecting that that is what took place.”

A more compelling theory was advanced yesterday by my UnHerd colleague Wolfgang Münchau. Wondering whether some bad commercial news was imminent, he wrote : “The Nvidia share price has fallen by nearly a third from its peak in early October. Will we hear the interim CEO declare her shock when she looks at the books?”

The most widespread speculation, though, is predicated on Huang’s championing of a wide and fast-growing ecosystem of AI developers. Many in this ecosystem use “open-source” AI. Namely: AI whose code is publicly available and thus easily augmented — by Chinese and Western developers alike. Techno-optimists, Huang included, view open-source as conducive to innovation and prosperity; it also ensures Nvidia a long queue of customers.

By Tom Ough

Those who are more fearful of powerful AI, however, consider open-source to be tantamount to nuclear proliferation. As such, the AI safety community, out of which grew the frontier lab Anthropic, wants powerful AI to be developed only by a small number of companies, each continuously scrutinized by third-party inspectors. These arguments have received friendly hearings in the Democratic Party, which, buoyed by its success in the midterms, is coalescing around the view that AI ought to be robustly regulated.

That adds up to plenty of enemies for Huang. But there are more: the US government’s China hawks. Seeking to keep its chief geopolitical rival away from the AI frontier, the White House has restricted the sale of chips to China. Somewhere in Inner Mongolia, though, the Chinese startup DeepSeek has been training its best model on Blackwell chips, the precursor to Rubin. Huang, who has publicly lobbied for the controls to be removed, is accused of turning a blind eye to large-scale smuggling of chips — with the suspicions exacerbated by his closeness to Alice.

So: whodunnit? Some in San Francisco have pointed the finger at Dario Amodei himself. Amodei is the chief executive of Anthropic and one of the figureheads of the AI safety movement. Could he be responsible for Huang’s defenestration? Was he heading off a secret Huang plan to develop frontier-class open models?

That it was Amodei specifically seems unlikely. Still, with only a little squinting, the hand of a rival can potentially be discerned in the reporting. Intriguingly, one of the New York Time s reporters who broke the story of that “close relationship” has related how a “tech industry contact” prompted him to look into Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s company. Tripp Mickle, the reporter, said on Tuesday that the source told him: “You really need to drop everything and look at this company.”

That conversation, according to Mickle, took place in August 2025. “And then about a month ago,” he continued, “we hear that our colleagues in Washington on the national security beat all of a sudden are hearing things about Alice Huang.”

Most telling here is the fact that the Times could refer to what ought to have been private briefings. Some part of the American deep state, it seems, lent the journalists a hand. It did so despite President Trump’s apparent affection for Huang — and despite the story’s potential disruption to Anthropic’s IPO, the success of which depends, to a significant extent, on investor confidence in the AI boom. The investigative journalist Glenn Greenwald, no friend to the deep state, writes that whoever wanted rid of Huang “wields extreme levels of power”. The briefing against Alice Huang, he said, was evidence-free, yet “instantly and uncritically ratified” by the American media. As for the infidelity: “Nobody actually believes that, in the age of Donald J. Trump, very powerful people rapidly fall due to extramarital affairs, right?”

Many additional questions present themselves, of which the most pressing is what happens next. Nvidia stock has nosedived, losing $550 billion of value . Huang, whom a Bloomberg report suggested is distraught, faces a congressional hearing. Perhaps the deep state will bring Nvidia to heel. Perhaps the leakers will be unmasked. Whether the American government will impose stringent regulation on the sector remains uncertain, and is likely to hinge on either an alarming demonstration of AI’s danger or simply a change of administration.

We can be confident, in the meantime, that the shenanigans, seen and unseen, will continue, that AI’s increasing geopolitical importance will manifest in further dossiers and defenestrations. Formerly the rockstars of technology, Huang and his peers have now been forced into the drearier role of hyper-scrutinized statesmen; scrutinized and threatened by their rivals, by their ideological enemies, by their own government and by foreign governments. More so than at any other time in modern history, senior appointments will need a clean record — which might come at the expense of some of the unorthodoxy upon which innovation depends.

For the moment, though, the honeytraps will continue. Security experts report that China is increasingly using the method to fish for intelligence about American startups. Opportunities for both espionage and espionage-related smearings abound. In San Francisco, the epicenter of frontier AI, there is a comically high preponderance of both nerdy men and what are affectionately known, even to themselves , as ABGs, or “Asian baby girls”. Huang is not the first businessman to develop a wandering eye, and he will not be the last.

What next, though, for the former CEO? For now, joked one wag , Huang’s nearly cleared diary will enable him to “spend more time with your wife”. Elon Musk, also the proprietor of a chip-making business, has said it would be an “honor” to hire Huang. Perhaps Huang might eventually return to his old job, as Sam Altman did when ousted by the OpenAI board in 2023.

In his final hours as Nvidia CEO, Huang reportedly called himself a “piece of shit”. In business, if not in marital, terms, he will be remembered as a titan, the man who, as much as anyone else, presided over the AI boom. Should the bubble burst, or should regulation arrive, it will not be on Huang’s watch. Similarly, if capitalist gravity eventually brings Nvidia’s market share back down to earth, Huang will not be to blame. The real threat to his legacy might be those GPUs in Inner Mongolia — and whatever other Nvidia equipment found its way across the border.

Tom Ough is a senior editor at UnHerd . He is the author of a book on existential risk .
