items.title: One-day general strike hits Spain in run-up to November 29 elections
items.summary: On November 11, workers walked out in Spain’s first nationwide strike in 14 years as social and political anger erupts against soaring rents, falling real wages and the rising cost of living.

scraped.title: One-day general strike hits Spain in run-up to November 29 elections
scraped.description: On November 11, workers walked out in Spain’s first nationwide strike in 14 years as social and political anger erupts against soaring rents, falling real wages and the rising cost of living.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
On November 11, workers walked out in Spain’s first nationwide strike in 14 years, protesting soaring rents, falling real wages and the rising cost of living. Calls for a general strike circulated widely amid mass housing protests in early October, and ultimately the Workers Commissions (CCOO) and General Labor Union (UGT) were forced to call a strike. At least 4 million workers struck on November 11, and hundreds of thousands marched despite pouring rain.

The strike pointed to the growing involvement of the working class in the wave of protests for housing, education, and against inequality, militarism and fascism that are spreading across Europe. It comes amid a wave of one-day national strikes called in France (November 17), Italy (November 20) and Greece (November 25) and amid mass youth protests against conscription in Germany. A sense of a new, emerging political radicalism permeated the Spanish strike, like protests elsewhere in Europe.

The stoppage hit hardest in heavy industry. Participation reached 90 percent in the car industry, with stoppages at Seat in Martorell, 85 percent in meat processing and 82 percent in refuse collection. In the Basque Country, production at Petronor, Mercedes and ACV was minimal. In Galicia, even the metal employers’ association Asime admitted 60 percent participation in shipbuilding. The ports were brought largely to a halt. The unions put participation there at 90 percent, especially in Valencia and Algeciras, and at 100 percent among Algeciras dockers. The marches were the largest in Spain in years. In Madrid, state officials counted 120,000 marchers in the rain, the Tenants’ Union 400,000. In Barcelona, officials counted 55,000, organizers 400,000. About 40,000 marched in Valencia, by the government’s count. Marches in Bilbao drew 70,000 people, according to union figures. Police repeatedly charged protesters; the Interior Ministry recorded 919 incidents, and at least 60 people were arrested nationwide.

They also exposed Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who after mass protests over housing on October 3 called snap elections for November 29. This aimed to hold a gun to workers’ heads, trying to force them to support his ruling Socialist Party (PSOE) or allied parties like Podemos and Sumar against the fascist Vox party and its ally, the right-wing Popular Party (PP).

In reality, the strike saw an outpouring of opposition not only to the PP and Vox but also to the record of militarism and austerity of the PSOE and its political and trade union allies. It is evident that the fundamental questions driving millions of people into struggle in Spain and across Europe will be resolved through the class struggle, not via maneuvers inside the capitalist political establishment.

WSWS reporters in Madrid interviewed workers and youth on neighborhood marches in the morning and the main protest march in the evening. They spoke to Blanca and Sergio, two public sector workers. Blanca said, “We have to support the strike, especially on housing. Salaries aren’t keeping up, everything is super expensive, it’s become impossible. … Public spending goes ever more to the military, if the right wins in the November 29 elections, there will be unrestrained hikes in military spending.”

While opposing Vox and the PP, Blanca added that she is disillusioned with the PSOE, Podemos and the Sumar-led Broad Front coalition: “If we are here today it’s because the PSOE, Podemos and the Broad Front all were worthless in terms of doing what had to be done, to meet people’s needs. If the housing situation got to this point, it is due to the cowardice of the government.”

Sergio was enthusiastic when WSWS journalists proposed to independently organize workers in rank-and-file committees of action in Spain and across Europe, to prepare a European general strike. He said, “Europe must develop a movement uniting all Europe’s nations, France and Italy like Holland and Portugal, all the European Union: We’re all in the same boat, ultimately. The situation is similar everywhere, and I think the mobilization can’t be just one day. What does a single day of general strike resolve? And it must be massive.”

He added, “I think the unions like CCOO and UGT just follow the government, in eight years of progressive government they were led by the hand, they did not press for any measure. We need something totally different—that is not tied to public funding, because in this case the unions in Spain receive a lot of public funding, and in that sense they’re pretty much controlled.”

Rafael, a retiree, told the WSWS: “We’re protesting for the right to housing, against high living costs, the rise of food, light, gas costs. Prices and salaries are not rising equally.” He added, “War is where Europe is investing a lot of money, but which belongs to us. … The poor always pay for war, workers are the cannon fodder. Plus, no country has in any way attacked Spain or France.”

He stressed his discontent with the union bureaucracies. They “called the strike, organized pickets, but then they failed to take this at all seriously, to organize assemblies in the workplaces.” Rafael added that they are “part of the system,” a term he applied to the ruling parties, as well: “Podemos is already out of government, now it’s Sumar and company, they are complicit in everything … by commission or omission.”

Africa, a university student who in October participated in the occupation of the Puerta del Sol to demand decent housing, told the WSWS she was enthusiastic about the growing radicalization of working people: “There is growing consciousness in youth and people of different ages. Struggles are coming together for public services, education, health, housing, a decent life. … Plus we need to struggle against fascism that is emerging.”

While she emphasized above all her concern with opposing fascists’ attacks on democratic rights, she also welcomed organizing struggles independently of the traditional bureaucracies. “The PSOE’s record is insufficient, many issues were abandoned, ultimately the left advanced very little while the far right makes big steps,” Africa said, adding: “Obviously the fact that this is emerging from below is very interesting, the most interesting is that it was born on the Plaza del Sol. People went there all day, we slept there, we went to study in the morning and then after to study. In my opinion it was a great step forward. It meant for the first time we saw things organized from below.”

Arturo, an immigrant worker from Mexico, said: “Even for people who work and have relatively decent salaries, it is getting impossible. On average 50, 60 percent of people’s wages go to housing, so that you get situations where you have to share rooms with lots of people, and it’s almost impossible to be independent. … The very rich are grabbing a large part of total income. It is a world problem, clearly.”

Asked about the role of the PSOE, Podemos and Sumar, Arturo replied: “That’s the big question. There are critics who say that in eight years of progressive government, theoretically of left-wing government, they did not manage to address the housing problem. The decrees they proposed were shot down by the opposition.” He compared them to the Mexican trade union bureaucracies, which he described as deeply corrupt.

When the WSWS asked what Arturo saw as the political basis for building an alternative to them, he replied: “The Marxist-Leninist injunction of internationalism, that the fight must be global. At the end of the day, if states become servants of capital, then even a moderately ‘left’ government continues to be overseen by global capital and will ultimately capitulate. This means that we are seeing rather that workers’ struggles will need to transcend the logic of the nation-state.”

Guillermo emphasized to the WSWS that the problem is rooted in the capitalist system. “The capitalist system arranges it so that capital is always more concentrated in fewer hands, and the rest of us don’t participate in cutting up the cake,” he said, adding: “The role of the PSOE is to preserve the system, seek as few changes as possible. The few changes that were promoted came from Podemos. … It was they who promoted changes that were more, in theory at least, left. But then they were cut off by the PSOE in parliament.

“I think a European general strike would be fantastic, a general strike on the entire planet. The initiative has not come from the trade unions, who are integrated into the institutions. Anyway, the best they can do of their own accord is to support something coming from somewhere else,” he said, adding: “Ultimately, Trotsky advocated for these sorts of things, for mobilizations in the street, for organizing among ourselves not in bureaucratic ways that absorb you and impose a series of things on you. So, as I see it, what is happening now in Europe is sort of a Trotskyist movement.”
scraped.lead_paragraph: On November 11, workers walked out in Spain’s first nationwide strike in 14 years, protesting soaring rents, falling real wages and the rising cost of living. Calls for a general strike circulated widely amid mass housing protests in early October, and ultimately the Workers Commissions (CCOO) and General Labor Union (UGT) were forced to call a strike. At least 4 million workers struck on November 11, and hundreds of thousands marched despite pouring rain.

items.title: “It’s about class”: Powerful strike by Harvard academic workers collides with the Democratic Party establishment
items.summary: The strike by more than 4,000 Harvard graduate student workers and first-ever walkout of non-tenure-track faculty and researchers is a direct conflict with the Democrats who oversee the richest university in the world.

scraped.title: “It’s about class”: Powerful strike by Harvard academic workers collides with the Democratic Party establishment
scraped.description: The strike by more than 4,000 Harvard graduate student workers and first-ever walkout of non-tenure-track faculty and researchers is a direct conflict with the Democrats who oversee the richest university in the world.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The strike by more than 4,000 Harvard graduate student workers, now in its third week, and the first-ever walkout of non-tenure-track faculty and researchers are colliding head-on with the Democratic Party establishment, which oversees the richest university in the world.

Members of the Harvard Graduate Students Union-United Auto Workers (HGSU-UAW) and Harvard Academic Workers-UAW (HAW-UAW) are demanding raises to address skyrocketing living costs, childcare benefits and protections for international students and academic freedom.

The Harvard Corporation, the board that governs the university, presides over an endowment that grew by $11.1 billion last year, a 27 percent increase, to reach $68 billion. It has frozen academic workers’ pay since July 2024, while Boston-area prices rose 7.9 percent. Harvard is now offering striking workers roughly 3 percent a year.

The Harvard Corporation is a veritable who’s who of the corporate-financial oligarchy. Its members include Sylvia Burwell, who held senior White House and budget posts under the Clinton and Obama administrations, in addition to the Bill and Melinda Gates and Walmart Foundations; billionaire Penny Pritzker, who served as US Commerce Secretary in the Obama administration; along with executives from major private equity and hedge funds, including Michael S. Chae, the vice president and chief financial officer at Blackstone, and Joseph Bae, the co-CEO of KKR.

A striking faculty worker explained to the World Socialist Web Site how this board is using the crisis. “Harvard has been in this very public fight with the Trump administration and that meant that among other things, they lost some funding from the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health. So basically some senior management at Harvard, working with the McKinsey consulting firm, decided they should make use of this crisis.”

Harvard paid McKinsey at least $250,000 to design cuts at the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, according to documents obtained by the Harvard Crimson. The plan to “cluster” administrative operations could eliminate as many as 25 percent of staff positions. “In some departments, they fired half the non-tenure track faculty,” the worker said. “They didn’t consult any of the professors... These are people [who] do most of the teaching and do a huge amount of research.”

“The cost of living is crazy here in Boston,” a striking graduate student said. “A lot of us are not full time and get something like $2,600 a month. I live with my partner, and we pay $2,600 per month in rent. So it’s more than half my pay.” He also spoke to the persecution of international students: “Everyone knows about ICE, how it got already into the university. The university has been cooperating with them.”

Sasha, another striking graduate student, rejected Harvard’s claim that it has no money. “It just doesn’t look true against the endowment, does it? They’re using political rhetoric as a means to deny economic justice effectively. It’s a real concern insofar as the Democrats here and other cities are using that as an excuse.”

The strike is taking place in the aftermath of the historic electoral defeat of Trump and the Republicans. Having taken control of Congress, the Democrats have pledged to seek “bipartisan common ground” with Trump. “They’re assuming that the status quo needs to be maintained,” the striking grad student said. “But clearly we’re not happy with the status quo.”

The same board that has postured as a defender of democracy is implementing Trump’s program on campus. It has fired the directors of centers studying the Middle East, punished undergraduates who protested the Gaza genocide, and rewritten campus rules so that undergraduates can no longer protest without prior authorization.

Harvard is also seeking to strip workers of employee status. The day after the graduate union’s contract expired in June 2025, it removed some 800 workers from the bargaining unit, and it now wants to carve out 300 to 400 stipend post-doctoral researchers. It has spent two years trying to force the union to file a petition that would put the question before Trump’s National Labor Relations Board. The aim is a ruling that would strip stipend post-docs of employee status at every campus where they are organized, including Columbia, Cornell and NYU.

In the face of this offensive, the UAW bureaucracy has confined the struggle to two bargaining units on one campus. Harvard has scheduled bargaining only every two weeks, a clear signal that it intends to wait the strikers out until the end of the semester.

The UAW’s record in academic strikes is one of isolation and capitulation: Harvard in 2019, Columbia in 2021 and 2026, the University of California in 2022 and 2024, and the New School in 2024. The graduate workers’ 40-day strike this spring ended without a contract, on the basis of verbal signals from Harvard’s negotiators. Five months later, the university’s position is essentially unchanged. The UAW apparatus, headed by President Shawn Fain, with Democratic Socialists of America members holding leading positions in Region 9A, campaigned for the Democrats in the midterms.

The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) has called on striking workers to demand what the UAW’s strategy is to win the strike. This includes:

The IWA-RFC urges strikers to form a rank-and-file strike committee now, uniting graduate and academic workers, and to demand an immediate mass membership meeting, with an open microphone and no restrictions on discussion, where the UAW must answer these questions and every member is free to raise proposals and put them to a vote.

“I support a mass meeting,” a grad student said. “We need to have a unified strategy that is in line with the members. We need to have in mind what’s going to hurt the administration rather than just what they’ve sort of done in previous semesters or what’s been done elsewhere. That’s going to mean keeping the strike going at least until grading for this semester and possibly longer if the administration doesn’t come to a settlement.”

The Harvard strike is part of a growing rebellion against the bureaucracies that have suppressed workers’ struggles for decades. The conditions confronting Harvard workers are the same ones facing workers in every industry and country: soaring inequality, austerity imposed in the name of crisis, and attacks on democratic rights. Harvard can outlast a strike confined to Harvard. It cannot outlast a movement of the working class as a whole.

“There are French Revolution levels of inequality. How can there be such an incredible magnitude of wealth and such poverty and mistreatment of others in the same world?” said Sasha, a striking graduate student. Addressing himself to broader sections of workers, he said, “We are all fighting the same fight. Even though our work looks really different at times, it is our labor that makes the rest of the world run.”

Another grad student pointed to the resistance of workers and young people across Europe. “Right now, people at Harvard are fighting for their own contracts, but it definitely resonates with some of the struggles that are happening in Europe. because I feel like there is something in the air about, like, Gen Z, rising up and demanding more rights. The future seems a bit dark, and we don’t want to be just economic growth, the same as we always were. The goal of capitalism is just for money to grow and grow. We think the important thing is not just for GDP to grow, but just for people to get a good life, and for everyone to be in decent conditions, and not just making rich corporations even richer.”

Asked what he would say to UAW members in the auto and other industries about the importance of the Harvard strike, he said, “The most important thing is, is not to take things for granted, that things can always be changed and that workers have power. We actually have all the powers, because without the workers, there’s no money. There’s no production, and we have the means of production. Therefore, we need to organize bottom up because the politicians are always going to try to be elected, get allies in the system, and do maneuvering. So always remember that the workers have the power and that our unity makes us stronger.”

scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Mary Peltola Widens Lead to 10,412 Votes in Alaska U.S. Senate Race, Campaign Says Victory Is Near
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola (Yup’ik) has widened her lead over Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan to 10,412 votes in Alaska’s closely watched Senate race, prompting her campaign to declare that her victory is all but certain.

With 49.84% of the total vote, Peltola, a Democrat and lifelong Alaskan, is approaching the 50% threshold needed to secure an outright victory in the first round of Alaska’s ranked-choice voting election.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Cheryl Bruce, campaign manager for Alaskans for Mary, said the remaining ballots are expected to strengthen Peltola’s lead and put her over the 50% mark.

“Alaskans have spoken, and it is clear that in the coming days Mary Peltola will be officially elected as their next United States Senator,” Bruce said in a campaign statement.

“Mary got into this race to take on DC corruption, lower costs, and put Alaska first – and when elected, she will hit the ground running. This campaign was built by Alaskans hungry for a change in leadership, and Mary is ready to deliver.”

According to the Peltola campaign, just over 10,000 ballots remain to be counted, with most expected from Anchorage and Southeast Alaska. Both areas have favored Peltola by significant margins in the ballots counted so far.

The campaign also pointed to Peltola’s strong performance in early in-person and absentee voting, which it says has helped widen her advantage over Sullivan.

The campaign maintains that Sullivan has no mathematical path to overtake Peltola and that the remaining ballots will confirm her election.

However, the Alaska Division of Elections must complete its ballot count and officially certify the results before the race is formally decided.

If Peltola’s lead holds, her election would mark a significant political shift for Alaska and return her to Washington, D.C., this time as the state’s next U.S. senator.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.title: Manitoba group needs $17M to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home
scraped.description: A Manitoba-based organization is trying to raise $17 million to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home from Switzerland.
scraped.author: Emma Honeybun
scraped.h1: Manitoba group needs $17M to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

(From left) Karl Stone and Coleen Rajotte are pictured Friday. The pair, along with Gerald Neufeld, make up Return the Sacred, a grassroots group committed to bringing 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home from Switzerland. Photo: Emma Honeybun/APTN News.

A Manitoba-based organization is trying to raise $17 million to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home from Switzerland.

“It doesn’t matter what tribe you’re from, it’s important that our people come together to bring these home to our Nations,” said Karl Stone, spiritual advisor of the group Return the Sacred. “And have these stored in a place where they can be kept for our own medicine people, within our own communities.

Return the Sacred, formerly called the Bringing Them Home Project, is a grassroots organization formed in 2025.

“That’s the way these sacred bundles should be taken care of, I believe. And these sacred bundles should be taught to the next generation.”

The group, headed by executive director Coleen Rajotte, returned from a week-long trip to Switzerland Thursday and held a news conference in Winnipeg.

Since June 2025, the group has been in communication with a private collector, Vincent Escriba, who ran the Indian Land Museum in Gossau, Switzerland.

The museum contained over 5,000 artefacts from North and South America, as well as several countries in Africa. They’re all part of Escriba’s private collection, which he has been growing for the majority of his adult life.

“He is actually a kind, gentle person,” Rajotte said. “He became enamoured with Indigenous people and Indigenous culture.”

She said he “spent his entire life travelling to North America,” 50 trips overall, collecting the items and purchasing other private collections in full.

“That’s how he’s collected such a vast quality,” she said. “We do believe him that he wants to work with us,” she said. “He’s now 70 years old, he’s put all his energy and all his money into this collection, and now he wants to sell it back.”

The Indian Land Museum closed in December 2025, when Escriba decided to retire. Since then, the artefacts have been stored in boxes in a private warehouse, awaiting sale.

Prior to its closure, the chief of Pikangikum First Nation , a community located in northern Ontario, had been advised of the collection’s fate. The chief told Gerald Neufeld, a long-time researcher based in Winnipeg, who created the group in an effort to bring the artefacts home.

The collection includes headdresses, unopened medicine bags, medicine and corn husk masks, pipes, totem poles, canoes, and several other types of artefacts that carry spiritual and cultural weight, Rajotte said.

Escriba also owns several boxes of textbooks, both in English and German.

Over several days, the group met with Escriba and took hundreds of photos of descriptions, contained in stacks of binders, which identified each object, along with its origin, in German.

They have not been able to confirm when all of the artefacts were made, but estimate most left Canada between 1840 and 1860.

Similarly, Rajotte said she is still working to figure out what came from where, but has so far been able to confirm several objects were from Nations in southern Alberta and North Dakota.

They also negotiated with Escriba and determined how much it would cost to purchase the items and return them to North America: $14.5 million, as well as an additional $3 million to cover transportation and handling of the items.

“Of course, there’s lots of opinions,” Rajotte said about Escriba’s decision to sell, rather than donate, the items back to the Nations they originally came from.

In California, she continued, the California Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act requires that all state-funded agencies, museums and universities must return any Indigenous cultural items, without a cost, by law.

However, even if the same laws existed in Canada, the situation with Escriba would be different, Rajotte said, due to his collection being private.

She said they are planning to negotiate with Escriba about lowering the price, or a long-term payment plan, but she doesn’t believe he’ll budge when it comes to the bill.

However, he has extended the sale’s deadline, which was originally set for payment by the end of December 2026.

Rajotte said she predicts it will take “at least” a year to appraise, document and pay for the entire collection.

So far, Heritage Canada has covered the initial trip to Switzerland, but there have been no additional conversations with public or private funders regarding the price of the collection itself.

“Our peoples’ sacred belongings that are in museums all over the world should be returned to the original people of this true land,” Stone said. “The bundles need to be protected … need to be cared for in a sacred way.”

Rajotte said, additionally, items are seen as living relatives, “ and the fact that they’re in a warehouse right now … no one’s spending time with them, visiting with them, makes me very very sad.”

She said her “biggest fear” was running out of time and not being able to purchase the collection, and that it will then be sold to private buyers and live out the rest of their days in office buildings in Dubai or New York City.

Stone said “it’s out of [his] hands,” but that he prays “that the right thing is done.

“It’s up to him [Escriba], but in our culture, we don’t believe there’s a price tag on anything that is sacred,” he said. “It’s sacred to us, that’s our way of life, that’s our culture, our belief, and hopefully something good will come of this.”

Return the Sacred will be hosting a fundraiser on Dec. 3. Money from the first event will go towards creating a digital archive and hiring a larger team.

The group’s short-term plan will be to translate each artefact description from German to English, with the use of artificial intelligence and a translator to double-check, to determine which artefact belongs to who.

Rajotte is encouraging “anyone with deep pockets” to reach out to the organization and donate to the cause.

“We’re working really hard to make sure we get all these items back to Turtle Island where they belong,” she said.

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

scraped.title: The taste we’ve been missing
scraped.description: syilx culinary storyteller kelsie marchand (kilawna) reflects on terroir, gentrification, and what the Okanagan forgot to savour
scraped.author: kelsie kilawna
scraped.h1: The taste we’ve been missing
scraped.body_text:
syilx culinary storyteller kelsie marchand (kilawna) reflects on terroir, gentrification, and what the Okanagan forgot to savour

kelsie kilawna

●

●

The clanking of pots and pans and the ringing of laughter while moving around the kitchen were always calming sounds to me growing up.

The most important lessons I’ve learned about food came as I stood at the hips of my grandmothers, watching them peel potatoes and listening to their stories.

I am a culinary storyteller of syilx foodways. In my work at Smoke on the Plateau , I teach through food. I share stories about my syilx/Okanagan homelands through a fully embodied experience bringing together taste, sight, smell and sound. My research has been lifelong and has taken place in kitchens, in berry patches, and while waiting for salmon and deer to return so I could help prepare it for the people.

There is a beauty to this way of knowing and living, because it is what taught me to be slow and patient with the offerings of our land.

The work I do honours the relationships that collapse time and place into story. It is a way of ensuring we never forget the importance of our Four Food Chiefs system. In essence, this is a reaffirmation of our governance system.

Now, today when you enter the Okanagan Valley, you see another food story being told. A palate cleanser for the gentrification of our foodways.

A rising culinary hotspot, the Okanagan has dressed itself in words like “local,” “seasonal,” “farm-to-table.” While wine glasses clink and tasting notes are murmured, words like “terroir” roll off the tongue as a somewhat promise to its authenticity. It is a beautiful and comfortable story.

Terroir is a French term embraced by the culinary industry to speak to “the taste of place.” The concept itself describes how the climate and land conditions of an area affect the flavour profile of local food crops.

In the Okanagan this is popularized through the wine industry. It’s often the terroir of a wine that is showcased through wine tastings. It speaks to the soil, weather, topography and tradition that shape what consumers taste.

“Local” has now become a premium label, “farm-to-table” has become marketing copy, and “terroir” has become a way to charge more for the same soil that syilx Peoples have been tending since the time of our Creation, without acknowledging who did the tending, or what was given back in return.

This is gentrification.

Not just through the extractive wine industry, but it’s become the gentrification of taste itself.

When terroir is extracted from its French roots and planted in the Okanagan, it lands on soil that is already alive with syilx knowledge and responsibility.

As a syilx culinary storyteller, I am responsible for reminding people of this, that our foodways should not be minimized for the sake of an entertaining evening.

Our foodways have and always will be prayed over. Ceremonies of health, and gratitude are held for all our homelands offer us. Young people go through their Coming of Age ceremony learning to pray for the health of our waterways. All of this is the missing spirit of the term terroir.

So I’ve been working to name what’s missing. One word, something that can hold the weight of kinship, of reciprocity, of generations coiled into one. Something that reminds us we are part of the land, not separate from it.

So I call it by it’s name, tmixʷ.

tmixʷ is the nsyilxcen word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is, it speaks far beyond just soil and climate. Rather it speaks to the kinships between all of it, our reciprocity, and our syilx/Okanagan obligation to give back, so that what you take can live again.

The syilx/Okanagan understanding of place is through tmxʷulaxʷ, which speaks to the life-force-place. It is a dynamic, regenerative relationship between all beings, which the culinary industry’s shallow “local” label cannot contain.

The Okanagan culinary industry wants you to taste place, so what they’re selling is terroir, but what its missing is tmixʷ.

Let me tell you a story about xusem (soapberries).

There’s a small spot in the Okanagan mountains that has the sweetest soapberries my family has ever tasted.

The oldest person in my family shared that those berries are special, he’s had xusem berries from all areas of the Okanagan Valley, and these are unique because of their sweetness. xusem is typically a rather bitter berry. But from this one particular spot, they are very sweet.

They hold memories for their sweetness. Our family talks about that spot and visits it every year just to give it thanks.

As I research the micro-climate of that place each year, I notice a specific dappling of sun unique to that area. It is rather open, so the berries get enough sun to sweeten but not so much that it kills them, because xusem loves its darker, cooler places.

The taste comes from the sun in that area, but it also comes from the water that feeds that place. I know the families who carry the ceremonial responsibility to caretake it, to pray over it, to give thanks for it, to ensure it remains healthy so that the berries can continue to sweeten, year after year, generation after generation. I know the specific prayer and ceremony said over that place.

And this is data — or knowledge — sovereignty. We have a story now about that particular place in our homeland, a story that helps us understand the relationship between land, its specific environment, and the taste of place.

But more than that, we have a responsibility. We know who holds the ceremonies, we know who carries the prayers, and we know that the taste of that berry is inseparable from the health of that water, and the health of that water is inseparable from the people who tend it with reverence.

That taste, the taste of that specific dappling of sun, of the hands that harvest, of the water that was prayed over, of the generations who knew to return, that is tmixʷ. That is the kinship I am speaking of that is missing from terroir.

Terroir speaks to what the land gives.

tmixʷ speaks to the responsibility, love and gratitude we have for how we are built into the system of a place.

But to fully understand tmixʷ, you have to understand its shape.

In syilx-centric understanding, time and relationship do not move in straight lines. They coil, they spiral, and they return. Like a rope being twisted, strand by strand, year after year, generation after generation.

tmixʷ is often described as the action of many strands continuously being bound and unified with each other to form one strong rope or thread, this coiling over time is what creates a living future.

Our name, syilx, carries this image. It loosely translates to those-who-twine/coil-(many)-into-one. This is who we are, and this is what we do as people, we coil the strands of life into a thread that carries us forward, so we may move into the future unbroken, generation after generation.

And there is another word that is used to describe us, sqilxʷ. It is the word for our people. And it translates as “to dream in a spiral.”

We are the ones who dream in spirals. We have the mind power to envision what could be, to create into reality whatever we can dream. So, unlike salmon, unlike roots, unlike bears, we humans do not automatically know how to live in ways that contribute to the wellbeing of future generations. It’s our responsibility to learn it, to dream it, and to choose it, again and again, this is our spiraling forward.

This is what it means to be syilx/Okanagan. We are the coil and the spiral, and we hold the past while we dream the future. We are the ones who must remember, and in that remembering, we create.

So when we harvest, we are coiling, and when we give thanks, we are coiling. As part of our agreement as people here it is up to us to ensure that what we take can be revived, we are adding our strand to the thread. And when we dream, when we envision a future where all life-forces can revive, we are spiraling, we are bringing the future into the present. This is how we collapse time and place and can share it as story.

The taste of place, through tmixʷ, is the taste of something being coiled, year after year, generation after generation, towards a time where all life-forces can revive. That rests on our responsibility as The People of this land.

The Okanagan culinary industry has taken the flavour of place and stripped it of the relationships that made it possible, but they don’t sell the obligation to give back.

Because you can’t sell what you don’t know, and you can’t taste what you’ve forgotten.

When you forget that you are part of a coil, a thread being twisted, strand by strand, generation after generation, you begin to believe that you are separate. That the land is just resources and that food is a product, that taste is just flavour.

This is the logic of extraction. It is the logic of the people-eaters, nəɬnasqilxʷtn, the monsters that Coyote, our teacher and trickster, was sent to transform. They consume without giving back, they take without gratitude, and they believe they are the only ones who matter.

I do not want to say that the Okanagan culinary industry is Coyote, because it doesn’t mean to be a monster, however it is dressed in the same forgetting. It has adopted the language of terroir without adopting the responsibility of relationship, and it speaks of a place without knowing who ceremonies for the water.

And so the coil weakens. The thread frays. The spiral loses its way.

To be sqilxʷ, to dream in a spiral, is to remember that we are the ones who must keep it coiling, and we are the ones who must keep it turning. We are to remember that we are torn from the earth and that our responsibility is to return.

To remember that we are not the only ones, that the water, the berries, the salmon, they are our relatives. They have their own life-force, and they have their own right to regenerate.

To remember that we are not just consumers, but we are participants, we are co-creators, we are the ones who must give back.

So what I know to be true, is that the taste of tmixʷ is still here, has always been and will always be. It is reaffirmed in the xusem berries that my family harvests every year. It’s reaffirmed in our salmon relatives that still swim up the rivers, it’s reaffirmed by the roots that still push through the soil, it’s reaffirmed by the berries that will continue to sweeten in the dappled sun of a place that has been tended by syilx Peoples for generations.

It will all remain and stay alive, surrounded by the sound of pots and pans and laughter moving about the kitchen where our children learn to stand and watch at the hips of their grandmothers. It’ll remain alive in the stories that collapse time and place into a single moment.

tmixʷ (pronounced tuh-MEE-kwuh) is the syilx word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is.

sqilxʷ (pronounced skee-lkhw) refers to the syilx people. It translates as “the dream in a spiral.”

syilx (pronounced see-ilkh) means those-who-twine/coil-(many)-into-one.

xusem (pronounced hoo-sem) is the syilx word for soapberry.

kelsie kilawna

A dedicated advocate for strength-based journalism and trauma-informed, culturally aware reporting, kelsie kilawna brings a compassionate lens to storytelling on her syilx homelands. Her writing is rooted in syilx protocol for self-location and grounded in the belief that storytelling is a form of ceremony. With a commitment to amplifying narratives that empower and uplift, kelsie navigates complex stories with sensitivity, ensuring that the voices of the syilx Nation are not only heard but honoured in every line of their work.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

scraped.h1: ‘It’s all about taking care of people’: How a smǝlqmíx farmer is building food sovereignty at ntámłqən
scraped.body_text:
The community garden is creating opportunities to process and store food in the Similkameen Valley, while passing farming knowledge and other life skills between generations

Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

The potato plants are so tall that their stems reach Dixon Terbasket’s eyes.

He remembers walking through his family’s garden when he was three or four years old, more than 60 years ago, in a community where his mom, all his aunties and uncles, grew food in gardens and orchards — and stored them in root cellars, too.

Now, Dixon finds himself leading his own food sovereignty initiative that he hopes will equip the next generation of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) people with the knowledge and skills to farm on their own.

“I want to give them at least a running chance, man,” Dixon told IndigiNews.

The ntámłqən garden is in unceded smǝlqmíx territory in the lower Similkameen Valley, in the southern Interior of “B.C.” It shares its nsyilxcən name with the adjacent community elementary school, meaning “gathering place.” Dixon said his people have gathered here since time immemorial.

At ntámłqən, a 7.5-acre community garden and food hub on Lower Similkameen Indian Band (LSIB) land near “Cawston,” he works with a small but dedicated crew of staff and volunteers to teach people life skills — from growing their own food; to sharing it with the community; and how to preserve what they grow.

At the peak of the harvest season, the garden hosted a free barbeque for the community on Sept. 28, in collaboration with the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association.

Dozens of people — Indigenous and non-Indigenous — came together around meals made with ingredients provided by the garden and its partners. Between all the mingling and laughs, they feasted on stuffed-peppers, colourful salads, watermelon, goat meat, apple pie and more.

“It’s all about taking care of people,” Dixon said, echoing the farm’s slogan of “For The People.”

The garden is working towards giving the community the ability to make decisions about their food — and having the knowledge, land and facilities to provide for one another. A processing facility expected to be completed by March 2027 will add space to prepare and store harvests, with opportunities for community food businesses.

Dixon’s niece, Coven Terbasket, joined the crew in 2024, a couple of weeks after moving back to her ancestral homelands. She was 29 and looking for work when she ran into Dixon at an insurance office in small-town Keremeos.

For most of her life, Coven had lived south of the colonial border in “Spokane, Washington.” During childhood summers, her mom would send her up to “roam around” LSIB lands with family, usually in their ancestral community of nkʷrulauxʷ (Blind Creek, Place of Yellow Dirt).

Like her uncle, she remembers family gardens all around Blind Creek, and the work that kept households fed beyond the growing season.

“Everyone had made the time to grow their own food, can their own food, to preserve,” she said.

Coven hadn’t seen Dixon since she was a child. As they reconnected in the insurance office two years ago, he learned she needed work and offered her a job at the community garden he had been building with a small crew of workers and volunteers for more than a year.

“He told me to show up at the garden the next day at 10 a.m., so I did,” she said.

Coven describes the encounter as fate, saying her uncle “found me” shortly after her return, during a difficult period in her life.

“It’s freaky how crazy it worked out … me looking for a job; me freshly back in the homelands after years of not living here – and being stuck in a really dark spot in life,” she said.

“Needing something to prove to myself that it’s worth living. That it’s worth giving another try.”

Working at the garden over the past two-and-a-half years, she said, “has been the growth and the movement that I needed in my life to be able to move through some of that.”

“It’s providing support for those who have once gotten forgotten about. It provides a place of well-being,” she said.

“This is a place where people can come and get grounded.”

The garden’s published priorities include supporting Elders, single-parent families and households with low incomes. Produce is available free or by donation to Indigenous and non-Indigenous community members experiencing food insecurity.

For eight weeks, beginning at the end of August, more than a dozen Elders received weekly “Elder Boxes” full of fresh produce from the garden for free. The program was carried out in partnership with LSIB’s health department, who helped deliver the boxes to the Elders’ homes.

The garden also has a library of seeds — from flowers, to herbs and vegetables — that community members can have access to, so that they can plant and garden at their own homes.

Workshops extend that work into the community’s kitchens and pantries, teaching people how to process and preserve what is available locally.

With support from the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Network (IFSA), ntámłqən has brought in Rumy Muenala of Ayapacha to lead harvesting, processing, and preserving sessions.

Participants learn to turn produce into meals, canned peaches, pickles, salsas and more. Muenala has also helped put on staff appreciation feasts and community dinners using ingredients from the garden. He was the lead chef at ntámłqən’s September community barbeque.

“To me, that’s food sovereignty: you have to adapt, you have to get creative with what’s available — and not depend so much on going to a grocery store,” said Muenala, whom Dixon met through Tea Creek .

Muenala, who is Quechua from Ecuador, delivers workshops and dinners at community farms around “B.C.,” most of them Indigenous-owned or Indigenous-led.

“It takes more work … to go out and find these ingredients. But at the end of the day, that’s more important to me, because it builds relationships: relationships to each other; to the land,” said Muenala.

“For me, Indigenous food sovereignty is reclaiming that power of not feeling like you need to depend on somebody anymore. The only people you should depend on are your close relatives, your community, to help one another.”

Before joining ntámłqən, Coven had spent about a decade working in hospitality. Her administrative job includes marketing and social media, but she spends just as much time out on the land, getting her hands dirty. She knows her way through the long rows of fruits, vegetables, sunflowers, tobacco and other plants.

“Harvesting, seeding, transplanting, weeding — all of it, man,” she said.

She arrived knowing little about farming. Over the past two and a half years, she has learned how to grow watermelons, squash and tomatoes, and to preserve what she harvests. Working on the land every day has been, as she put it in October, “probably the biggest culture shock I’ve ever experienced.”

Coven sees the work as part of building a food system guided by the community’s needs and its responsibilities to the land. She envisions being able to feed one another on their own terms, so that “we don’t rely on the food systems that have been set up, as far as the whole capitalistic ideal.”

Learning to grow food has also changed how she understands her place in that system.

“I feel like there’s a sense of self in growing your own food. You identify with that food – you know what it took, and what it takes to grow.”

The Okanagan Nation Alliance’s teaching resources describe syilx food knowledge learned through the territory’s seasonal changes. When saskatoon bushes first bloom, bitterroot is ready to harvest. Learning when to gather one food means paying attention to other life around it.

“I’ve found this calling here at the garden,” Coven said. “To be a good person. And to give back – to have this reciprocal way of living. I give as much as I take, and find that nice balance between the two.”

Returning to the simplicity of farming has taught Coven the patience and sustained care that living things need to thrive.

“To take care of the things that take care of us … a deeper appreciation and understanding of where food comes from, and how water feeds every source of life that surrounds us on a daily basis.”

Through the garden’s volunteer program , people can help tend to crops, process produce or clean seeds, and leave with a harvest bundle. First-time volunteers receive a site and cultural safety orientation.

Earlier this fall, Hannah Field, who co-manages the ntámłqən Community Garden as its coordinator, said more than 600 people — including volunteers and guests — had come through the farm this year alone.

At an Okanagan Food System Summit gathering at Okanagan College in kiʔláw̓naʔ (Kelowna) in October, Field described ntámłqən as a place where people could find belonging and learn to “work together in a good way.”

“I’m from England. I showed up on Dixon’s doorstep in 2023, and became entwined in making this vision a reality,” she said.

Coven remembers how different community life felt while she was living south of the border.

“That’s the beauty of it – you could be from any walk of life and come here, and feel comfortable and feel welcome,” said Coven.

“The sense of community is something that I very much lacked living in the States. I didn’t really know what that meant, as far as what it means to show up for each other.”

The garden’s development drew on years of community planning and consultation. LSIB has supported the project through core funding and an in-kind land lease, according to the garden’s published history .

Funding includes a $193,873 grant through the federal Local Food Infrastructure Fund grant for the farm and food hub and $747,704 listed among the province’s 2024-25 rural development awards for the processing facility. A separate $289,759 federal contribution supports a well, irrigation equipment and facilities to preserve and store food.

The garden’s irrigation system is sourced from a well, which was implemented during the farm’s development.

About two acres of the site are devoted to infrastructure, including a greenhouse, chicken coop, office, workshop and community space above a root cellar. Some buildings are finished, while others are nearing completion.

The two-storey food-processing facility will have a walk-in cooler and freezer downstairs, with storage that can be used for commercial purposes. The commercial kitchen downstairs is equipped with meat grinders, dehydrators, and other tools to help support food processing and preserving.

A ramp leads upstairs to a rental kitchen, a podcast room and washrooms.

“You can start to imagine the kinds of things the community can do once they have these types of infrastructure in place,” said Field.

“You can chop a thousand pounds of peaches through there, can it, and take it up to the North Okanagan. Or store apples in the walk-in cooler. There are endless possibilities, really.”

Power for the facilities is currently being funded by grants. But Field said that within the garden’s operational business plan, they envision a future where diverse revenue streams can support the garden’s operation costs.

Potential revenue streams include different workshop programming; wholesale produce distribution; and renting out the commercial kitchen and other facility spaces, like the freezer or cooler.

Kwantlen Polytechnic University’s 2021 Okanagan study describes how spending at locally owned food businesses can circulate among growers, suppliers and repair services. It also identifies concentrated supply chains as a vulnerability during disruptions.

The garden donates fresh produce to community members and gives people a place to spend time together. Dixon said people can learn to fix a chainsaw or take part in growing, processing and preserving their own food.

The teaching model also helps democratize practical knowledge by offering paid training and describes every team member as a potential mentor, with local Knowledge Holders involved in particular tasks.

“That’s the whole thing — we want people to come here and just hang out,” said Dixon.

In a 2026 YMCA online survey , 64 per cent of people in “Canada” wished their communities had more “third places,” or informal gathering spaces outside of home and work.

Longtime residents and newcomers to the valley are welcome to volunteer at ntámłqən , with no gardening experience required.

“A lot of people believe in — they want to help. There are a lot of settlers who want to do something, and feel like they’re contributing. This is an opportunity for that,” Field said.

In a 2023 account published by the Economic Trust of the Southern Interior , Dixon outlined a plan to feed the community first and sell surplus produce, with processing and storage eventually bringing in income to help keep the garden running.

The garden’s apprenticeship program describes it as an organic operation. Its training plan includes cover cropping, composting and seed saving, alongside irrigation and food preservation. Keeping seeds gives growers something to sow the follow season; compost returns organic matter to the soil, helping it retain water and nutrients. Cover crops help protect the soil between harvests.

A nursery for native plants is also in the works at the garden. Its 2026 growing list includes native seedlings and cuttings intended to restore the territory, including black huckleberry and wild strawberry.

Connections with Young Agrarians, Tea Creek and the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association have also supported the garden’s development.

Dixon sees opportunities for the community to farm elsewhere on reserve land, too. He said soil mapping had identified 7,200 acres of Class 1 agricultural land, opening possibilities for community members to grow food for their families and earn a living from farming.

In 1978, when he was 21, Dixon planted his first garden at his mother’s place, next door to where he lives now by the ntámłqən garden. The plot was no bigger than his kitchen.

He developed a business plan to farm on a larger scale and involve more of the community. On the same lands where ntámłqən garden would be built nearly 40 years later, he launched the Similkameen Native Organic Produce company in 1987, beginning as a market garden and later moving into commercial growing.

“We had quite a few people — similar to what we’re doing right now — training people from the reserve,” he said.

They started with five acres of potatoes. With help from his staff and a 100–horsepower irrigation pumping system, they started growing “rows and rows of vegetables,” he said.

“Putting in 5,000 tomato plants and 4,000 pepper plants. It got bigger and bigger.”

The tomatoes they were growing were a major seller – not just locally, but even into the U.S., he said.

He highlighted that the Similkameen Native Organic Produce company was producing 40,000 to 60,000 pounds of tomatoes every season for at least four years.

“I became quite the market. After a while, sometimes, I’d run out of tomatoes,” he said.

By the end of the 1990s, Dixon got busy raising a family and returned to a life of local governance. He later worked as a natural resource technician with the Okanagan Nation Alliance and retired in 2024 after more than a decade in that role.

But even before he announced his retirement, Dixon was already making plans to return to farming.

In 2018, Dixon sought community support and permission to farm a piece of band land near his home. His request was approved.

“I just thought I was going to retire here, grow some tomatoes and some peppers. The good life,” he said.

Now, Dixon has found his fourth wind in life, passing on the lessons that began at an early age in his family’s garden.

“I think you die after you slow down,” he said of retirement.

Farming runs deep in his family history. Dixon’s 93-year-old mother, Theresa Ann Terbasket, grew up farming on a ranch operated by his great-grandfather Paul Terbasket at nkʷrulauxʷ.

But farming isn’t the way his ancestors traditionally lived, Dixon said.

“Maybe my grandfather did — maybe his grandpa, too. It’s a couple generations back. But prior to that, it was hunting. Everything was there — berries were there; the roots were here; the deer were here; the fish were here. The garden was everywhere,” Dixon said.

“Then they started putting us on the Indian reserves, and then we became farmers. We were good farmers.”

The Working Group on Indigenous Food Sovereignty describes the right to food as sacred, alongside responsibilities to care for the lands, plants and animals that provide it.

As IndigiNews reported in 2022 , Paul was farming 50 acres by 1909, diverting water from Blind Creek through an irrigation ditch.

That year, the province’s Water Act asserted Crown ownership over water and required licences to divert it. Indigenous water licences were often improperly recorded, altered or cancelled, according to legal researcher Kathryn Gullason’s history of water regulation .

Paul’s application for a water record was refused in 1911. Instead, the provincial Board of Investigation confirmed the Similkameen Fruitlands Company’s water record, historian Duane Thomson wrote in a 1994 study in BC Studies.

Author and historian Harold Rhenisch, who grew up with Dixon, said the attempt to block Paul’s water use dates back to 1913. In his 2022 account , he wrote that Paul carried on using the land and water because “he had never relinquished title to it, and he had been promised water long before.”

In 1923, the dispute went to court, Rhenisch wrote. Paul continued watering his orchard and was eventually jailed for contempt of court.

“We were banned from selling our food in the 1930s and ‘40s. They took away water licenses from us in the ‘50s and ‘60s. We were food sovereign until the end of the ‘60s – we were becoming reliant on a thing called social assistance,” Dixon said.

Dixon and the ntámłqən crew worry about climate change, political instability, and disruptions to food supplies.

This fall, cyberattacks reportedly disrupted the refrigeration systems that grocery stores depend on to keep food safe. In October, attackers reportedly remotely took control of cooling systems at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores in France, forcing some to discard food.

Governments have also been emphasizing household preparedness. In 2025, the European Commission called for guidelines to help people meet their own needs for at least 72 hours during a crisis. Federal emergency guidance in “Canada” also advises households to keep enough food, water and other essentials for at least three days.

The federal National Food Security Strategy also calls for growing and processing more food domestically. It sets a target to increase the domestically produced share of healthy food available in “Canada,” measured against Canada’s Food Guide, from 75 to 85 per cent by 2032.

Closer to the garden, preparing for disruptions begins with helping people grow food and keep the harvest available year-round. That ability depends, in turn, on the health of the territory where the food grows.

In May 2026, the syilx Okanagan Nation declared a watershed emergency across the Similkameen and five other watersheds, citing drought, ecosystem decline and growing threats to water security. The Nation identified declining streamflows, threats to fish, and the early die-off of bitterroot as signs of a deepening crisis.

Nearby, nməlqytkʷ (the Similkameen River) winds through agricultural land and surrounding ecosystems. At nearly 200 km long, the waterway has been described as “the lifeblood of the valley” by LSIB Chief Keith Crow.

Coven remembers swimming in its waters as a child.

“I’ve seen the changes (in the river) since I’ve been a kid. I’ve seen how it’s getting grittier, nastier – something that I preferably don’t want to swim in anymore, which is really sad,” she said.

“We all have a responsibility to the land and to the water.”

The region has also experienced how quickly transportation routes can fail. In November 2021, flooding and mudslides closed major highways and rail lines connecting the Lower Mainland and “B.C.’s” Interior, interrupting the movement of food.

“Food can become scarce. I think a lot of people don’t really know how much risk we’re at. How vulnerable we are. We take it for granted,” said Dixon.

In the event of an emergency situation where local food systems are disrupted, he explained that the garden would step-up and manage whatever food they have readily on-hand. Part of that process is to identify any food surpluses, which they would then compile into a “stockpile” to support the community’s needs.

“You have to manage it. You might even have to protect it,” he said.

Emergency response also includes working with other nearby farmers and ranchers to see how they can pool their resources together for the community, he added.

“It’s dependent on the time of year,” Field emphasized in November.

“If it’s now, obviously there’s nothing in the field. But what we’ve got in the cellar, or processed, would be what we would have.”

The food processing facility comes equipped with a back-up generator, so the community would still be able to access stored food and food processing equipment, in the event of an emergency food systems situation.

Dixon sees a “generational gap” in the knowledge needed to grow and preserve food. Teaching is his way of giving back to the community that taught and supported him through his years of farming.

“I care so much, man. … Why do I do it? I really think that people need to learn. As a young guy, I was trained. A lot of older men and women trained me. They showed me how to do these things.”

Passing those skills on is his way of giving back to the community that supported him through his years of farming.

“I didn’t realize how valuable it is, how to do that.”

In the garden, Dixon can see the results of his work. He contrasts that with years spent in board meetings.

“You sit there for 20 years and don’t get any results. At least here, it feels like I did something,” he said.

Coven described her uncle as “a git-r-done kind of uncle,” and called it a privilege to work and learn from him.

“I see a man that is very vision-led, vision-driven. I see a man of action. The man just does, and will figure it out in the process,” she said.

For Coven, caring for the ntámłqən garden is part of revitalizing smǝlqmíx food systems, culture and customs. She imagines that work extending into people’s homes.

“I see a lot of the community members being able to sustain their own fridges, to sustain their own pantries,” she said.

The work gives her hope for a future in which her people can “survive and thrive.”

“The hope that we can do this as one people. Because it takes all of us.”

If there’s anything the community takes away from the garden, Dixon said that he hopes that people can develop the confidence to know that they can farm and grow food at home, too.

“You can do this. Grow a couple tomato plants. Grow some peppers. Grow a few potatoes. Grow some beets. Grow some carrots. Throw a couple onions in there – in your own little patch. That’s how I started,” he said.

Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

Aaron Hemens is an award-winning photographer, journalist and visitor in unceded syilx Okanagan territory. He is Filipino on his mom’s side, and has both French and British roots on his dad’s. As a settler, he is committed to learning and unlearning in his role as Storyteller for the Okanagan region, and to accurately and respectfully tell stories of Indigenous Peoples throughout the area. Aaron’s work is supported in part with funding from the Local Journalism Initiative in partnership with The Discourse and APTN.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

scraped.author: Jourdan Bennett-Begaye
scraped.h1: New Indigenous senator, representatives learn the ropes of Congress
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Jourdan Bennett-Begaye ICT

WASHINGTON — The incoming Indigenous congressional members who made history descended upon the nation’s capital this week for freshman orientation.

Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan’s first photo was of her by a sign that read, “This elevator is reserved for SENATORS ONLY at all times.” Her caption, “Going up!”

Comments ranged from “It’s really happening!” to “Omg YESSSS!!!” to “I wish I could like this post 100 times!”

Flanagan, White Earth Nation, will be the first Native woman elected to the U.S. Senate in American history.

New York Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, posed for a photo with Reps.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York.

Michigan Rep.-elect Sean McCann, Citizen Potawatomi Nation, stood with other freshman members from Michigan, ready to take off to Washington, D.C.

Valdez and McCann are the first Native people to represent their respective states in Congress.

The three new Indigenous members will be sworn-in at the start of the 120th Congress, joining Tom Cole who is Chickasaw, Choctaw citizen Josh Brecheen and Sharice Davids of Ho-Chunk Nation.

Alaska is still waiting on election results for Mary Peltola, Yup’ik, in the U.S. Senate race and Bill Hill, Dena’ina Athabascan, who is running for the U.S. House.

Flanagan, Valdez, and McCann were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week — the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party’s sweep of the midterm elections, and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans.

New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on Jan. 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

This week’s orientation included training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or those retiring it’s the start of figuring out what’s next. Briefing rooms were filled with information about office setup, payroll and benefits, and there was a room to take official portraits.

It’s also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House.

Selfies, besties and tough votes ahead

The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate.

Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection. President Donald Trump backed Cornyn’s rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated.

“I’m so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes,” Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas as well.

And Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews, Roy Cooper, Peggy Flanagan, Josh Turek and others.

“First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn’t ask for a better team,” she posted as the caption.

Leadership elections test the new members

One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they’re sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership.

Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices — House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer — in favor of a fresh start.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support— the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation’s first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters’ sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate. Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan announced they would not support Schumer.

Sen.-elect Chris Pappas, D-N.H. — who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator — said their class is “a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington.”

He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him.

Republicans chose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party’s election defeat. Ohio Rep. Jim Jordon won the race against the No. 2 Republican Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana to become the minority leader, continuing a rivalry stretching to 2023, before Johnson rose to power.

Senate Republicans tapped Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to stay on as leader, despite those agitating for a change.

A diverse new class arrives

As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday’s session with a prayer, “some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats.”

On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones — Flanagan will be the first Native American female U.S. senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more.

Rep. Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats’ campaign chief, called the party’s candidates “all very unique.”

“We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy award-winning musician,” she said earlier.

“They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp.”

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol’s stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Jourdan Bennett-Begaye, Diné, is the digital news director of ICT and based in its Washington bureau. Follow her on X: @jourdanbb or email her at jourdan@ictnews.org. More by Jourdan Bennett-Begaye

scraped.author: Mark Trahant
scraped.h1: Don’t waste brain cells on Interior’s plan to sell off public lands
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Mark Trahant Substack

I am not sure it’s worth spending many brain cells on the Interior Department’s 2026-2030 Strategic Plan. If it was released before the election, then we’d all be mad and worried. But now? Not a chance.

Even Western Republicans don’t like the idea of a sell off of public lands. Former Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke told the Associated Press that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands.” And he would vote against any measure.

Of course the Trump administration will try to do much of this by executive order. And that means a lot of litigation ahead.

The report, really a love letter to oil and gas, misappropriates history. In his letter Interior Secretary Doug Burgum writes:

As President Theodore Roosevelt, who helped shape and define our department, explained: “Conservation means development as much as it does protection.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Perhaps it’s worth thinking about Roosevelt’s actual record. He added roughly 230 million acres to the public land base.

A summary from the The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History:

“In the early twentieth century, President Theodore Roosevelt was a dynamic force in a relatively new movement known as conservationism. During his presidency, Roosevelt made conservation a major part of his administration. As the new century began, the frontier was disappearing. Once common animals were now threatened. Many Americans, including Roosevelt, saw a need to preserve the nation’s natural resources. He wanted to protect animals and land from businesses that he saw as a threat. Roosevelt said, “the rights of the public to the natural resources outweigh private rights, and must be given its first consideration.” By the end of his time as president, he had created five national parks, four game refuges, fifty-one national bird reservations as well as the National Forest Service. It could be said that Theodore Roosevelt, through laws, executive orders, and his strong personality, opened the nation’s eyes to the natural wonders of the land. Roosevelt had changed the attitude of America. As we begin the twenty-first century, conservation is once again an issue that the United States faces.”

Roosevelt was imperfect, but these ideals remain worthy.
