scraped.description: Previously, New Mexico had an MMIP task force within the state Indian Affairs Department. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham scrapped the task force in 2023
scraped.author: Source New Mexico
scraped.h1: New Mexico Missing and Murdered Indigenous Peoples task force proposes creating state-level office
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by Source New Mexico.

Joshua Bowling Source New Mexico

New Mexico state lawmakers in the upcoming legislative session may consider a proposal to create a state-level office dedicated to the crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons.

Members of the New Mexico Department of Justice’s MMIP Task Force testified Thursday, Nov. 12, in Santa Fe before the interim Indian Affairs Committee, where they said “many members” of the task force have been advocating for a state-level office.

State lawmakers had several questions for the task force members about how such an office would coordinate with other state agencies. The task force members said they have had varying levels of success getting in touch with state agency heads and hope to make more progress in the weeks between Gov.-elect Deb Haaland’s inauguration and the beginning of the legislative session .

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

“While there has been really strong interest and we want to push this forward, we do recognize the need for additional expertise and guidance to determine how such an office should be structured, what its responsibilities should include,” Birga Alden, a task force member who also works as the chief communications officer of the anti-human trafficking nonprofit New Mexico Dream Center , said at the hearing held at the Santa Fe Indian School. “We welcome your input as we continue to develop the proposal.”

Previously, New Mexico had an MMIP task force within the state Indian Affairs Department. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham scrapped the task force in 2023 , and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez created one within his New Mexico Department of Justice in early 2024 after the Legislature passed a joint memorial directing him to do so .

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Any legislative proposals will come during Haaland’s first term as governor. Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, previously served as secretary of the U.S. Department of the Interior, where she established a Missing and Murdered Unit within the Bureau of Indian Affairs . At the time, she said the unit would coordinate with tribal governments, law enforcement agencies and families of missing people to help address the crisis.

Before her June primary election for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, Haaland told Source NM that she would revisit the state Indian Affairs Department’s defunct task force and “be transparent about the issue and bring people to the table and find out what we need.”

State Sen. Shannon Pinto (D-Tohatchi), a Diné woman who chairs the interim Indian Affairs Committee, said that efforts to find missing and murdered Indigenous people often proves difficult because “jurisdiction has always been the conundrum.”

“We shouldn’t be having to do this because our current law and our justice system — it’s for everybody,” she said. “There should be no conundrum on having any kind of action taken for a loved one…but that’s not where we are with this issue.”

scraped.title: ‘We don’t play about our babies’: Monica says she is fiercely protective of Kobe Bryant’s daughter Natalia
scraped.description: Monica opens up about her honorary aunt relationship with Natalia Bryant, praising the model's accomplishments and describing her protective approach.
scraped.author: Bobby Pen
scraped.h1: ‘We don’t play about our babies’: Monica says she is fiercely protective of Kobe Bryant’s daughter Natalia
scraped.body_text:
The R&B singer describes herself as an honorary aunt to the 23-year-old model, who credits Monica with being a dependable source of support and guidance.

Monica is making it clear that when it comes to Natalia Bryant , the protective instincts are real.

The Grammy-winning singer recently opened up about her relationship with the 23-year-old model, the eldest daughter of the late NBA legend Kobe Bryant and Vanessa Bryant. Monica, who has maintained a longtime friendship with Vanessa, considers herself an honorary aunt to Natalia and says she takes that role seriously.

Speaking exclusively with PEOPLE at the 2026 EBONY Power 100 Gala in Los Angeles, the singer offered a glimpse into their relationship, describing herself as someone who is not afraid to be direct when it comes to looking out for the younger Bryant.

Monica even joked that she is probably the most aggressive aunt, although Natalia offered a slightly different description of her approach.

“Not aggressive. We’re direct,” Natalia told PEOPLE, reframing Monica’s protectiveness as a sign of her straightforward personality.

Monica agreed, adding, “Because we don’t play about our babies. It’s no exception to the rule.”

For Natalia, that protectiveness comes with a sense of reassurance. She described Monica as someone she can reach whenever she needs advice, support or simply someone to talk to.

“Well, Auntie Mo here, she is seriously the most down to earth, so supportive. You can call her any moment, anytime, about absolutely anything, and she’ll always pick up and she’ll always be there,” Natalia said.

The exchange offered a glimpse into a bond that extends beyond celebrity friendships and public appearances. Monica’s relationship with Natalia reflects the kind of extended-family connections that are common in many Black households, where close friends can become aunties and uncles who play meaningful roles in children’s lives even when there is no biological connection.

Monica also has plenty of reasons to celebrate Natalia’s accomplishments.

The young model graduated cum laude from the University of Southern California in May 2025 while continuing to develop her fashion career. She signed with IMG Models in 2021 and made her runway debut for Versace during Milan Fashion Week in September 2023.

“I’m so incredibly proud of Nani, not only graduating from college, but aspiring to do everything in the fashion field,” Monica said. “Everything she puts her mind to, she does it. And it’s just amazing to see.”

Monica also connected Natalia’s determination to the work ethic associated with her father, who died alongside her sister, 13-year-old Gianna, and seven others in a helicopter crash in January 2020.

“It’s Mamba Mentality from top to bottom over here,” Monica said, referencing Kobe’s well-known philosophy of discipline, dedication and continuous improvement.

“But she’s just a hard worker, and she’s such a sweetheart at the same time,” the singer added. “I adore her.”

Natalia has continued building her own identity in the fashion industry while honoring her family’s legacy. Her modeling career reached another milestone in October, when she debuted at the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show.

At 23, Natalia is continuing to establish herself professionally while navigating the attention that comes with being part of one of basketball’s most recognizable families.

For Monica, however, the accomplishments are only part of what makes her proud. Her comments suggest that her investment in Natalia extends beyond the modeling industry, public recognition and the Bryant family’s legacy.

Whether she is celebrating Natalia’s academic achievements or encouraging her as she pursues opportunities in fashion, Monica appears comfortable occupying a role that is both supportive and protective.

And if Natalia’s description is any indication, Auntie Mo is only a phone call away.

scraped.title: 'A sheer joy': Tom Hanks pays tribute to former co-star Irma P. Hall after powerhouse actress dies
scraped.description: Tom Hanks pays tribute to Irma P. Hall, his The Ladykillers co-star, after her death at 91, calling the Soul Food actress 'a sheer joy.'
scraped.author: Odafe Oghen
scraped.h1: ‘A sheer joy’: Tom Hanks pays tribute to former co-star Irma P. Hall after powerhouse actress dies
scraped.body_text:
The actor shared a personal tribute to his co-star from 'The Ladykillers,' who died Nov. 10 in Dallas.

Tom Hanks is remembering Irma P. Hall , his co-star in the 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers,” after her death at 91. Hall, who famously played Big Mama in 1997’s “Soul Food,” helped ensure the film has a lasting legacy in Black cinema.

Hanks shared a photograph of Hall on Instagram on Friday, Nov. 13, along with a brief tribute. “Irma P. Hall was a sheer joy…May her memory be eternal…,” he wrote. The two actors worked together on Joel and Ethan Coen’s dark comedy more than two decades ago.

A post shared by Tom Hanks (@tomhanks)

Hanks played Professor G.H. Dorr, an eccentric criminal who rents a room in the home of Marva Munson, a devout and sharp-tongued character played by Hall. His plan to use the house as a base for a robbery runs into trouble when Munson grows suspicious. Hall won a jury prize at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival for her performance in the film, which features an all-star ensemble cast including Marlon Wayans, J.K. Simmons and George Wallace.

During her recovery from a January 2004 car crash and open-heart surgery, Hall heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers, who signed her pillow.

“Whenever I miss them, I hug it.” she told the Associated Press at the time.

Hall died Nov. 10 in Dallas, her family confirmed in a statement released the next day. Her relatives remembered her as an actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker, and asked for privacy as they mourned. No cause of death was announced.

Before finding wider fame as an actress, Hall spent more than two decades teaching in Dallas public schools. Director Raymond St. Jacques cast her in the 1973 film “Book of Numbers” after hearing her recite poetry. Her later screen credits included “A Family Thing,” “Beloved,” “Collateral,” and “Meet the Browns.”

For many viewers, Hall will remain Big Mama, the matriarch whose Sunday dinners held her family together in “Soul Food.” Hanks’ tribute offers a glimpse of the affection she inspired among the people who worked alongside her.

scraped.body_text:
The three-year-old appears on six Arena Homme+ covers, including one with Rihanna wearing her red jumpsuit from the 2023 Super Bowl pregnancy reveal.

Rihanna and A$AP Rocky ‘s 3-year-old son Riot Rose has landed six covers of Arena Homme+ Issue 66, marking his magazine cover debut.

Five of the covers feature the toddler alone, while a sixth pairs him with Rihanna in her red Super Bowl jumpsuit from the performance where she revealed she was pregnant with him. The milestone follows his September concert appearance in Copenhagen alongside both of his parents.

On her Instagram account, Rih shared the six covers on Instagram, captioning the post, “RIOT ROSE. Arena Homme+ Issue 66.” The photographs include a portrait of mother and son, with Rihanna wearing the red Loewe outfit from the 2023 Super Bowl halftime show.

Photographed by Oliver Hadlee Pearch and styled by Jahleel Weaver, Riot appears in designer outfits from Chanel, Louis Vuitton and other labels. One image shows him standing on stacked Louis Vuitton trunks in denim, while another shows him wearing an oversized tweed jacket. He also wears Chopard jewelry in the fashion spread.

A post shared by badgalriri (@badgalriri)

Rocky hinted at the shoot before its release.

“One of my sons has a modeling gig in like three days, you know, the day before my birthday, and it’s — I’m so proud of him,” Rocky told The Cut in September. “This is his first magazine cover, so I think it’s just fascinating to see these little people grow into personalities of their own. I mean, they’re still relatively little and small, but you know, they kind of speak up for themselves and have their own kind of swag and sh-t. It’s crazy.”

“It's trippy.” A$AP Rocky reveals that his and #Rihanna 's son is going to be on the cover of a magazine for the first time … and it's coming this week!! 👀💗 pic.twitter.com/qlUdfacUbC

Rihanna has also given her thoughts on Riot’s personality. Speaking with Harper’s Bazaar in 2025, she called him hilarious and said he often wakes up squealing and singing. She joked that his noisy mornings make him her alarm clock.

Riot Rose is the middle child of Rihanna and Rocky’s three children, all of whom have appeared on magazine covers. Older brother RZA joined their parents for British Vogue in 2023. Younger sister Rocki appeared with Rihanna on the U.S. edition of W and with Rocky on W China this year.

items.title: Zohran Mamdani Pauses Trump’s New SNAP Rules—Giving Corner Bodegas a Crucial 90-Day Lifeline
items.summary: Mamdani gets Trump to delay SNAP rules, but Black communities facing disproportionate food insecurity still have much at stake.Read more...

scraped.title: Zohran Mamdani Pauses Trump’s New SNAP Rules—Giving Corner Bodegas a Crucial 90-Day Lifeline – The Root
scraped.h1: Zohran Mamdani Pauses Trump’s New SNAP Rules—Giving Corner Bodegas a Crucial 90-Day Lifeline
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Mamdani gets Trump to delay SNAP rules, but Black communities facing disproportionate food insecurity still have much at stake.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

WASHINGTON, DC – NOVEMBER 21: U.S. President Donald Trump meets with New York City Mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani (L) in the Oval Office of the White House on November 21, 2025 in Washington, DC. Trump congratulated Mamdani on his election win as the two political opponents met to discuss policies for New York City, including affordability, public safety, and immigration enforcement. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has struck a 90-day deal with President Donald Trump to pump the brakes on enforcing new federal SNAP rules that threatened to shutter thousands of corner bodegas—the very spots Black folks, people of color, and working-class families rely on to put food on the table.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

The agreement marks a historic moment of direct negotiation with an administration whose policies have created uncertainty for millions of folks relying on federal food assistance . And for Black communities, where food insecurity remains disproportionately high, the stakes extend beyond the survival of small businesses.

Bodegas are more than neighborhood convenience stores in New York City. Across all five boroughs, these businesses are woven into the cultural and economic fabric of working-class communities, providing accessible groceries and everyday essentials in neighborhoods where full-service supermarkets can be difficult to reach.

At the same time, families rely heavily on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), so losing the ability to use benefits at these stores could mean another barrier between them and a reliable source of food.

Mamdani celebrated the deal with the Trump administration that gives bodegas and neighborhood grocery stores another 90 days to comply with USDA stocking standards or risk losing their ability to accept SNAP benefits.

RELATED : Why SNAP Adding Hot Rotisserie Chicken Is More Important Than You Might Think

“When hundreds of bodegas came to our administration asking for help, we stood with them,” Mamdani wrote in a statement shared with The Root . “Without more time, many of these stores risked losing the ability to accept SNAP – threatening their livelihoods and making it harder for families to put food on the table.”

And the racial disparities surrounding food insecurity are hard to ignore. Black families are disproportionately affected, with nearly one in four Black, non-Hispanic households (24.4%) experiencing food insecurity in 2024, compared with 10.1% of white, non-Hispanic households, according to the USDA . Black Americans also made up 25.7% of SNAP recipients in fiscal year 2023, highlighting just how important the program is to Black communities.

The USDA was set to begin enforcing the new stocking requirements on Nov. 4. Under the rule, stores accepting SNAP must carry at least seven varieties of food across four categories: dairy, grains, protein, and fruits and vegetables.

But small retailers and anti-hunger advocates have been pushing back, arguing that the timeline doesn’t give neighborhood stores enough time or resources to make the changes. Nearly 250 stores reportedly signed a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins asking for a delay, while lawmakers from both sides of the aisle also called for more time.

“For those living in areas with no major grocery stores, the loss of these authorized SNAP retailers means losing the only accessible point of purchase for groceries,” Crystal FitzSimons, president of the Food Research & Action Center, said in a statement.

New York City has more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores, and SNAP benefits provide billions of dollars in annual purchasing power. Deputy Mayor Julie Su said the extension gives retailers additional time to make changes they want to implement but lack the resources and guidance to accomplish immediately.

The 90-day extension gives bodegas some much-needed breathing room, but it’s only a temporary fix. As we head into 2027, there are still big questions about the future of SNAP, including funding, eligibility and whether families will continue to have access to the food assistance they depend on.

For Black families, who are already more likely to experience food insecurity, what’s decided in the coming months could have a real impact—not just on their grocery budgets, but on the neighborhood businesses and communities that help keep food on the table.

scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Now that the holiday season is upon us, we thought we’d whet your whistle for the new Black movies coming in 2027.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Thuso Mbedu plays Zélie and Damson Idris plays Inan in Children of Blood and Bone from Paramount Pictures.

While the holiday season of 2026 is just getting underway, that’s not stopping us from looking ahead and anticipating the new Black films and TV shows that are set to drop in 2027! And believe us when we say there’s a whole bunch of goodness in store!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

From Denzel Washington and Michael B. Jordan to Whoopi Goldberg and Tyler Perry—this next year will be filled with top-tier series and films you need to put on your radar NOW! Keep reading for more.

Gina Prince-Bythewood is pulling all the stops for the film adaptation of “Children of Blood and Bone” and bringing in some serious star power to go along with it. Viola Davis, Damson Idris, Cynthia Erivo, Thuso Mbedu, Regina King, Chiwetel Ejiofor and more. This film is going to be one that we can’t stop talking about!

Release Date: January 15, 2027 in theaters

Related: Children of Blood and Bone Black All-Star Cast Revealed

This Danai Gurira and Denzel Washington-led film is shaping up to have the things you love about heists, cons, and bank robberies—complete with a knockout cast to really elevate the story! Yeah, sign us up for this one immediately.

Release Date: January 15, 2027 on Netflix

Forget a Black James Bond, Oscar-winning actor Michael B. Jordan is giving us all the shaken and stirred feelings with his version of “The Thomas Crown Affair.” Expect this one to be sleek, chic, and full of a very suave and debonair Jordan.

Release Date: March 5, 2027

Miles Morales is back in “Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse” and continuing on from the events that happened in the previous film. You know, the one where he got trapped in a whole alternate reality and was tied up by another variant of himself? Yeah, we’re beyond ready to see how this unfolds!

Release Date: June 18, 2027 in theaters

“Women Like Us” is set to tell the story of a recently widowed woman who gets dragged to the Hamptons by her lifelong best friends and sister on what should have been her 30th anniversary. As the days go by, the weekend becomes a reckoning, with grief, marriage, sisterhood, and the realization that dreams don’t have an expiration date. But if the plot wasn’t enough to convince you to see it, maybe the cast will: Whoopi Goldberg, Vivica A. Fox, Jenifer Lewis, and Vanessa Williams!

Release Date: Some time in 2027

While the upcoming season five of “Bridgerton” will do as it normally does and follow the eponymous family, this season is set to have a bit more melanin in it thanks in large part to the addition of Tega Alexander, Jacqueline Boatswain, Gemma Knight Jones and more! We can’t wait to see how the ton reacts to this!

Release Date: Some time in 2027

If you’re a fan of shows like “Chicago Fire,” “Station 19,” “9-1-1” and “Fire Country” but feel like they needs a bit more melanin in them, look no further than Tyler Perry’s upcoming show, “Where There’s Smoke.” Similar to the aforementioned series, this one will also follow the lives of a group of firefighters as they navigate the challenges of their high-stakes profession, all while grappling with personal struggles, imperfect relationships, and the emotional toll of saving lives.

Release Date: Likely 2027

The delicious messiness of Beauty in Black will return for the third and final season in 2027. But trust and believe, they’re going to go out witha bang, so you better mark your calendars for the presumed explosive end!

Release Date: August 27, 2027 on Netflix

While Ice Cube may not be involved in Prime Video’s TV adaptation of his film , “Barbershop,” the forthcoming series still looks promising. And it’s all thanks to star Jermaine Fowler and other cast members like Brett Gray, Punkie Johnson, Roy Wood Jr., Bresha Webb, Bokeem Woodbine, Langston Kerman and more. Others like Zack Fox, Ego Nwodim, Ziwe, and other funny folks are all slated to made guest appearances so you can expect this one to be filled with laughs from start to finish!

Release Date: February 10, 2027

Writer S.A. Cosby’s compelling novel “All Sinners Bleed” is finally going to get the small screen treatment and some serious acting gravitas thanks to stars like Ṣọpẹ́ Dìrísù, Nicole Beharie, and Daniel Ezra. If you loved the serial killer suspense from the book, then you can assume this one will play up on that even more!

Release Date: The first half of 2027

“Sinners” star Miles Caton will make his return to the big screen in a highly-anticipated crime-adjacent film starring Denzel Washington and Teyonah Parris. While the film has yet to get an official name, we know when it’s set to come out and what it’s about.

This movie follows a former police detective serving a life sentence who gets diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. As a result, he gets a compassionate release and a prognosis of only six months to live. While living out the rest of his days, he decided to rekindle his relationship with the estranged daughter he left behind and a grandson he never knew existed while his past follows close behind him.

Release Date: October 1, 2027 int theaters

Cynthia Erivo will be lending her beautiful voice to the wonderful, animated world of whimsy and pixie dust for the new film, “Bad Fairies.” You can expect this movie to be filled with some good, old wholesome fun so be sure to bring the kiddos out for this one!

Release Date: May 21, 2027

items.title: Justice Clarence Thomas To Teach Racial Equality At Texas University After Decades of Disappointing Black Folks

scraped.title: Justice Clarence Thomas To Teach Racial Equality At Texas University After Decades of Disappointing Black Folks – The Root
scraped.h1: Justice Clarence Thomas To Teach Racial Equality At Texas University After Decades of Disappointing Black Folks
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, whose views on racial equality have drawn decades of criticism, will now help shape tomorrow’s leaders at UT at Austin.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

AUSTIN, TEXAS – APRIL 15: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas speaks at the University of Texas on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas is headed back to college to teach a course about civil rights. But for some, that may sound like an unlikely assignment for a justice whose views on race and equality have sparked decades of criticism and controversy. The conservative has long challenged policies and legal protections that civil rights advocates consider essential to addressing racial inequality. Yet Thomas will soon bring his perspective to the University of Texas at Austin, where he is preparing to teach students about race, equality and the American political tradition.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Beyond simple academia, Thomas will have a rare opportunity to influence how the next generation of leaders understands one of the most consequential struggles in American history. And everyone should be paying attention to how he plans to do so.

Thomas will lead a week-long undergraduate seminar titled “ Equality and the New Birth of Freedom” from Feb. 1 through Feb. 5, 2027, through UT Austin’s School of Civic Leadership. The one-credit course will enroll just 17 students, selected from 65 applicants, and will include two hours of instruction from Thomas every day.

The curriculum is set to explore American political thought, race and equality through the writings and speeches of influential Black thinkers and civil rights figures like W.E.B. Du Bois, Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington, the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. Students will also break down how questions of race and equality intersect with recent Supreme Court decisions.

RELATED : Oh Lord, Republicans are Pushing for a Clarence Thomas Statue, But Here’s Why This Should Never Happen

But Thomas’ presence at the head of the classroom is particularly interesting given his judicial legacy.

Since joining the Supreme Court in 1991 , succeeding legendary civil rights attorney Thurgood Marshall, Thomas has developed a conservative constitutional philosophy that frequently challenges civil rights traditions. He opposed affirmative action, questioned federal voting rights protections and rejected certain legal remedies for racial discrimination. That’s, of course, all on top of decades’ worth of allegations of sexual misconduct and corruption , which has not been proven in a court of law.

Regardless, Thomas’ positions have drawn decades of criticism from civil rights organizations, legal scholars and advocates who argue that his colorblind interpretation of the Constitution overlooks the systemic inequalities that continue to affect Black Americans. Supporters, meanwhile, view his philosophy as a defense of individual equality and constitutional principles.

The opportunity presents a significant moment for the 17 students who will learn directly from one of the most influential figures in American law. Whether students embrace or challenge his worldview, they will encounter a perspective that has helped shape the country’s legal landscape for generations.

This opportunity, therefore, is bigger than just Thomas. As future lawyers, policymakers and civic leaders grapple with the meaning of equality, they will do so in a country still wrestling with the legacy of slavery, segregation and the civil rights movement. Thomas is now charged in directly helping to shape that conversation.

scraped.title: Scott Colom’s Unexpected Wardrobe Choice Sparks a Frenzy After His Historic Mississippi Victory
scraped.description: Mississippi Senator Scott Colom’s historic victory draws attention to his Richard Pryor hoodie and his use of fashion to celebrate Black culture.
scraped.author: Sharmaine Johnson
scraped.h1: Scott Colom’s Unexpected Wardrobe Choice Sparks a Frenzy After His Historic Mississippi Victory
scraped.body_text:
Mississippi Senator Scott Colom’s historic victory draws attention to his Richard Pryor hoodie and his use of fashion to celebrate Black culture.

Senator Scott Colom ’s victory in Mississippi’s Senate District 14 race marked a historic political shift, making him the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since Reconstruction and flipping the seat from Republican to Democrat.

But beyond the political headlines, Colom’s fashion choices are also catching people’s attention.

Reports say Colom wore a Richard Pryor hoodie when he learned he had won the election. Fans applauded his choice and the message behind it.

X user Jay Scott Smith tweeted , “That hoodie!” Another user shared the same sentiment , writing, “If anyone knows where that hoodie can be purchased please post. Thx.”

Richard Pryor’s daughter, Elizabeth Pryor, also joined the conversation, explaining that the message was especially powerful for this moment and expressing her gratitude in an Instagram post .

“My heart is absolutely bursting. But even more because when he found out the news, he was wearing this T-shirt,” she shared before showing a picture of Colom. “I’m processing what it means about Scott Colom not only to be a Richard Pryor fan to celebrate my father’s ability to speak truth to power in a way that was vulnerable and open-hearted. But I know one thing: my father would be so proud, and I’m so proud that this moment happened with my father emblazoned on Scott Colom’s chest.”

This isn’t the first time Colom has showcased his Black pride and used clothing to make a statement. Throughout his campaign, Colom has represented several HBCUs, including Alcorn State and Jackson State University. He has also promised to show love to Mississippi’s other schools in due time.

Beyond HBCU apparel, Colom has also used his wardrobe to highlight important messages about Black history and culture. One hoodie from his collection features a quote from Bob Moses , a civil rights organizer who played a significant role in Mississippi’s fight for voting rights.

The hoodie reads, “When you’re in Mississippi, the rest of America doesn’t seem real. And when you’re in the rest of America, Mississippi doesn’t seem real.”

The Richard Pryor hoodie carries a similar message. Pryor built his reputation on unapologetic comedy, using humor to tackle racism, classism, and the realities of Black life. His work challenged audiences to confront uncomfortable truths while giving Black Americans a voice through comedy.

Colom’s choice to wear Pryor on such a historic day resonated with people who recognize the comedian’s legacy. The online reaction also showed that the hoodie made a statement of its own. Colom’s historic win even caught the attention of President Donald Trump , who had some unexpected praise for the newly elected senator. When asked about Colom, Trump recalled seeing him campaign at one of his Mississippi rallies.

“I heard it the other day when I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line telling everybody on the line what a good job he did,” Trump said. “I give him a lot of credit for that.”

Scott Colom in Mississippi, finding out the race was called for him while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Nov. 11, 2026 (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) pic.twitter.com/8z8Lfeuopi

scraped.title: 'I Dare Him': El-Sayed Is Done Playing Nice with Trump; Now He's Coming for the President with a Golden Opportunity He Knows He Can't Refuse
scraped.description: Abdul El-Sayed is dangling an offer aimed straight at Trump’s ego — and daring the president to explain himself if he turns it down.
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: ‘I Dare Him’: El-Sayed Is Done Playing Nice with Trump; Now He’s Coming for the President with a Golden Opportunity He Knows He Can’t Refuse
scraped.body_text:
Abdul El-Sayed is dangling an offer aimed straight at Trump’s ego — and daring the president to explain himself if he turns it down.

Michigan’s new Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed isn’t wasting any time. He’s been making the rounds on Capitol Hill and talking with media outlets since his hard-fought election victory in the midterms.

He’s also apparently ready to start treating President Donald Trump like the bully he is, escalating a growing war of words between himself and Trump.

The Rhodes scholar and former Detroit Health Department executive director is suggesting a possible way to pass universal health care or Medicare for all and get Trump on board with it or at least force a veto.

During an interview with NPR on Wednesday, El-Sayed appealed to Trump’s vanity, suggesting a bill to provide health care to all Americans could be named after the president himself.

“Put his name on it,” the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate told NPR’s Leila Fadel on the video podcast “Newsmakers.”

“He’ll probably pass it. I’m not above doing that. I don’t care what it’s called,” a serious El-Sayed said.

Then he went a step further.

“I dare Donald Trump to veto. I dare him,” the Michigan Democrat challenged, “because if you want to make the argument that Democrats want to deliver for you, do that. Make him veto it.”

He doubled down on the offer, too, in a social media post directed squarely at the president.

“This is a message for @realDonaldTrump Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed baited Trump in a caption over an image showing a gold “TRUMPCARE” card.

The post had almost 4 million views by noon on Thursday.

A day before his NPR interview, El-Sayed told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins the same thing about naming universal health insurance “Trumpcare-For-All.”

“Donald, if you’re watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff. You can finally meet the unmet promise in America to guarantee everybody health care. So, it’s on the table if you want to do it,” he offered.

In the same interview with NPR, the incoming U.S. senator threw caution to the wind and repeated what he said about Trump on the campaign trail.

“You recently called President Trump the dumbest effing guy who ever was president,” Fadel said.

El-Sayed agreed. “True.”

Fadel continued, “You’ve also said Democrats should drop the decorum and treat the president as the unserious fool that he is.”

Again, El-Sayed agreed. “True.”

“Why are you taking that approach?” Fadel asked him.

El-Sayed didn’t hold back, explaining how to handle a “bully.”

“Because he’s a bully alongside being a narcissist. And the only way you deal with bullies is to stand up to them. Bullies don’t bully you because they necessarily care for the thing you have. They bully you because they like to bully you because it makes them feel strong,” the Democrat stated.

“And the way you take on a bully is to bully back because then they learn that this does not make them feel strong. It makes them feel weak, and they don’t like to feel weak. So they back off,” he continued.

He also said you can’t let a “bully” get away with it because then they just continue the behavior.

“So, I think it’s important for us to stand up to him.”

Trump and his mini-me JD Vance spent the months leading up to the Nov. 3 midterms calling El-Sayed the worst names possible, from Jihadist and terrorist to a member of the political Islamist group, the Muslim Brotherhood.

Trump also accused El-Sayed of being a “jihadist lunatic” who was “on the side of terrorists,” NPR reported.

Unfortunately for Vance, he will be tasked with swearing in all the new senators in January, including El-Sayed.

“I hope he doesn’t make it awkward,” he told NPR. “There is, as I said, a delicious irony in the fact that he is constitutionally obligated to swear me in.”

Social media is fully backing El-Sayed.

“Finally, someone who can meet the moment we are in,” an X user proclaimed.

Author Joyce Carol Oates agreed, commenting “spoken like a true leader,” above a clip of the El-Sayed’s NPR interview.

Another poster may have said it best about El-Sayed comments on Trump’s bullying and how to handle a bully: “Perfect answer.”

This is a message for @realDonaldTrump . Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave. pic.twitter.com/f32IYs3FXG

scraped.title: ‘That’s So Raven’ Star Kyle Massey Was Already Locked In for a Movie with Morgan Freeman When Disney Put a Stop to It
scraped.description: Kyle Massey had already booked the movie and attended a table read with two Hollywood heavyweights. Then Disney stepped in with one demand that cost him the role.
scraped.author: Danielle Jones
scraped.h1: ‘That’s So Raven’ Star Kyle Massey Was Already Locked In for a Movie with Morgan Freeman When Disney Put a Stop to It
scraped.body_text:
Kyle Massey had already booked the movie and attended a table read with two Hollywood heavyweights. Then Disney stepped in with one demand that cost him the role.

Kyle Massey is 35 years old now, but more than two decades ago, he was a teenager working on one of Disney’s most popular TV series.

​From 2003 to 2007, he played Cory Baxter, the annoying little brother of Raven Baxter, played by Raven-Symoné , on “That’s So Raven.”

​He later went from a supporting character to a lead, still portraying Cory in the spinoff series “Cory in the House.” It ran from 2007 to 2008 and ran for 34 episodes. Though both series gave Massey a great start in his acting career, playing Cory also cost him other on-screen opportunities.

​The Atlanta native told the truth about what happened behind the scenes regarding what could have been his first big movie.

In an interview with “The Art of Dialogue,” he revealed that Disney made him turn down a movie with Morgan Freeman and Edward Norton because he was Cory.

“I actually booked a movie with Morgan Freeman and Edward Norton and I did a table read for the movie. We was locked in and then Disney I guess read the script and they was like, ‘You can’t do this. You’re Cory.’”

Massey admitted he had to “relinquish” the role, even though he’d already booked the job. He even has pictures with Norton at the table read.

​Further explaining what happened, he said, “I had to, like, relinquish the role because it conflicted with the character that I was portraying on the Disney Channel and that was the priority.”

Massey could not name the movie because it still had a “working title” at the time. The filmmakers had not finalized its name.

The studio may have scrapped the movie entirely. No documented film release features both Norton and Freeman.

​Despite not being able to play the role, Massey has a positive outlook on the situation.

He said, “This is how God works. Like I had to turn down that role. But once I turned down that role and I gave my all to Corey on ‘Raven,’ that turned into ‘Cory in the House.’ So everything always just kind of works out.”

“Sometimes the big letdown is not a letdown,” Massey added.

Fans online expressed shock after learning that Disney had forced Massey to give up the role.

​One person said , “So he is saying Disney wouldn’t let him be in a movie that either didn’t get made or flew so under the radar he can’t even remember it! Ok. From what it sounds like even if he had done this supposed movie it wouldn’t have done much for him anyway.”

​Another fan who felt similarly wrote , “Whatever this movie was supposed to be.. It never happened.”

Two supporters wrote, “I loved him on ‘That’s So Raven!” and “‘Cory In The House was the s–t.”

Before booking “That’s So Raven,” Massey came close to landing a role on another Disney show. “Even Stevens,” which starred Shia LaBeouf and Christy Carlson Romano, ultimately went in a different direction.

Massey auditioned for Beans, the quirky, pestering neighbor of the Stevens family, but Steven Anthony Lawrence won the role.

​But he later got to play Cory.

Massey also auditioned for Beans, the quirky, pestering neighbor of the Stevens family. However, Steven Anthony Lawrence ultimately landed the part.

After “That’s So Raven” ended in 2007, Massey took on the lead role in its spinoff, “Cory in the House.”

​He recalled that he was in Utah filming a Disney movie called ‘Life Is Ruff’ when he suddenly confessed to his mom, Angel Massey.

​“I’ll never forget my mom and I, we’re going over lines on the bed and then while she’s like reading my lines to me, I just looked at her, and I was like, ‘You know, I don’t want to stop acting,’” he recalled.

​His mom reminded him that even though “That’s So Raven” was over, he was still working on a movie.

​He said, “And then the next morning, they call me about ‘Cory in the House,’ you know? So, it’s like as soon as I start to feel something, the universe reacts. And I’ve learned to just trust it wherever it takes me, you know?”

​After ‘Cory in the House,’ Massey went on to do voice acting in the animated Disney series “Fish Hooks.”

Other projects he starred in over the years include “Gotham,” “Being Mary Jane,” and “Millenials.”

A post shared by The Art Of Dialogue (@theartofdialogue)

scraped.title: Meet the Man Behind Scott Colom’s Viral Senate Campaign Ads
scraped.description: Ryan Sayles helped create two videos that spoke to Mississippians and the nation as a whole.
scraped.author: Camila DeChalus
scraped.h1: Meet the Man Behind Scott Colom’s Viral Senate Campaign Ads
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

Ryan Sayles was exhausted the day he shot what would become one of the most-talked about political ads of the 2026 midterms.

The 27-year-old content creator was celebrating homecoming at Alcorn State, his alma mater, when Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate campaign team wanted him to film the commercial that would go viral. “I’m really tired, and I’m out here for homecoming,” he said. “But OK, I’ll drive.” On a Friday morning in early October, he drove about two and a half hours to Columbus, Mississippi, to shoot it. “I filmed that video, and then I went back and enjoyed homecoming, and then I edited on a Sunday,” Sayles said.

The spot was a response to comments made by Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in February, when she was asked in an interview with WLOX about rising beef prices. She said that Mississippians had “so many proteins to choose from,” suggesting shoppers pick a different protein should beef be too expensive. In the ad, visibly irritated Mississippians at the grill, in a diner, and in a grocery store said they would rather “pick another senator instead.”

After Colom posted the ad on X on Oct. 13., it drew 2.8 million views in its first 36 hours, and had passed 16 million by Nov. 6, Yahoo News reported — at least four times as many as the video of Barack Obama’s endorsement of Colom. “Pick another senator” became a slogan for the campaign.

“It crazy,” Sayles said of the ad’s success.

Colom went on to defeat Hyde-Smith, becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator in more than 150 years . At his victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11, he spoke in front of a sign that read “Picked Another Senator,” Newsweek reported .

Sayles also gave the campaign’s viral Halloween ad its name. The spoof of Ryan Coogler’s Sinners , the film set in the Mississippi Delta, casts Colom and his identical twin brother, Andrew, as the movie’s twins, guarding a door against a Hyde-Smith lookalike who begs to be let in. Sayles titled it “Sinators.”

Colom has been quick to give Sayles, who had never worked on a political campaign before, credit for his work. The day after the election, he wrote on X that Sayles should be considered the breakout star of the cycle and did “GAME CHANGING work with SO little.” Sayles is just as quick to pass it along.

“I’m getting a lot of credit right now, and I appreciate it,” he said. “But make no mistake, this was a collaborative effort.”

Capital B spoke with Sayles about how the protein ad came together, why the campaign took the risk, why he thinks it resonated with people within Mississippi and across the country, and how he coached the delivery of the ad’s breakout line — “Shiiii.”

Capital B: Walk me through how the protein ad came together.

Ryan Sayles: Andrew Colom, Scott’s brother, along with Scott and Gerard Henderson, wrote the script for it. Basically presented it to me as like, “Hey, we really need to do this. I think it’d be a really good idea.” I had no idea that it was gonna be what it was. I definitely did not know that it would be this big.

When did you realize the protein ad was going viral, and what were those first few days like?

President Obama endorsed Scott the day before we dropped it, and so I was like, “We’ll never have a video to do what that just did.” That’s President Obama.

And literally, the night [we published it], I was at my nephew’s game. I saw him playing football, and I was watching the post. Over two hours, got 8,000 likes. I was like, “Oh, this might be up there with the Obama ad.” And when I woke up in the morning, it was crazy. I was like, oh, this is definitely gonna pass the Obama endorsement. It’s about to do something I didn’t have no idea it could do.

I realized that it was actually going to be a pivotal piece of the campaign [when] Fox News pushed the ad on national television and graded it an A. I was like, OK, we just did something that is not normal.

I don’t like the idea of political ads that anger people or put people in fear. I like political ads that motivate people, that make people feel a part of something, and speak to how people really feel. I just want people to see stuff, care about it, and if they can identify with it, cool. I don’t like the idea of scaring voters or bashing people.

And what’s your favorite moment?

I mean, come on now. You know it was my guy saying “Shiiii.” That was the part that did it, man. He changed the course of history with that, and that was definitely the best part. I had to coach him through that part a little bit, because the first time he said it, it wasn’t from the soul. You know what I mean? We needed to reach down and get that one. So that was very fun, though. And I knew from then. I was like, it’s gonna be good.

Our content was well known around Mississippi. When I thought about a video doing good, I’m like, yeah, a lot of people in Mississippi see it. I wasn’t in the mindset of, a lot of people in the world gonna see this. That had never crossed my mind. I was on CNN [Thursday], and I was like, “What am I doing on CNN?”

Another breakout ad for Colom’s campaign was “Sinators.” Walk me through it. How did it come together, and what were you trying to say about Mississippi?

With “Sinators,” [cameraman] Kayland Partee did his thing. You would think a lot of people filmed that. Kayland Partee filmed that with one camera by himself, and some guys helped with lighting. Andrew Colom wrote that script, and he did an amazing job. That is Scott’s identical twin brother. A lot of people thought that was like an AI thing or something, but that was Scott and his identical twin brother, Andrew.

I did come up with the name “Sinators.” That’s the one thing I did. Like two hours before we posted, I was like, “What if we named it ‘Sinators’ instead?” That was my little sprinkle.

I think the reason it worked [is] because, of course, a lot of people love the movie Sinners , but also it’s Mississippi. The movie Sinners was based out of Mississippi. It spoke to so many stories and had so many analogies, and I think that was something that we tapped into, while also showcasing the fact that people want to move in a new direction and elect Scott Colom. So I think it was dope.

You thought mostly Mississippians would see it. What has the response from around the country been like?

I ain’t gonna lie to you. I’ve been trying to take this in, and I got so many family members and friends that are just expressing how happy they are about the recognition. They’ve seen me working for a very long time. They’ve seen the stress that a campaign brings to me. I’ll make a joke: I got two gray hairs. I named one Scott and the other Colom. But yeah, it’s been great.

Around the country, I’m seeing so many people just quoting the ad and saying how much that ad has meant to them. I’m getting thank-you messages from people in California, and I’m like, thank you for what? And they [say], The ad, it helped. It inspired us. It made us feel hope.” And Mississippi now has a Democratic senator, the first Black senator to be elected by Mississippians. All of that is just amazing. I’m blessed to be a part of it.

Why do you think the ad landed with people who can’t even vote in this race?

I think the main thing that landed with people is, of course, he was speaking how a lot of people in America feel right now. People are fed up. The other part of this that made this ad be appreciated in a different way was the fact that Scott was in the ad for five seconds. It wasn’t about him. It was about Mississippi. It was about people and how voters feel. And I think a lot of times in these political spaces, a lot of candidates can forget that this is not about them. It’s about the people that they are serving, and I think that’s one thing that Scott holds dear and close to his heart, is that his responsibility is to the people of Mississippi.

What does it mean to you to be part of this history-making campaign?

Man, it means the world to me. I’m getting a lot of love nationally, a lot of credit. But I do want to say that the biggest thing in this moment for me is really making sure I stay grounded and understand that this is because of the work of so many people. This moment that Scott is able to have right now is because of the work of so many people, and I’m just blessed to be a part of it.

My grandmother graduated from Tougaloo [where Colom’s victory rally was held]. My auntie Alva graduated from Tougaloo College. My grandmother marched alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. There’s so much history in Mississippi. People have fought very hard for this moment.”

And being from Mississippi, being from Jackson, I know what Mississippi faces. I know the struggles that we have. I know that a lot of times, people don’t feel seen in Mississippi. But I know for a fact, this moment right here, Mississippi feels seen. Everybody in Mississippi feels this. They feel love, they see the support, and it brought hope back to Mississippi, man. A lot of people leave saying Mississippi will never change, but this is a huge step in a new direction for our state. I’m glad to be a part of it.

scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

On the front line of the human-elephant conflict, coming up with non-lethal methods of protecting crops means getting creative. In one village in Zimbabwe, a multilayered approach is taken – first a fence covered in chili infused rags and chili powder traps, if that fails elephant dung covered in chili oil is set alight, finally as a last resort a makeshift bazooka (powered by a deodorant) fires chili-oil filled ping-pong balls at persistent elephants. The last elephant who took a pingpong ball to the face did not return to the village for over a year.

Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman examines how this change is playing out: conservationists welcome the wolves’ return, ranchers vilify them due to livestock losses, and others seek coexistence at a time when wolf numbers are growing. scraped.h1: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

The South African Supreme Court of Appeal recently dismissed the government’s appeal against a ruling that struck down plans for 1,500 megawatts of new coal-fired power.

The so-called #CancelCoal case was brought by a coalition of environmental NGOs that argued the new planned coal capacity violates children’s constitutional rights to a healthy environment. Already, air pollution from coal-fired power plants kills more than 2,200 South Africans each year and “causes thousands of cases of bronchitis and asthma,” according to a statement from the Centre for Environmental Rights.

The Minister of Electricity and Energy argued that additional coal capacity is necessary for energy security. A previous High Court judgment ruled against the plan “on the basis that it violates the right to an environment not harmful to health and well-being,” per the statement.

“The High Court further found that government’s arguments about grid stability offered by coal, was not sufficient justification for the violation of constitutional rights,” said Michelle Sithole in an email to Mongabay. Sithole is senior associate in the pollution and climate change program at the Centre for Environmental Rights, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the court case.

The Minister appealed the High Court decision. The recent Court of Appeal’s decision dismissed the Minister’s appeal, meaning the previous High Court decision stands.

“While this does not mean a definitive end to the development of new coal-fired power as part of the energy security policy, it does mean that government has a higher onus/standard to justify choosing coal for electricity,” Sithole said.

“Our and our clients’ position has been that there are cheaper, cleaner and more sustainable sources of energy. Energy security should not come at the expense of people’s lives, health and well-being. We would like government’s electricity plans to reflect that,” Sithole said. She noted that the Minister of Electricity and Energy can appeal the Supreme Court of Appeal ruling to the South African Constitutional Court if he so chooses.

Banner image: South African coal-fired power plant. Image courtesy of JMK via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 4.0 ).

After nearly a century’s absence, gray wolves are recolonizing California, altering ecosystems and landscapes in the U.S.’s most populous state. Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman examines how this change is playing out: conservationists welcome the wolves’ return, ranchers vilify them due to livestock losses, and others seek coexistence at a time when wolf numbers are growing. scraped.h1: How California Gov.-elect Becerra could be better on climate than Newsom
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

13 November 2026

Supported by

This is California Wire , a weekly newsletter from Jeff St. John on the state’s clean energy transition. Subscribe to get it weekly via Substack.

Welcome back, everyone! Well, we may have finally caught a break when it comes to making progress on climate and energy. The midterm elections have given Democrats control of Congress and dramatically expanded the party’s power in state legislatures and governors’ mansions. That’s opening up big opportunities for reinvigorated clean — and affordable — energy transition policies and actions across the country.

In California, Canary Media just held what amounts to a big party for Golden State climate and energy aficionados: our fourth annual Canary Live Bay Area show, which brought nearly 400 people to The Freight in downtown Berkeley on Tuesday night. The vibe was fantastic — with so much exuberance at the blue wave lifting our common climate ambitions. And onstage and off, there was a whole bunch of gritty, detail-oriented discussion about how to best proceed on all the work ahead.

I was thrilled to share the stage with Leah Stokes , the Anton Vonk Associate Professor of Environmental Politics at the University of California, Santa Barbara; author of top-ranked climate books ​ “ Short Circuiting Policy” and the newly released ​ “ The Carbon Wave” ; writer of the Substack ​ “ Notes from the Electric Era” ; and one of the chief behind-the-scenes architects of the Biden-era climate triumph, the Inflation Reduction Act. She even created a Carbon Wave Calculator to help people understand how to make climate progress in their communities.

Stokes has a lot to say about outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom’s climate and environmental justice policy record — much of it not very flattering. She’s particularly angry that Newsom clawed back nearly $ 200 million in funding for schools to upgrade their heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, and plumbing systems — a move he made right when schools in Santa Barbara were reporting classroom temperatures of 93 degrees Fahrenheit. ​ “ Half a million kids were under extreme heat-modified days at the same time that Gov. Newsom gutted that program,” she said.

She’s also critical of the way the Newsom administration has undercut the state’s biggest virtual-power-plant program, Demand Side Grid Support. While Newsom did sign into law a number of bills this year that will tap distributed energy to help solve the state’s rising electricity-cost crisis, his administration has consistently undercut DSGS in budget negotiations. That leaves the program without enough money to pay out would-be participants in 2027 — absent some intervention between now and then. That’s particularly unfortunate since, according to Stokes’ own research , the program offers disproportionate benefits to lower-income participants in the Central Valley and Inland Empire.

She and I eventually turned to Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra’s potential climate agenda. She, for one, is feeling hopeful. ​ “ I think that there’s more of a focus on affordability, on holding the utilities accountable, on delivering on environmental justice,” she said. ​ “ I think that these are things that actually matter to Becerra.”

In particular, she’s a fan of Becerra’s free ​ “ Power Hour” proposal for no-cost utility power when solar is flooding the state’s grid — an idea that’s been pioneered in Australia and floated for California by Stokes herself and a number of other climate thinkers .

For more than a decade, California has been trying to design energy policy to solve for the ​ “ duck curve” — excess solar at midday, not enough grid power as the sun goes down. Batteries can soak up that power, obviously. But so can heat pumps and air conditioners that preheat or precool homes and buildings, as can heat-pump water heaters, which store energy in tanks of hot water, she said.

Structuring utility rates to charge customers less when power is cheap and clean will require raising them at times when it’s scarce and dirty, she said. But she sees a way to ​ “ either shift the prices up at the peak time in the 4 to 9 [p.m.] period, or keep them flat and use taxpayer funds to backfill that.”

Utilities’ wildfire liability is the most immediate crisis facing the incoming governor. Stokes has ideas for how to tackle that, too. She contends that utility shareholders, not customers, should pay those costs. Or oil companies, whose products are responsible for the climate crisis, could be forced through lawsuits to pay up as well, although she conceded that these solutions haven’t gained any political traction yet.

“ But I’d rather be pie in the sky and on the side of everyday people, who should not be paying for wildfire costs in their bills,” she said.

One idea I was particularly excited to get into with Stokes was avenues for replacing that lost funding to finance on-site solar, batteries, electric school buses, and efficient, all-electric HVAC systems for the state’s nearly 10 , 000 public schools. The way I see it, that’s a public good that goes well beyond climate. With those systems in place, schools could be positioned as resilience centers for communities in the midst of wildfires, heat waves, and other climate change–intensified disasters.

Stokes, who collaborates with the nonprofit UndauntedK 12 to find funding streams for projects like these in California schools , proposed the idea of a ​ “ children’s climate bond” ballot measure to raise money for this kind of work. ​ “ It’s crazy living in like the fourth-largest economy of the world, and yet there’s never any money to do the things that need to get done,” she bemoaned.

During the intermission, I heard another idea of how to cover the cost of school electrification from Lorenzo Kristov, who helped transform the operations of the California Independent System Operator for the renewables age. Kristov is also a luminary in the world of distributed and community energy policy — and, full disclosure, a Canary Media supporter . Kristov told me his plan for transforming California’s schools into solar-and-battery-powered revenue generators and allowing them to sell their excess power to their neighbors.

Unfortunately, the economics of school solar have gotten worse, not better, in recent years. Regulators weakened compensation for shared-solar systems at schools, farms, and apartment buildings back in 2023 , and Newsom vetoed a bill meant to restore the old system for schools in 2024 . Perhaps Becerra will take a different approach.

My colleague Alison F. Takemura has a story out this week on the state’s latest consequential — yet confusing — step on its long march toward shifting buildings from fossil-fueled to electric-powered heating.

On Nov. 4 , the Bay Area Air District board voted on final amendments to a measure setting requirements for new water heaters starting in 2028 . It’s an important milestone for the district’s 2023 plan to phase out appliances that emit nitrogen oxides, which have harmful human health and air quality impacts. The regulation will significantly restrict new installations of gas-fueled furnaces and water heaters in the Bay Area.

Last week’s vote doesn’t go as far as initially proposed. Affordability exemptions for low-income households and other buildings that could struggle to find electric options that work for them are likely to apply to about half of the region’s installations in the coming years. Multifamily buildings will have until 2033 to do the upgrade work to make the switch to all-electric heating. And the district has yet to finalize rules on space heating, which makes up a bigger share of emissions than water heating. Still, it’s a big ​ “ first” for getting gas out of buildings.

My Canary Media compatriots live all over the country — Asheville, Nashville, Seattle, New York City — so we don’t get to hang out in person nearly as often as we’d like. And like so many modern-day information workers, I spend a lot of my time interacting with people on tiny screens. That’s one of the reasons I look forward to our live events so much — we all get to meet each other, talk face-to-face, and celebrate our common humanity and common purpose. This week’s Canary Live Bay Area event was no exception. Check out our photos from the event!

Lily the corgi normally spends a lot of her time relaxing. But this week has been one of great vicarious excitement for her, vibing to her mom’s and dad’s general enthusiasm about the course of human events. So we can’t blame her for seeking out the comfort of her friends Barbara the stuffed-animal corgi and Henry the monkey for some quiet time in her favorite spot on the Eames chair ottoman by the front door.

scraped.title: The US Has Officially Lost Its Measles Elimination Status
scraped.description: In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized in the US due to preventable measles outbreaks.
scraped.author: Amy Maxmen
scraped.h1: The US Has Officially Lost Its Measles Elimination Status
scraped.body_text:
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized in the US due to preventable measles outbreaks.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States.

“It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate . States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren’t vaccinated before they’re a year old.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts. Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.

But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks. For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children’s immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.

After health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations “without reviewing the evidence.” She added that “we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years” and that, “if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return.”

Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, including Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. “The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading. That’s no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative , a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.

Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children’s hospital in Minnesota during the nation’s last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems. Two children at the hospital died of measles. “That changed my career forever,” she said.

Back then, she said, the federal government “saw the urgency.” Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC’s flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.

When data suggested that some children weren’t mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot. When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn’t been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.

Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated. “Elimination” allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can’t be protected by vaccines.

People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity. With at least 95% of people within communities immunized, outbreaks petered out and vulnerable people were protected.

It would be 14 years before a significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC’s Schuchat to testify on the situation. “Vaccination wasn’t a partisan issue,” she recalled. “This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?”

National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street ’s Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.

In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak concentrated in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.

“Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable,” Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.

Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the “importance of on-time vaccination.”

And during the 2014 , 2015 , and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC’s MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. “The MMWR is the voice of the CDC,” Schuchat said, “alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action.”

Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16. Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to “deaths every year.”

Congress didn’t call a hearing, and HHS didn’t send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn’t publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.

“A lot of this is the dog didn’t bark,” said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law-San Francisco. “Something that normally happens isn’t happening.”

Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. “There’s a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration,” one official said.

“Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved,” another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that covid vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.

“The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false,” Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News. She said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.

More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC’s journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced potentially lethal brain swelling due to the virus.

The MMWR still hasn’t published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC’s national measles update hasn’t appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.

CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently .

“We have two CDCs now,” an official at the agency said. “One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website.”

The CDC’s measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.

Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year. It now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order “to prevent vaccine hesitancy.”

The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal,” and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism. Stephen Miller, now Trump’s White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors “pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences.” Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied .

Kennedy has made such claims for two decades , including as health secretary . “Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable,” Schuchat said.

When pressed by journalists and Congress , Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven’t repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.

Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.

At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.

To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn’t on the horizon.

“Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire,” he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

Amy Maxmen is a contributor at KFF Health News.

Get the news you want, delivered to your inbox every day.

Truthout must raise $39,000 in the next 5 days to meet our basic publishing costs. We are funded almost entirely by readers like you — the average gift is just $30. Please give if you can!
