scraped.title: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
scraped.description: These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.
scraped.author: Petala Ironcloud
scraped.h1: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
scraped.body_text:
These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Eureka, a small city in Northern California, provided Roger “Chapreges” Jones an anchor in his Yurok culture. He took public K-12 Yurok language classes and Indian Ed covered school supplies. But when his parents divorced and he moved to Redding at 13, those resources vanished — and so did his appetite.

Chapreges got his first job at a Native American mental health clinic while grappling with an eating disorder hidden in plain sight. His new role at Two Feathers Native American Family Services became a kind of Trojan horse: He walked through the door looking for employment and found therapy waiting inside.

Founded in 1998 by a tribal consortium to strengthen Native family units in Humboldt County, Two Feathers has grown significantly since 2018, when its current executive director, Virgil Moorehead, joined. It went from having four staff members to having 32, including mental health clinicians, substance abuse counselors, and cultural coordinators.

Two Feathers serves a disproportionately large Native population across Northern California, where many Tribes and their citizens are either unrecognized federally or have been disenrolled. Critically, it serves Native families regardless of enrollment status — a stance that resists the disenrollment politics that plague underfunded tribes across Indian Country.

Chapreges is one of dozens of Native youth accessing Two Feathers services in a region where waitlists are long and federal funding cuts have gutted alternatives. A 2022 study from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health echoes mounting research on the importance of cultural connection to Native youth’s mental health.

Chapreges’s experience speaks to that truth. He had struggled to acclimate to Redding without other Native youth or regular cultural resources beyond the annual Stillwater Powwow. In his sophomore year, he and his father, overwhelmed by the isolation, returned to Eureka, where Chapreges completed high school.

The following year, he became a youth ambassador at Two Feathers, promoting their culturally tailored programming: stick games, flower dance, trips to the local powwow, and the Young Bucks and Spotted Does programs for youth ages 8 to 12.

Moorehead is also a licensed clinical psychologist and has helmed a new era for the organization, implementing circular Native philosophy by creating a continuum of school- and family-oriented treatment services for Native youth and their families. Two Feathers’ approach reflects a broader Indigenous understanding of mental health that recognizes the effects of historical trauma while at the same time accounting for the distinct experiences of different Native communities.

One such program, the Acorn Youth Wellness Program, works with youth individually to bolster their cultural identity. “But I think giving them hope, you know, sense of belonging,” said Moorehead, “Those are all things that are measured.”

Moorehead said the program tracks attendance, cultural identity, and hope for the future. “I always say that if you don’t have kids that come to the program, you don’t have a program. And so through the way we did Acorn, it engaged kids and had them show up in the sense of coming back and back and back.”

In 2020, the California State Assembly’s Select Committee on Native American Affairs conferred the honor of a plaque, letter, and on-site visit recognizing the organization’s work to improve and stabilize the lives of Native youth and families in Northern California. The program’s success has attracted interest from other Native Nations seeking to replicate the model. Moorehead said he’s in early conversations with one tribe planning to launch their own version next year, though he declined to name specific nations in preliminary stages.

Another member of the Two Feathers staff, Jayla, who asked to be identified by first name only to protect her privacy, joined the organization at age 15 after seeing an employment ad. A year into her time at Two Feathers, in 2025, President Donald Trump proposed consolidating behavioral health funding. Despite the fact that Trump’s proposal has only been partially implemented , Jayla still sees the impact of it firsthand: “After there were all the budget cuts, they got hit pretty hard with that … They were getting both federal and state funding, and I think a lot of what they’re getting now is just from California.”

Despite these cuts, Two Feathers’ budget has grown roughly twentyfold since Moorehead’s arrival, from about $594,000 in fiscal year 2018 to $11.7 million in fiscal year 2025, according to IRS filings, with grants and contributions making up nearly 95 percent of revenue. Two Feathers draws on all three levels of government. Its largest grant is a five-year, $7.2 million SAMHSA award for school-based youth mental health that runs through 2028. It bills Medi-Cal through a Humboldt County contract and holds state grants for youth opioid prevention.

Those filings run only through June 2025, before the full weight of federal cuts; Moorehead said the organization’s biggest challenge is escaping the cycle of one-, three-, and five-year awards. Two Feathers now bills for services, which Moorehead acknowledged has made it “a little bit more mainstream,” because billing requires diagnoses. But he rejects the idea that federal and state money forces programs to abandon their values.

“You think that you can receive federal and state funding and still not lose your values and your identity,” he said. “But I think that it takes leadership.”

Moorehead said long-term funding remains a central challenge for Two Feathers, which relies on grants while seeking more sustainable funding arrangements. “How do we create more sustainable funding?” he asked. “So that we can continue to build and get better, and not be stuck in just chasing after those grants, chasing after that funding.”

He compares the work to being a coyote, a trickster figure in many Native traditions, playing the game of federal funding and diagnostic billing without losing yourself to it. Whether these programs can truly keep doing that may depend far less on proving they work than on funders willing to commit for longer than a grant cycle.

In 2026, Moorehead and his program manager Amy Mathieson each received the James Irvine Foundation Leadership Award , which included a $350,000 grant conferred toward their organization to expand bespoke Native youth mental health programs, according to Moorehead. The award comes as Two Feathers continues to navigate funding challenges in the wake of Trump’s federal funding cuts.

Once at Two Feathers, Chapreges quickly realized what the organization could offer beyond employment. Under staff supervision, Chapreges’s manager suggested he seek support from the mental health clinicians on staff. Chapreges agreed.

“I feel a lot better. I have someone to actually talk to about how I’m feeling throughout the week compared to before, where I wouldn’t really tell anyone because I didn’t want to feel like a burden,” Chapreges told Truthout .

Outspoken about his support for the program, Chapreges encourages others even outside the scope of the Two Feathers program to seek mental health support. “I would recommend all Native youth to talk to someone, if it’s a federal one [Indian Health Service mental health program] or if it’s Two Feathers,” he said.

Jayla, Seminole, is also a youth ambassador and moved from South Carolina, where she was raised, to work at Two Feathers in McKinleyville, California, over five hours’ drive north of San Francisco. She supports the Young Bucks and Spotted Does program, among others.

“They try and use local teachings and elders and understand how trauma goes through generations of people and how it just lingers,” Jayla said. “It’s always kind of there through each generation. But how can we fix it? How can we help our generation so other generations in the future don’t have to struggle so hard?”

Culturally competent care is a central goal at Two Feathers, aiming to mitigate the many physical and mental health effects of colonization. “Last year we made little dresses that the girls were able to take home that they created and got to make their own designs,” said Jayla. “Every year, Two Feathers takes a group of kids to the Stillwater Powwow, and it’s a very intentional time where they’re able to see not only their own culture but other cultures as well.”

They also organize a trip to a conference co-produced by Two Feathers, the Wiyot Tribe, Blue Lake Rancheria, and Queer Humboldt for two-spirits — the inter-tribal term for the unique historical and contemporary social roles tied to LGBTQ Natives. Amplifying two-spirit youth voices has remained at the core of Two Feathers programming, despite widespread attacks on DEI under the Trump administration.

“I think that what success looks like in this program … it’s people being able to move on from the program eventually,” said Jayla. “And to be able to use the connections they made from Two Feathers to further along their own careers and their passions.”

This model — employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community — isn’t isolated to Humboldt County. In Oakland, the American Indian Child Resource Center (AICRC) bucks Western metrics that are often used to qualify health organizations for federal grant funding.

AICRC offers similar programming to Two Feathers: tobacco prevention, youth employment through gardening, after-school academics, and culture.

Three vehicles pick up roughly 20 Native youth from three to four schools in the afternoon for the 4-6:30pm program. Gardening offers a trifecta of camaraderie, modest pay, and education on living in good relations with the land — a striking tradition for Native youth who are the fourth generation to inherit Oakland as their homeland since the urban Indian relocation program started over 75 years ago.

“We have three plants that are interconnected and help one another,” said the California Native garden coordinator Joshua Hoyt. “[We’re] kind of juxtaposing that with modern Western agriculture, which is, you know, everything’s in rows and squares … using that as a way of thinking about how Native people see the world differently.”

Twenty-five-year AICRC veteran Mary Trimble Norris hesitated to give Truthout exact participant numbers for its after-school program, underscoring the organization’s refusal to define operations by metrics and instead emphasizing its intimate, student-focused approach.

“We’re not funded at that scale to generate the kind of metrics,” said Trimble Norris. AICRC operates on roughly $1.1 millon a year , nearly all of it grants: federal Indian Child Welfare Act dollars from the Bureau of Indian Affairs, state funding for its Indian Education center through the California Department of Education, and Bay Are foundations such as the East Bay Community Foundation. The budget has barely grown at all since 2011.

Manny Lieras, a youth services director who has worked at AICRC for 25 years, described the program’s intergenerational impact: “The institution’s size hasn’t shaped its intergenerational popularity,” he said. “One of two staff members whom I supervise is a former alum of the program when I ran it. On the other side of the coin are now several of the youth who are part of our program, that are offspring of alumni.”

In D.C., the Center for Native American Youth (CNAY), housed within the Aspen Institute supports leadership development among urban and reservation-based Native youth. For Jazmine Wildcat, a Northern Arapaho graduate of CNAY’s Champions For Change fellowship, the Center offered economic and social support after leaving Wyoming’s Wind River Reservation for college. After earning three bachelor’s degrees at the University of Wyoming, she moved to Washington, D.C., where she is pursuing a master’s in public health at George Washington University. “Being surrounded by like-minded individuals was really reassuring and was also just very empowering and motivational,” said Wildcat.

That support also had a lasting impact on how Wildcat thought about her own well-being. “I don’t think I’m going to be truly understood by anyone at these schools … as much as I have been understood by people at CNAY [and] my fellow youth and my peers because they’re all going through the same thing that I am,” said Wildcat. Her ability to see other Native youth incorporate traditional practices into their daily lives helped her find ways to stay grounded, she said. “I was able to see and observe what other people were doing that worked for them, and kind of take that and kind of see what works for myself.”

Katy Stewart, a CNAY staff member, says the organization has spent several years developing a rich Indigenous framework for its leadership curriculum, grounded by cultural and spiritual practices, elders, and activities such as medicine pouch-making and other in-person gatherings. Its core values include identity and culture, respect, relationships, responsibility, community, and humility.

“Sometimes a clinical model isn’t always inclusive of the Indigenous models and traditional ways of knowing that our youth really understand,” Stewart said. She argues that well-being cannot simply be reduced to individual outcomes but must also account for young people’s living relationships to their communities. CNAY’s Democracy is Indigenous Program is one unusual example, offering microgrants to youth ages 11 to 24 to develop community projects; staff help applicants write a budget and proposal, that is often their first. The program distributed $500,000 so far, Steward said. In Oakland, one recipient hosted a “beats and beading” event, where community members beaded together during a DJ set while talking about mental health. In Philadelphia, a 20-year-old graphic designer used her grant to design and place Missing and Murdered Indigenous People Awareness posters across the city’s bus and subway system for two months, an effort she estimates reached more than 600,000 riders.

Though CNAY is housed within the Aspen Institute, it actually raises its own money, Stewart said, including a 2025 grant from the Decolonizing Wealth Project’s new Youth Mental Health Fund . So far, she said, federal cuts haven’t touched its programs, but many of the young people it works with are finding urban Indian health centers and other behavioral health services hard to access. “Our goal is to figure out ways to sort of like supplement the support that youth would find in other places,” she said.

Taken together, these programs suggest that culturally grounded care can draw Native youth in and keep them coming back, but their growth has been uneven and precarious. Two Feathers’ budget has grown twentyfold since 2018, while AICRC operates on about the same shoestring budget it had in 2011. All three organizations depend heavily on grants that expire every few years, and the Trump administration’s cuts have shrunk the clinics and behavioral programs that young people would otherwise turn to. Their leaders say the biggest gaps lie in what short-term grants can’t buy: long-term, intensive support for the young people carrying the most trauma, continued care after youth age out of school-based services at 18, and staff rooted enough to stay in one place with these kids for years. Other Native nations have already approached Two Feathers about replicating its model, Moorehead said. Whether it spreads may depend less on proving that the model works than on finding financial backers who are willing to take the plunge beyond a grant cycle.

For Wildcat, healing has meant becoming more comfortable with herself and learning to share what she has learned with others finding their way. The connections she found through CNAY helped her feel understood in spaces where she often felt alone.

“There are plenty of people out there who understand and have gone through similar feelings and issues,” said Wildcat. “I just hope that they know they’re not alone, and … there’s resources out there.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

scraped.title: Residents in CA Agricultural Town Face Down ICE Facility and Amazon Data Center
scraped.description: Residents and activists in the town of Gilroy are drawing links between Big Tech surveillance and immigration jails.
scraped.author: Blanca Missé
scraped.h1: Residents in CA Agricultural Town Face Down ICE Facility and Amazon Data Center
scraped.body_text:
Residents and activists in the town of Gilroy are drawing links between Big Tech surveillance and immigration jails.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation .

South of San Jose, California, residents of the city of Gilroy are fighting a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility and an Amazon data center. Organizers with ICE Out of Gilroy, a coalition that launched in May of this year, have linked the two fights in a united struggle against detention and Big Tech surveillance. The coalitionincludes Community Agency for Resources, Advocacy, and Services ( CARAS ), a Gilroy-based immigrant-rights group; Services, Immigrant Rights & Education Network ( SIREN ), based in San Jose; and Bay Resistance , a Bay Area coalition for racial and economic justice which formed after Trump’s 2016 election and reactivated in 2025.

Gilroy’s farms and service economy depend on immigrant labor . The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure. The projects have distinct origins, but both raise the same question: Who gets to use Gilroy’s land, labor and infrastructure — and who gets to decide how?

On August 23, 2026, local residents joined the “Dump Big Tech” march opposing the ICE facility on Holsclaw Road, Amazon’s data center on Camino Arroyo, and the 54 automated license plate readers (ALPRs) owned by Flock throughout Gilroy. Mateo, an organizer with CARAS and the rapid-response network who asked to use a pseudonym due to concerns about potential repression, summed up why the coalition has linked the fights: “The data centers take our resources; the detention center takes our people.”

Kim Woo, a community organizer with SIREN, traced the connection in another direction: “Flock cameras lead us to the data center, and then to detention facilities.” Kim is concerned with how surveillance data moves across agencies to circumvent sanctuary policies. R ec ords show out-of-state police searched the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) Flock data for ICE-related purposes. Separately, an SFPD audit found a regional fusion-center network routed 299 federal and out-of-state queries; none were marked immigration-related. Kim calls these indirect channels “side-door sharing.” Rebeca Armendáriz, chair of the ICE Out of Gilroy Coalition and now a council-member-elect, says Flock data are being used to identify local rapid-response activists and monitor journalists. She calls all these technologies part of “the authoritarian state machine.”

The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure.

A WIRED investigation found that, since 2023, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have spent at least $515 million on services from Palantir, Microsoft, Amazon and Google. Palantir supplies investigative and case-management software; the others provide cloud and computing services. ICE’s Palantir case-management system runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and the companies also have a technology partnership . The government contracts are separate: ICE committed $86.3 million to Palantir on April 30, 2026, for case-management modernization; on September 8, the Department of Homeland Security committed $18.3 million to AWS for cloud infrastructure supporting ICE. All together, these figures exceed $619 million today.

The proposed ICE facility in Gilroy would generate rent and construction payments for a private landlord, Elmwood Capital Group, which is based in Beverly Hills. On January 8, 2025, the Trump administration awarded Elmwood a 20-year lease for up to $26,551,532 in rent. A March 2026 amendment authorized up to $8.66 million in construction reimbursements, bringing potential federal payments to the Elmwood Capital Group subsidiary ECG6 to $35.2 million over 20 years, according to the court order . Rent begins when General Services Administration (GSA) accepts the completed site, under a 20-year lease with a 15-year firm term. This arrangement uses public money to prepare private property for detention and then lease it to the government for profit.

On May 14, residents and immigrant-rights advocates rallied with county officials, who pledged to fight the project and said they were coordinating with Attorney General Rob Bonta, which led organizers to hold a community briefing and a mass organizing call on May 22. In response, the state of California and Santa Clara County sued after federal agencies began construction without the environmental review required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Gilroy’s then at-large city council, which had no Latino members, declined to join the lawsuit.

The complaint alleges Elmwood described the project to county planners as “office and operations space,” without disclosing its holding rooms or the scale of construction. ICE’s court filing estimates about 10 detainees on a normal day; the state and county say plans show rooms for up to 150. A judge found the state and county likely to prevail on their NEPA claim and halted construction ; the court later extended the pause.

The Gilroy lease is part of a national detention buildout. An internal ICE memo from February outlined to expand capacity to 92,600 beds across the U.S.

Seven ICE-contracted detention facilities have been active in California in 2025, according to the DOJ ; the eighth, the Central Valley Annex , began holding detainees in April 2026. The California Department of Justice says , affirming what families and attorneys are saying, that facilities are remote and hard to reach.

The Beverly Hills capital group’s reach extends beyond Gilroy: The state and county’s complaint alleges the firm leased at least two properties to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in Montana and Texas. In Billings, Montana, Elmwood’s portfolio lists a 14,444-square-foot GSA property; city records identify an ICE facility at 1711 6th Ave. N. A 2022 remodel permit lists Noah Zeligman as the owner of the property and describes jail processing spaces and holding cells.

The contracts reach beyond detention operators to surveillance firms, deportation contractors and property owners, as part of a broader detention-industrial complex. In the first year of Trump’s second term, ICE obligated about $5.4 billion to 679 contractors; the top ten received roughly $3.8 billion, according to a joint POGO–IRW analysis . Those top recipients included Palantir (surveillance analytics), CoreCivic and GEO Group (private detention), and CSI Aviation (deportation flights). ICE paid $129.3 million for a warehouse formerly majority-owned by Goldman Sachs and $68.2 million for one sold by a Carlyle-linked entity, CoStar and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Those are sale prices, not the firms’ disclosed profits. WIRED found ICE and CBP had spent at least $515 million with Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Palantir since 2023. Some firms, executives or PACs donated to Trump-aligned campaigns or initiatives, and some lobbied on ICE-related issues. More than 50 members of Congress launched separate investigations into six contractors, brokers and property owners, Salon reported .

Armendáriz warned KTVU that construction of an ICE facility may push farmworkers to leave Gilroy: “Our community is going to live in fear because this is going to be so close.” Law enforcement pressure is already palpable at county jails: On October 28, federal agents pursued two men after they were released from Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas; one was tased. Observers reported seeing 10 to 12 agents at county jails daily the week before. Sheriff’s office figures show about 70 people detained near county jails since June 2025, local reporting found .

Farmworkers have the legal right to organize, but only about 10,000 of California’s 800,000-plus farmworkers arecovered by union contracts, a UC Davis review estimated in 2025. In a UC Merced survey of farmworkers in the state, 19 percent of respondents said an employer had withheld payment of wages; 43 percent said employers never provided the required heat-illness prevention plan. A national study found that spikes in immigration arrests cut noncitizen farmworkers’ weekly hours by as much as 23.1 percent that month. The threat of detention compounds workers’ risk of retaliation when they report wage theft or unsafe conditions.

Mateo said early marches in May drew mostly white allies from San Jose, Santa Cruz, and Salinas. In a small town, he said, residents feared detention, violence, or provocations that could lead to mass arrests. As more Latino residents saw other communities stand with them, they began joining — and calling for more people to join them in the streets.

The organizing efforts drew people from beyond Gilroy — from Stockton to Salinas and across the Bay Area. Organizers say about 800 people joined an emergency online call to action on May 22 after news broke that the ICE processing center was being built. Union members joined rapid-response work; Pacific Printing donated thousands of red-and-yellow campaign materials; SEIU 2015 and other health-care workers’ unions helped organize actions, while nurses brought material aid and joined protests. SEIU-USWW and the local labor council also supported the campaign.

More recently, on October 25, the coalition screened When ICE Melts , a documentary about Minneapolis resistance to Operation Metro Surge, in San Jose. The film follows unions, immigrant groups, and rapid-response networks as they defend their neighbors and build toward a mass strike. The film’s organizing argument has a local echo: Immigrant defense belongs inside labor organizing.

Amazon’s 56-acre data center at 8050 Camino Arroyo is a reported $2 billion project with two planned buildings. Its first phase requires a 49-megawatt connection to Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E). That is the first building’s peak demand; the full site could require 98 MW , with any effect on household bills depending on who pays for grid upgrades.On July 3, 2025, Gilroy’s Community Development Director approved it under existing industrial zoning, without a planning commission hearing or city council vote. The Council later adopted new public-notice and hearing requirements for future large projects; Amazon’s approval remains in force. Resident Georgine Scott-Codiga told KSBW , “What they have done is they shut the people down; the people have no voice.”

Gilroy’s approval findings say the project’s benefits outweighed its unavoidable environmental impacts, including converting prime farmland and increasing vehicle travel above California’s environmental review threshold, which increases pollution from employee commutes. The city described the parcel’s long period of underdevelopment as “detrimental to the economic development of the City as a whole” and cited its goal of attracting technology companies seeking less costly locations. The city projects $40 million in revenue over the first decade, about 70 percent from a 5 percent tax on electricity use, according to its revenue FAQ . The city’s tax revenue rises with the facility’s power consumption.

The project requires off-site PG&E transmission upgrades. Gilroy’s Community Development Director says Amazon will fund a dedicated substation, but the California Public Utilities Commission’s Public Advocates Office issued a statewide warning that ratepayers could bear transmission costs if projected demand falls short. The city says newer state protections may limit that risk, though it remains unclear whether they cover Gilroy’s approved project.

Kim Woo of SIREN says the centers will “drastically deplete our electricity and water resources.” The project’s Water Supply Assessment estimates up to 23 acre-feet of water a year — about 7.5 million gallons — for cooling, irrigation and domestic use. Once recycled-water service is connected, expected by 2030, potable use should fall to about 2 acre-feet annually. Amazon must pay for the recycled-water infrastructure, which the city says will also serve future customers.

Gilroy City Council’s jobs argument centers on construction: The city projects hundreds of temporary jobs under a project labor agreement that prioritizes local hiring and prevailing wages. Those jobs matter to workers, but they end when construction does. The approval report’s employment projections estimate up to 25 full-time employees initially and 50 after Phase II. At full buildout, up to 125 employees and contractors, including part-time workers, could be on site. The figure of up to 125 people on site includes part-time workers and contractors. Hundreds of workers may build the reported $2 billion project ; only a few dozen are expected to run it.

That is the point. Data centers are a massive fixed-capital investment designed to produce more output with less workers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said generative AI and agents will mean fewer people doing some of today’s jobs, while his company announced two rounds of cuts affecting about 30,000 office-based corporate roles: 14,000 in October 2025 and 16,000 in January 2026, according to its October notice and January notice . A Fairwork investigation documents how AI and robotics intensify warehouse work, while algorithmic monitoring narrows workers’ control over their pace and tasks.

Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) research director Alex Hanna describes AI as “making our expertise an add-on, and making us more interchangeable.” Alongside replacing some jobs, these systems can speed up work, expand surveillance and make the workers who remain easier to replace. A Truthout investigation found that Amazon’s Atlas model draws on hundreds of data points — including worker feedback, injuries and proximity to union activity — to assess “labor risk” and anticipate organizing. Workers build and power this infrastructure while Amazon gains new tools to reorganize their work and contain resistance.

After the court injunction paused work at Holsclaw Road, Gilroy’s Council passed a 45-day moratorium on new detention facilities on October 5, then extended it through October 4, 2027. The ordinance covers detention and custodial-facility applications where city authority applies, but not Holsclaw Road, outside city limits. Mateo calls the injunction and moratorium partial victories. The coalition’s tactic, he says, is “to delay these projects while we build a broader opposition.”

“We need to fight these systems of mass surveillance now with a mass united front that brings immigrant defense together with the fight for civil liberties.”

On October 5, 2026, a community-backed proposal to bar immigration-enforcement staging on city property failed to advance . Kim had pressed for no-staging zones: “Our city property belongs to us, the community, not the ICE agenda coming here to harass and kidnap us.”

On October 19, the Council extended its moratorium on new data-center applications through September 3, 2027, but Amazon’s project remains exempt . The coalition is using the pause to press for the Holsclaw project’s cancellation, and a permanent data-center moratorium.

As a result of this grassroots movement, Gilroy’s political representation is changing. Before district elections, its at-large Council had no Latino members despite a population that is nearly 60 percent Latino, according to local reporting . After a lawyer’s December 2024 letter threatened a California Voting Rights Act lawsuit, amid Latino residents’ calls for greater representation, the Council voted in February 2025 to switch to district elections. The first were held in November 2026, when voters chose three Latinas—Diana Sanchez Bentz, Christina Tovar, and Rebeca Armendáriz—for the three seats on the ballot. Armendáriz, ICE Out of Gilroy’s chair, was among those elected and campaigned on protecting residents from ICE.

The struggle also crosses city lines. Kim sees the proposed Gilroy facility and the former Dublin federal prison as parts of one regional system, with Gilroy processing people and Dublin detaining them. Armendáriz wants the newly elected Congress to defund ICE, reverse its inhumane policies, and end qualified immunity for ICE agents. She is looking ahead to 2027: “It is a key year, and the community is ready for a general strike.”

For Betty, a San Jose teacher who asked to use a pseudonym due to fears of state repression, said that fight must unite immigrant defense with civil liberties. “We need to fight these systems of mass surveillance now with a mass united front that brings immigrant defense together with the fight for civil liberties,” said Betty, who is active with Workers’ Voice. “That means unions, immigrant rights groups and civil liberties organizations organizing together across the Bay Area, across California and nationally.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

scraped.title: Privacy advocates push Dems to do something about warrantless surveillance
scraped.description: In a letter first shared with Mother Jones, civil society groups urge the incoming Democratic-majority Congress to curb Trump’s spy powers.
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Privacy Advocates Push Dems To Do Something About Warrantless Surveillance
scraped.body_text:
A video surveillance system on the East front of the Capitol building. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty

A growing coalition of political and civil society groups is pushing the new Democratic-majority Congress to curb the executive branch’s warrantless surveillance powers once they take over in January. Trump officials and even some Democrats, meanwhile, are encouraging Republicans to renew those powers during the lame duck session, making it more difficult for a bluer Congress to add guardrails to those powers next year.

As we reported earlier this week , Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA)—a provision used by US intelligence agencies to spy on the electronic communications of thousands of people outside the United States without a warrant—lapsed in June. The National Security Agency can continue operating under the law until March 2027, but a renewal would extend that timeline. Privacy advocates and civil libertarians have long decried Section 702, which was introduced in 2008 to retroactively legalize a post-9/11 wiretapping program, as unconstitutional. Earlier this year, seven Republicans defied Trump and voted against renewing it .

Incoming House Intelligence Committee head Rep. Jim Himes (D–Conn.), a surveillance hawk, told Republicans this week to “get this thing done” and renew Trump’s warrantless spy powers. Himes is joined by top national security officials in the administration—Attorney General Todd Blanche, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe. In a joint letter, the three said President Trump has asked them to extend Section 702 now—as a renewal next year by the Democrat-controlled Congress would likely impose stronger warrant requirements on searching for information about Americans in the Section 702 database.

Many Americans are increasingly frustrated with being watched—from the 120,000 Flock cameras on our roads to the electronic monitoring of anti-ICE protesters—and last week’s elections reflected that. In a letter to Democratic leaders shared exclusively with Mother Jones , 80 civil rights groups outlined an anti-surveillance agenda they hope Democrats will pursue come January.

“We write to urge you to make protecting Americans’ privacy and reining in surveillance an urgent congressional priority. The unprecedented assault on privacy by the Trump administration underscores a fundamental reality: civil liberties cannot depend on who occupies the White House,” wrote the groups, which included American Federation of Teachers, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, Demand Progress, the Project on Government Oversight, and Demand Progress.

“Federal surveillance capabilities now extend far beyond FISA,” they wrote. To match, that means that surveillance reform needs to extend beyond FISA too, they argued, toward federal rules that would govern access to location data—like the information gathered by Flock cameras—curb spying by agencies like ICE, and prohibit government data-broker use, which has expanded with little oversight.

That’s because it is entirely legal for the government to buy people’s personal data from third-party data broker sites, allowing them to access reams of personal information without a warrant by paying for it. “Basically, it’s like a police officer giving your landlord an envelope of cash to go into your apartment rather than getting a warrant,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Project on Government Oversight, said.

This sort of broad, uncontrolled government surveillance is not popular: In last week’s elections, cities across the country voted to get rid of Flock cameras or to prevent their cities from installing them without public approval. So, as Democrats figure out how to keep voters’ goodwill, pushing against surveillance could be a good option, Bell said. “I think Americans have sent a resounding signal to Congress that they need to do something now to protect privacy and civil liberties.”

scraped.title: The post-election vibe shift is real
scraped.description: Even the Trump administration is trying to distance itself from itself.
scraped.author: Tim Murphy
scraped.h1: The Post-Election Vibe Shift Is Real
scraped.body_text:
Donald Trump and JD Vance attend a ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier for Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. Mark Schiefelbein/AP

If you’ve forgotten what the world felt like after the 2024 election, I don’t blame you. That was like a decade ago, and a lot has happened since. But here’s what I remember most clearly: a succession of billionaires, corporations, celebrities, and institutions slowly (or quite rapidly) bending the knee. Mark Zuckerberg told Joe Rogan we needed to celebrate “masculine energy.” The NFL took the words “End Racism” out of the end zone. Corporations backed away from their commitments to diversity with the urgency and alacrity with which you always wished teens in a horror movie would back away from the door. The story was that the Great American Middle had spoken, we were in the midst of a historic realignment, and we all had to figure out what a Nelk Boy was or get left behind. A Republican finally won the popular vote—must be a vibe shift !

The vibe shift was never a particularly fact-based proposition, and the eagerness of all of these institutions and elites to fall in line with an aspirationally fascist government really said a lot more about those people than it did about the country as a whole. But in the days since the Trump administration’s historic midterm repudiation, change is afoot. Some of these changes were in the works well before, some of them may be unrelated, but taken together, I think it’s fair to say something’s up. It’s time for Zuck to sit down with Heather Cox Richardson and welcome his Woke 2 overlords.

LIV Golf, the Trump-backed Saudi venture that advertised itself as “golf, but louder,” officially folded . Russell Brand, who was recently featured at a “Make America Healthy Again” conference alongside JD Vance, was convicted of rape and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. Elon Musk announced that the Cybertruck was being discontinued. Susie Wiles, Harmeet Dhillon, and a significant percentage of the Department of Justice almost immediately left . Alina Habba Mildon was fired by the company that was set to pay her $50 million. Laura Loomer and Vivek Ramaswamy both logged off . Kalshi, which joined forces with Donald Trump Jr. just before the inauguration last year, parted ways with Donald Trump Jr. one week after the midterms. Ken Paxton finally got divorced and then dropped his years-long harassment campaigns against immigrant aid organizations in El Paso and Houston. Calley Means accused the administration he just left of trading health policy concessions for campaign donations. Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who has spent the last however many months sounding like someone who builds a machine to kill Spider-Man, told Politico he’s “been a Democrat my whole life” and that he’s “been saying in private” that the administration’s immigration agenda has gone “too far.” OpenAI announced a new slate of data center-policies designed to placate policymakers and the public. The NYPD’s notorious Strategic Response Group—ostensibly an anti-terror squad that has been used for crowd control and sweeps of homeless encampments—is finally getting disbanded . Former NFL coach and Trump surrogate Rex Ryan getting arrested for allegedly running over someone’s foot in Nashville? You may not call it a vibe shift, but I’m banging the gavel.

Even the Trump administration is trying to distance itself from the Trump administration—witness JD Vance running away from the war he helped start, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent throwing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under the bus.

Maybe the ur-vibe-shift story right now is Jensen Huang, who was forced to resign from Nvidia last week after three alleged affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who was also a business partner and two with employees at his company. Nvidia was one of Trump’s second-term darlings and he and Huang appeared to become fast friends. The US government took a cut of Nvidia’s chip sales in China, and Huang gave the president $25 million to build a stately pleasure dome. When Trump was briefed on Huang’s connection to a possible spy, he took no action and later urged Huang to stay on as CEO amid the scandal. And in October, that might have been enough. But Nvidia, and the rest of Big Tech, can no longer afford to just keep Donald Trump happy.

And that, really, captures the essence of the post-election vibe shift. Unlike the last one, it’s rooted in a basic recognition of how American democracy works and what checks and balances really mean. Companies like Nvidia acted in 2025 as if they’d reached the conservative End of History. Now they have to come to terms with the fact that they haven’t. They are about to be dealing with a Democratic Congress that has warned everyone in close contact with the president to be ready to explain themselves next year—and maybe, just maybe, that leather jacket wouldn’t look so good in a hearing room right now.

scraped.title: The death of the Cybertruck is actually great news for the electric vehicle market
scraped.description: Cancellation of two oversized EVs this year could make smaller ones more affordable.
scraped.author: Brian Kahn
scraped.h1: The Death of the Cybertruck Is Actually Great News for the Electric Vehicle Market
scraped.body_text:
A Cybertruck parked outside a Tesla service center in Burbank, California, November 2026. Justin Sullivan/Getty

This story was originally published b y WIRED and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Tesla will end production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory next year.

It’s a uniquely toxic electric vehicle, between its divisive design and Elon Musk’s embrace of you name it. That toxicity certainly contributed to subpar sales, along with a number of recalls .

But the end of the Cybertruck is also another sign that the era of big EVs—particularly big trucks—is waning. That’s great news for pedestrian and biker safety , but also for the battery supply chain at a time when more people need to get behind the electric wheel.

The Cybertruck uses a massive 123 kilowatt-hour battery that clocks in at around 1,600 pounds, or around a quarter of its weight. That’s on par with the battery that powered Ford’s F-150 Lightning, another electric truck that was canceled late last year . (The company also killed a three-row EV in 2024.) Ford’s behemoth batteries ranged from 98 kilowatt-hours up to 131 kilowatt-hours.

EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature.

Seeing both trucks canceled within a year of each other, while automakers have announced a bevy of smaller EVs and gas-powered autos with electric motors that can extend range , indicates there may be a shift afoot. Ford is planning to launch the Fathom next year. The sub-$30,000 electric pickup is expected to be about the size of the automaker’s compact gas-powered Maverick pickup. Though Ford hasn’t announced the battery sizes available in various trims, it’s a safe bet they won’t be anywhere near the size of the F-150 Lightning or Cybertruck. The company is also planning to relaunch the Lightning as an extended-range model.

Startup Slate is also launching a tiny electric pickup that can be converted to an SUV, with a bare-bones base model starting below $25,000. It also features a svelte battery and has seen a massive surge in preorders—though, to be fair, so did the Cybertruck, and we saw that turned out .

Then there’s the Rivian R2 , which launched this year. While the SUV isn’t as tiny or cheap as Ford and Slate’s vehicles—its battery has 88 kilowatt-hours of capacity and weighs in at around 1,200 pounds—it’s still smaller than the company’s flagship R1S. Rivian has also teased the R3 , an even more-slimmed down SUV, in the coming years.

That’s not to say big EVs are dead. The Kia EV9, for example, is among the top 10 EVs by sales in the US, as is the R1S. There’s also a torrid resale market for the F-150 Lightning. But the rest of the top 10 new EV sales are all crossovers, sedans, or mid-sized SUVs with moderately sized batteries, and a number of newly announced EVs are trending on the smaller side or function as extended range vehicles.

Building smaller vehicles is, of course, one way to make EVs cheaper. With less weight to propel, you can rely on a smaller battery. And given that the battery pack is the most costly component of an EV, that can in turn help automakers offer more affordable vehicles at a time when the price of so many other consumer goods is skyrocketing. That includes the current crop of EVs: The average transaction price for a new model is now $55,800, according to Cox Automotive.

Going small—or smaller, anyway—also means making the most of a limited battery supply chain. The vast majority of Cybertruck drivers are doing the same thing with their vehicles as Hyundai Ioniq 5 drivers: getting groceries, commuting, and driving kids to soccer games. But a standard range Ioniq 5 driver is doing it with a battery about half the size.

After President Donald Trump’s administration killed EV incentives last year, sales plummeted. The Iran War and rising gas prices have led to an uptick in interest, though sales still lag behind the global average. (Used hybrid sales have also picked up , reflecting the pain people have been feeling at the pump.) Even with a Democratic-controlled Congress , EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature. But should Democrats take the White House in 2028, marking the culmination of Woke 2.0, support for would-be EV buyers becomes much more likely.

Automakers pivoting to smaller cars could be much better-positioned to meet pent-up demand if that happens, while also lowering the risks of delivery delays.

Even Elon’s announcement killing the Cybertruck points to where the market is heading: He claims Tesla is ending production to make room for cranking out more Cybercabs . The battery size in those vehicles? Just 48 kilowatt-hours.
